News.title: Coke dealer who thinks he’s doppelganger of James Bond star was snared by cops after posting on Strava
News.content:
LAST LAP Coke dealer who thinks he’s doppelganger of James Bond star was snared by cops after posting on Strava

A COKE dealer who claimed he looked like James Bond was snared by cops after revealing his location by posting a jog on Strava.

Andrew Doran, 42, was part of an audacious plot to smuggle a whopping 172kg of cocaine into the country hidden in gas canisters.



He thought he bore a resemblance to the iconic 007 secret agent when sharing his supposed doppelganger on social media.

But Doran turned out to be no James Bond, and was caught by police hiding out in Spain after he posted a jogging route on the fitness app Strava under an alias.



The details of the route in Estepona, Spain helped the National Crime Agency track the apparent wannabe secret agent down to his Iberian hideout.

He was arrested in Spain and then extradited to the UK in October last year.



Doran, from Kirkby in Merseyside, admitted to drugs importation charges at Newcastle Crown Court in December.

Last week he was sentenced to 18 years in prison.



Doran had pleadeed guilty to his part in smuggling the huge quantities of coke from the Netherlands to the UK.

The court heard that the drugs were packed into gas canisters.

Twelve of the canisters were collected from locations in Chatham, Kent, Corby and Northampton and Peterborough between October 2019 and April 2020.

Each bottle was packed with up to 16 kilos of coke, with 172kg seized in total.

Doran commanded international criminals in the Netherlands and Kevin Taylor, 44, from Newcastle upon Tyne, to orchestrate the plot.



He also gave orders to Taylor to shift huge amounts of cash from drug sales from the North East to the South and abroad.

Taylor was sentenced to 27 years behind bars in September last year.

Another foiled plot of Doran’s saw him arrange the importation of 42 kilos of cocaine from the Netherlands between March and June 2020.

The combined street value of both schemes was estimated at £18million.

NCA branch commander Gavin Heckles sent a warning to other Brits on the run abroad that they are “not beyond our reach”.



He said: “Andrew Doran had a central role in this plot, telling criminal associates at home and overseas how the drugs should be transported and distributed once in the UK.

“His extradition shows that criminals living in Spain are not beyond our reach, and we will never relent in securing justice.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Class A drugs like cocaine cause huge amounts of harm to communities across the UK, and create violence and exploitation at every level.

“We will continue to work with partners at home and abroad to pursue the criminal networks behind this trade and protect the public.”

News.title: One killed and five injured including 2 cops after shooter opened fire as FBI rush to block of flats
News.content:
AT least one person has been killed and five injured, including two police officers, as a mass shooter opened fire at a block of flats.

Cops rushed to control the active shooter situation in Minneapolis on Wednesday afternoon, with the FBI pledging support.



Conflicting reports suggested that several civilians were killed, KSTP news reported.

A law enforcement source told the network that several civilians had been killed in the attack.



KSTP reported that one officer had been shot in the stomach and the other shot in the leg at the shooting near 15 East Grant Street.

Police did not immediately say how many people were shot, but the Hennepin County Medical Center spokesman Jonathan Comito told the Star Tribune the hospital had received seven patients, one dead.

Read More in World News KILLER'S RAMPAGE Moment fast food staff scramble for cover as mass shooter fires into store

FBI director Kash Patel wrote on X: “FBI is aware of the shooting in Minneapolis involving law enforcement and our personnel are responding — we will offer any and all resources necessary to assist local authorities.”

The unidentified shooter is reportedly dead at the scene.

Photos show a huge police presence in the city.

The City of Minneapolis confirmed that the incident had multiple victims, and urged residents to avoid the area of the Shoreline Plaza apartment building.



It wrote on X: “The Minneapolis Police Department is on the scene of a shooting in the area of 15 E Grant St. involving multiple victims, including two police officers.”

Two men were shot and killed at the same block of flats last year.

Building resident Umecua Agnew told the Star Tribune the shooting was “terrifying”.



She was in the lift when the shooting began, and said: “It was three adults and one child in the elevator, we were all together and when we got to the first floor it was when we heard the massive shooting.”

Umecua ran and hid in the bathroom before another resident helped her flee.

She said: “I just thank God for being alive because that could have been me or he could have killed another girl or her mom or anybody that could have got shot right there.”

Witnesses said the shooter was on a high floor of the block.

Social media videos showed police aiming rifles upward at the building.



Anthony Strong said he was smoking behind the building when he heard the “pop-pop-pop-pop” of shots going off.

He said he went upstairs and saw several people lying on the floor, adding: “I’m trying to process it.”

Minnesota Governor Tim Walz said state officials are on the ground at the scene of the shooting.

He added: “Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon.

“Minnesota is praying for our first responders.”



People have been asked to avoid the area from 12th Street to Franklin Avenue and Hennepin Avenue to Third Avenue South, with the Hyatt Regency hotel on lockdown.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth said she is “praying for the victims of this heinous crime”.

She wrote on social media: “I’m incredibly thankful for the massive response of our brave law enforcement officers.”

News.title: Burnham’s 70s-style Socialism and big-state agenda are a toxic mix designed to deliver only economic ruin
News.content:
Road to ruin

Andy Burnham is so wedded to 1970s-style Socialism that he appears to have no clue how economic growth actually works.

Despite all the evidence from history, our Bus Conductor-in-Chief remains determined to let the dead hand of the State throttle all aspects of our lives.



It is a terrifying misunderstanding of how modern economies work.

Governments DON’T create growth, they can only summon up the best conditions for it. That should mean the State getting out of the way and freeing individuals and businesses to invest.



But yet again the PM and his deputy Louise Haigh told MPs they would deliver the very opposite: public control of energy, housing and water, plus a costly programme of devolution.

The problem for them and Chancellor John Healey is that for a second day running, the markets simply weren’t buying it.

They sent the cost of Government borrowing to the highest level in 28 years, blowing a £14billion hole in the nation’s finances.

Burnham still insists that tackling the cost of living is his top priority.

But how does he square that with the fact that Labour’s addiction to welfare and spending is guaranteeing interest rate spikes, food price surges and tax rises that clobber working families?

As for creating the best platform for growth, Net Zero has saddled Britain with the highest electricity costs in the world, making the PM’s plans for “reindustrialisation” a pipe dream.



National Insurance and business rates have crippled businesses and left a million young people jobless.

That’s a toxic left-wing mix designed to deliver only economic ruin.

Firing blanks

Yesterday Andy Burnham told MPs he would commit to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence — only for Downing Street to later insist it wasn’t confirmed.

While he dithered, Kemi Badenoch’s Tories have a sensible alternative plan: re-introducing the two-child benefit cap to cut the welfare bill and ditching the Chagos Islands giveaway.

As Kemi rightly says, a country that spends more on benefits than bullets is guaranteeing its own surrender.



Deal is sunk

Whether or not the hopeless “one in, one out” migrant deal with France is scrapped, it will make no meaningful difference to stopping the boats.

Britain remains a magnet for young men from countries who don’t share our culture or values but want to exploit a system offering free housing, welfare, health and other benefits.

Small deals with the French are no substitute for what we really need: a Rwanda-style return scheme.

News.title: King Charles and Macron share a joke as they view the Bayeux Tapestry together at the British Museum
News.content:
King Charles and Emmanuel Macron try to show there is no needle between Britain and France as they view the Bayeux Tapestry together.

His Majesty and the French president enjoyed a joke while walking the artwork’s 230ft length at the British Museum yesterday.



The 950-year-old masterpiece, which depicts the 1066 Battle of Hastings and Norman Conquest, is in the UK temporarily in an act of diplomacy agreed after Mr Macron’s State Visit to Windsor Castle last year.

The King hailed it as an “unprecedented loan”.



Charles, Camilla, Mr Macron and his wife Brigitte viewed the work along with PM Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel.

They paused at key points along the 11th century artwork to hear from curators about the historic moments depicted.

They included King Harold’s death after supposedly being shot in the eye at Hastings.

Charles, speaking later in both French and English at the London museum, said the tapestry is a reminder “that our two nations have been bound together for almost a millennium”.



He said that although the artwork depicts a conflict, “here it is today, nearly a thousand years later, as a precious symbol of trust, at a time when trust seems sadly to be in short supply between nations”.

He added those involved in it would be “pleased our two great nations have prospered together across the tides of history”.

The tapestry is on display from September 10 to next July, and tickets until December 31 — costing up to £33 — are already sold out.

Britain is sending the treasures of Sutton Hoo to France in return.

News.title: Woman fighting for life after being shot with air rifle as man, 28, and woman, 26, arrested for ‘attempted murder’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

STREET SHOOTING Woman fighting for life after being shot with air rifle as man, 28, and woman, 26, arrested for ‘attempted murder’

COPS have arrested three people after a woman was left fighting for her life after reportedly being shot with an air rifle.

The victim was rushed to hospital with serious injuries following the alleged horror attack yesterday evening.

Police were called to Windsor Street in Thurnscoe, near Barnsley, at around 9.50pm yesterday after reports of a person with a suspected firearm.

It was reported that a woman had been shot with an air rifle.





Officers and ambulance crews raced to the scene and the woman was taken to hospital for treatment.

She suffered serious injuries and remains in hospital in a stable but life-threatening condition.

Cops recovered an air rifle from the scene before launching a search for the suspect.

A 26-year-old woman was arrested at the scene on suspicion of attempted murder.



She remains in custody.

Then today, cops arrested two more people as the investigation continued.

A 28-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder.

A 37-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.



Both men remain in police custody.

A police scene remains in place on Windsor Street as detectives continue their investigation.

DI Claire Moss, from the Armed Crime Team, said: “The thoughts of all those involved in this investigation remain with the victim and her family in the wake of such a vicious attack.

“I am thankful for the work of the first officers at the scene and emergency services staff who attended the scene and provided essential and immediate medical care to the victim.

“We are carrying out detailed inquiries to get a better understanding of the circumstances which resulted in the victim being seriously injured.



“If you saw what happened yesterday evening, or have any information which may assist our enquiries, please get in touch online or by calling 101, quoting incident number 1076 of 1 September 2026.”

News.title: Burnham urged to stop stitch-up as French promise just 45 more small boat cops on day Bayeux Tapestry displayed in UK
News.content:
Andy Burnham was last night urged to prevent a stitch-up by the French after viewing the returned Bayeux Tapestry.

President Emmanuel Macron will today promise just 45 extra cops for the small-boats crisis.



He and the PM were at the British Museum to see the medieval embroidery depicting King Harold getting shot in the eye with an arrow in 1066.

They then held talks, with Mr Burnham urged to confront Mr Macron over a Dunkirk detention centre that is still incomplete, despite being paid for by the UK three years ago.



It was part of a £1billion package announced under the Tories and extended by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood.

Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: “It’s shocking that it’s not operational. Forget the Bayeux Tapestry, this is a stitch-up.”



No10 will hail a fall in Channel crossings, with this summer seeing the fewest since 2020.

But more than 16,000 migrants have arrived this year amid a change in tactics by gangs, with a record 230 on a mega-dinghy last month.



An extra 45 French cops are to be sent to beaches to help. An intelligence and judicial unit is also rising from 18 to 30 officers.

But Mr Philp claimed he recently witnessed ten armed French cops “standing around doing nothing” as around 100 migrants boarded a boat.

He said: “A gendarme said they had orders not to intervene. The £660million we pay should be withheld until they stop all embarkations in shallow waters.”



Meanwhile, the future of the controversial “one in, one out” returns deal is also said to be under threat. It was extended into autumn, with the Home Office saying more than 1,400 arrivals have been removed.

But French reports say Paris has been pushing for it to be scrapped in the longer term.

The PM insists the latest figures show cooperation is working, but he added: “We cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead.”



Ms Mahmood said: “We are boosting officer numbers to record highs to crack down on small boat launches and the gangs behind them.”

News.title: Kemi Badenoch pledges huge welfare cuts to fund £10bn a year boost to defence spending by 2030
News.content:
KEMI Badenoch has pledged a £10billion a year boost to defence spending by 2030 — via huge welfare cuts.

The Tory leader’s savings would include £4billion from housing benefit reforms and £3billion by reimposing the two-child benefit cap.



If she wins office, she would also scrap the Chagos Islands deal.

Ms Badenoch has heaped pressure on PM Andy Burnham and his Chancellor John Healey to urgently spell out plans to hit three per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.



She said: “The first duty of every government is defence — and the Conservatives will always put our defence first.

“That’s why we are setting out our plans to reach three per cent on defence spending by the end of this parliament.



“John Healey resigned from Keir Starmer’s government saying Labour weren’t keeping our country safe.

“Now he is Chancellor he should adopt our plans and make sure our armed forces have the funding they need.”

At Mr Burnham’s first Prime Minister’s Questions in the job, Labour MP Tan Dhesi, who chairs the Defence select committee, told the PM “vibes alone are not going to be enough”.

He added that rather than “kicking the can down the road” the PM should commit to three per cent by 2030.



Mr Burnham replied he had “made that commitment very clear”.

But Government sources have pointed to the Chancellor saying this week that the target date would be set out at the spending review in the spring.

Mr Healey quit as Defence Secretary in June during Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership over the Armed Forces spending plan.



Lord Dannatt, the former head of the British Army, told Times Radio last night: “My heart bleeds for John Healey.

“He resigned over Keir Starmer’s unwillingness and Rachel Reeves’ inability to fund defence.

“He now realises the wider financial issues that the Government has got.”

News.title: Footage shows boy racers causing ‘pure chaos’ on roundabout as locals warn someone will be killed weeks after A66 crash
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment thuggish boy racers cause “pure chaos” as they tear around a busy residential roundabout.

Footage shows cars racing at high speed and making dangerous turns as crowds of yobs gather around the road to watch.



The clips were filmed in Dartford, Kent, where residents say groups of predominantly young men regularly gather to race and speed.

Drivers can be seen hurtling around roundabouts while crowds line the roads and entrances to nearby estates.



Locals say they are being “terrorised” by the late-night meets, with fears someone will be killed.

One mum said the meets had turned Friday and Saturday nights, as well as Sundays, into “hell”.

She said: “Everyone weekend, Friday and Saturday nights and Sunday are hell.

“There’s organised meet-ups, with terrible sorting. It’s hell.



“They drift around the roundabouts at high speed.

“The spectators block the entrance to the local estates. It’s a nightmare.

“There’s groups of dozens of them. It’s so disruptive.

“Someone will end up getting killed. They are dicing with death.”

Another mum, Sonia, 32, said: “We’re being terrorised. It’s pure chaos.”



The issue has now been raised in Parliament, with Dartford MP Jim Dickson comparing the behaviour to the circumstances surrounding the deaths of two police officers and five teens.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, were killed in a horror crash on the A66 near Middlesbrough last month.

The two officers were in a marked armed response vehicle when it was hit head-on by a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way along the road.



Five young men travelling in the Passat also died in the devastating collision on August 22.

They were named as Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Jacob Matusiak, 23, and Makai Saddington, 18.

The tragedy has renewed fears over the dangers posed by reckless driving and illegal racing on Britain’s roads.

In Parliament, Mr Dickson said Dartford residents had experienced “very similar” incidents involving racing and speeding.

He told MPs: “My constituency of Dartford has experienced very similar, deeply antisocial and incredibly dangerous experiences of racing and speeding on our roads.



“Groups of predominantly young men gathering along our roads, watching cars, speeding down those busy roads as content is filmed to be posted on social media.

“This activity is clearly dangerous for other road users, really disruptive for local residents.

“Would the Home Secretary agree with me that we must do absolutely everything we can to tackle this lawlessness.”



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood thanked the MP for bringing the issue to her attention.

The Dartford footage comes amid a series of devastating road tragedies involving dangerous driving.

Just days before the A66 crash, five teenagers were killed in a separate wrong-way motorway smash in Ireland.

The teenagers were travelling in a stolen BMW the wrong way along the M9 in County Kildare after police tried to stop them.

The BMW then smashed into a Hyundai carrying innocent members of a family.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Three sisters and a seven-year-old boy were seriously injured in the devastating collision.

Now Dartford residents fear it is only a matter of time before reckless driving at the late-night meets ends in another tragedy.

News.title: Man accused of robbing £137,000 diamond-encrusted watch in London says ringleader threatened to ‘set me on fire’
News.content:
Man accused of robbing £137,000 diamond-encrusted watch in London says ringleader threatened to ‘set me on fire’

Ali Eldahouzze, 22, and Abdel El Habchi, 30, are accused of being part of a plot to target entrepreneur and fashion designer Catalin Botezatu's £137,000 Richard Mille watch

View 2 Images Catalin Botezatu, fashion designer, had his £137,000 watch stolen in Mayfair

A Moroccan man accused of robbing a fashion designer of his diamond-encrusted £137,000 watch says he was threatened with being “set on fire” if he did not take part in the crime, a court has heard.

Ali Eldahouzze, 22, and Abdel El Habchi, 30, are accused of being part of a plot to target entrepreneur Catalin Botezatu after he had dinner with his assistant and a friend in Mayfair, central London. Mr Botezatu had been smoking a cigar on the terrace of Latin American restaurant Amazonico in Berkeley Square on the evening of January 28, and shortly before midnight his Richard Mille watch was cut from his wrist.

Younes Djoudi has pleaded guilty to robbery while El Habchi and Eldahouzze have pleaded not guilty to the charge. Last week El Habchi told Southwark Crown Court he had “no idea” of a plot to steal a watch before the timepiece was snatched.

On Wednesday, Eldahouzze told jurors Djoudi had threatened his life and “told me to go and grab the watch”.

“He was threatening me, cursing my mother, threatening that he would kill and set me on fire”, he said. “I was looking at the floor, I was very scared.

"He kept telling me to go and grab that thing. I didn’t understand what he meant because I’m Moroccan and I couldn’t understand exactly what he meant.”

Prosecutors say Eldahouzze assisted Djoudi by pushing Mr Botezatu and grabbing hold of his arm. But Eldahouzze insisted there was not any physical contact, telling the court: “As soon as I saw what he (Djoudi) was doing, I just fled.”

He told jurors he refused to follow Djoudi’s instruction to “grab the watch”, and feared for his safety in the aftermath.

View 2 Images The pair appeared at Southwark Crown Court (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

“To be honest, that evening, I thought he was going to do something to me, going to kill me or set me on fire while I was at home,” he said.

El Habchi, a social media influencer in Morocco, told the court that he and his friend Eldahouzze had been travelling from Slough to Soho, central London, hours before the alleged robbery when Eldahouzze received a call from Djoudi telling him to meet in Mayfair.

Prosecutor Arizuna Asante said last week that after leaving the restaurant, Mr Botezatu “stood near the car smoking for a few minutes with his friend before he was approached by three males”.

Mr Asante told jurors: “The three males surrounded Mr Botezatu and robbed him of his watch by wresting it from his left wrist. It is believed a knife was used to cut through the rubber strap because the victim had cuts on his wrists after the watch was taken.”

El Habchi told jurors that Djoudi met the pair the following morning with the watch. In his evidence, Eldahouzze said friends of Djoudi took his phone after the robbery, and he said they had sent messages and taken pictures, including an image of the stolen watch.

El Habchi and Eldahouzze each deny one count of robbery.

Article continues below

The trial continues.

News.title: Buckingham Palace planning 'major security upgrades' amid growing Russia threat
News.content:
Buckingham Palace planning 'major security upgrades' amid growing Russia threat

Buckingham Palace officials have confirmed a major cybersecurity upgrade will go ahead as the threat from Russia operating in the 'grey zone' grows, three years after the Royal Family website was targeted

View 3 Images Buckingham Palace is in line for a huge upgrade (Image: © 2026 PA Media, All Rights Reserved)

Russian hackers have forced Buckingham Palace into making major upgrades amid a growing threat from Moscow, reports suggest.

‌



The Palace’s cybersecurity systems will be upgraded after officials from the King’s household admitted its ‘ageing’ IT needs a revamp, reports The i .

‌



The move comes amid rising tensions between the UK and Russia, with the US warning on Wednesday (September 2) a ‘limited’ attack from Russia on NATO countries was more likely to happen sooner than the previous estimate of 10 to 15 years.

‌



In the meantime, Russia appears to be operating in the ‘grey zone’ of war, launching a drone attack on a Ukrainian plane stationed at Leipzig Airport in Germany. Russia has also previously targeted the Royal Family website, managing to take it offline for around an hour and a half in October 2023.

It’s against this backdrop that Palace officials have decided to spend a portion of the annual Sovereign Grant on upgrading cybersecurity at Buckingham Palace.

View 3 Images King Charles has reportedly stepped up his Royal work significantly (Image: Max Mumby/Indigo, Getty Images)

‌



“The new level of the grant will ensure that the Royal Household can continue to deal with property maintenance backlogs following some years of constrained funding during the pandemic,” Treasury minister Dan Tomlinson said.

“It will also allow the Royal Household to replace ageing systems to strengthen cybersecurity and to install energy-efficient heating systems.”

The £99.9 million annual Sovereign Grant is the settlement given to the Royals by the government, funded by the taxpayer. Last year, it was worth £137m.

‌



The ‘core element’ of the grant will rise from £72m in 2026 to £99m in 2027 as King Charles and Queen Camilla conduct hundreds of engagements every year, and 100 more than the late Queen Elizabeth II carried out in the final years of her reign.

Mr Tomlinson added: “That reflects this bottom-up assessment that has taken place, looking across the needs of the Royal Household and making sure that it is being funded adequately for the work, for the public duties that His Royal Highness the King and the royal family carry out.

“And it is worth pointing out, of course, that those activities have increased significantly in recent years.

‌



View 3 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin (Image: Getty)

“Towards the end of her reign, the late Queen was not carrying out a large number of foreign engagements, and also was hosting a smaller number of state visits.

“The King has increased the engagements that he is carrying out on our behalf as part of his public duties, and that has involved more expenditure in terms of staff costs and making sure that those engagements and the benefits that in terms of the representation of our country and supporting good causes here in the UK can get the funding and the support that they need.”

Article continues below

However, the overall grant will reduce from 2027, as funding for the renovation of Buckingham Palace is removed as work is completed.

Buckingham Palace was contacted for comment on this story.

News.title: Doctors baffled as boy, six, dies from disease barely seen in over 200 years
News.content:
Doctors baffled as boy, six, dies from disease barely seen in over 200 years

Doctors were left 'baffled' after it was found a six-year-old boy suffered a heart attack and died from scurvy - a disease that has barely been seen since the 19th century

View 3 Images Queensland Children's Hospital

Doctors were left baffled after a six-year-old boy died from a disease so rare it has not been seen in over 200 years.

‌



The child from Queensland, Australia, Connor Dean, died on August 10, 2024 at the Queensland Children’s Hospital in Brisbane.

‌



A coroner found that Connor died of a heart attack associated with a severe vitamin C deficiency consistent with scurvy.

‌



View 3 Images Doctors were left baffled by the boys condition

Deputy state coroner Stephanie Gallagher said: “I am of the view that, publishing these findings may be sufficient mechanism to draw attention to this death so as to prevent death in similar circumstances happening in the future”.

Scurvy was a common disease up until the 19th century.

‌



It was caused due to the lack of availability of vitamin C rich foods and was very common among sailors on long voyages. The condition breaks down blood vessels, tissues and organs and can lead to death due to infection and internal bleeding.

Connor had Down syndrome and a heart defect, with slow developmental progress meaning he spoke mostly only using single words.

On July 11, 2024 he was taken to the doctor after he began suffering from symptoms including knee pain, a shuffling gait and limping, all thought to be related to a fall in the playground.

‌



However, when their was no improvement, he was admitted to Queensland Children’s Hospital for X-rays and an MRI scan.

These showed no other obvious abnormalities, but he was diagnosed with para-influenza. Connor's mum said he was taking a multivitamin and his vaccinations were up to date.

His condition gradually worsened and on one occasion he had to be resuscitated.

‌



It was thought that Connor could be suffering from Leukaemia, but this was quickly ruled out.

By the end of July, Connor was showing symptoms of renal disease, multi-organ failure and sepsis.

It was at this point that scurvy became the most likely condition to unite all of Connor’s symptoms, which could have explained his earlier heart attack.

‌



Connor died in early August after all invasive treatments were stopped.

The coroner was told by Connor's doctor that he had “long standing concerns” about the boy’s growth and height, noting that the boy was partially fed by gastric tube until February 2020.

Up until June 2022 he ate a variety of foods according to his mother but by May 2023 he was branded by a paediatrician as a “very fussy” eater.

‌



The coroner heard he essentially has no fruits of vegetables in his diet. The paediatrician observed he had gained just 300g in 11 months.

He said: “I told his mother that I was very concerned about Connor’s diet, specifically that it did not contain enough calories or the vitamins and minerals he needed to grow and be healthy.”

It was suggested that Connor take a specific multivitamin supplement which came in gummy form.

‌



View 3 Images It was recommended that Connor took a specific multivitamin (stock image)

The doctor noted that when he saw Connor in late 2023, ”his diet was still very poor with lots of white bread, some beef sausage, custard and chocolate.

“He was being offered vegetables at daycare but I don’t believe he was eating them.

‌



“He was drinking apple and blackcurrant 100 per cent juice poppers which would contain vitamin C.”

The multivitamin Connor was taking did contain “small amounts” of vitamin C but it wasn’t the supplement he had recommended.

The doctor added: “I discussed with Connor’s mother that Connor’s diet was inadequate to meet his vitamin and mineral requirements but that I believed that we were covering these requirements with the multivitamin, vitamin D3, Ferroliquid and vitamin A injection”.

‌



When Connor was admitted to hospital he was taking the multivitamin the doctor recommended, however the doctor noticed it contained no vitamin C.

The doctor expressed his concerned that a product labelled as a multivitamin could be sold if it was lacking in vitamin C.

However the manufacturer of the multivitamin said the vitamins in the product were all clearly listed.

‌



Connor's parents confirmed he was a “very fussy eater” from about four-and-a-half year's old.

He was given multivitamins, iron and vitamin A injections – as instructed – but they said they did not realise he had a specific vitamin C deficiency until it was too late.

The disease used to be common when sailors reached Australia due to a lack of fresh food during winter, but the year-round availability of fresh produce and vitamin C supplements was thought to have wiped out the condition.

Article continues below

Some Australians do still have vitamin C deficiencies but scurvy is almost unheard of these days.

News.title: Water firms accused of dumping sewage in rivers and seas over 43,000 hours over summer
News.content:
Water firms accused of dumping sewage in rivers and seas over 43,000 hours over summer

PM Andy Burnham is facing calls to tackle a "glaring public health crisis" as a charity reveals it received 636 sickness reports from people who said they became ill after swimming in the nation’s rivers, lakes and seas this summer

View 5 Images Reports of widespread sewage discharges have prompted calls for urgent action (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Water companies dumped sewage into England’s rivers and seas for over 43,000 hours during July and August, figures released by a charity have revealed.

‌



The deluge included more than 2,000 hours when sewage was allowed to pour into the country’s designated bathing waters, including popular spots for holidaying families.

‌



The data was published by Surfers Against Sewage amid mounting anger at the privatised water industry's track record on pollution. Campaigners are calling on the Labour government to do more, including bringing the critical sector under public control.

‌



It came as Surfers Against Sewage revealed that it received 636 sickness reports from people who said they became ill after swimming in the nation’s rivers, lakes and seas during the peak summer months of July and August. Those included cases of gastroenteritis, skin, ear and eye infections and, in some severe cases, hospitalisations.

View 5 Images Readymoney Cove in Cornwall was identified by the charity Surfers Against Sewage as a bathing spot impacted by sewage discharges (Image: Education Images/Getty Images)

It says the data showed sewage pollution is a “significant public health concern” but, as many cases go unreported, it was likely the tip of the iceberg.

‌



Surfers Against Sewage’s Safer Seas and Rivers Service app issued 290 alerts over the summer months, with nearly 85% in designated bathing waters rated as ‘good’ or ‘excellent’ water quality by the Environment Agency.

Locations with the most discharges included Wallasey Beach and Moreton Beach in Merseyside, Readymoney Cove in Cornwall and Plymouth Hoe East in Devon, the charity said.

View 5 Images The charity Surfers Against Sewage - and others - are delivering a 330,000 strong petition to Downing Street (Image: PA)

‌



Water companies in England are only permitted to spill sewage into rivers and seas through storm overflows when there has been heavy rainfall.

However, the new data shows that, across the three heatwaves between May right through to August, sewage spilled into bathing waters alone for nearly 14,000 hours - aside from rivers and seas.

‌



It comes after the Mirror revealed last month that firms in England and Wales carried out 8,576 so calls “dry spills” last year, totalling 14,873 days.

The latest figures were released as the charity prepares to deliver a petition with more than 330,000 signatures to Downing Street, demanding Prime Minister Andy Burnham put people before water company payouts and end what it calls a “profit-driven sewage scandal”.

View 5 Images Andy Burnham has talked tough about the need to tackle failures by privatised water firms (Image: House of Commons/AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Among those who fell ill this summer was eight-year-old Keeva Hollow, after swimming at Avon Beach in Dorset – a designated bathing water site awarded ‘excellent’ by the Environment Agency.

She swallowed seawater whilst swimming at her local beach and was hospitalised afterwards, with tests showing she had contracted campylobacter, a bacteria found in contaminated seawater.

Mum Aisling McCarthy said: “Watching your child becoming so seriously ill is terrifying. No parent should have to see their child go through what Keeva did after simply going on a trip to the local beach.

‌



“We were hugely upset that when we raised this with the relevant authorities, the concern was not taken seriously: we were given advice about washing hands and cooking chicken.

“Our family enjoys our local beaches, but now we are scared to. If there are issues affecting our sea and rivers, and putting the safety of our children at risk, we want answers.

“We want people to be held accountable. Above all, we don’t want another child to be hospitalised just because of swimming in the sea.”

‌



View 5 Images Giles Bristow, of Surfers Against Sewage, says the amount of sewage dumped must not become 'the norm' (Image: Getty Images)

Giles Bristow, chief executive at Surfers Against Sewage, who will deliver the petition on Thursday, said: “A day at the beach should leave families with happy memories, not vomiting, bacterial infections or hospitalisations.

“We must not accept these shocking figures as normal. It isn’t and must never be. This is a glaring public health crisis, and a direct result of water companies putting profits above all else.”

‌



He went on: “Over 330,000 people have signed a petition telling the Government it must end this privatised water system to fix the sewage scandal.

“Andy Burnham has a golden opportunity with the Clean Water Bill to demonstrate the leadership we have been crying out for. The Bill could smash the shackles of the privatised system that has destroyed our waters and reset the industry so that it operates for people, not profiting polluters. We cannot afford his government to waste this opportunity – doing so will mean the government fails our seas, rivers and safety.

Julie Maughan, the mother of eight-year-old Heather Preen, who tragically died from an aggressive E. coli infection after coming into contact with contaminated water on a Devon beach in 1999 and whose story inspired Channel 4’s Dirty Business, will join those handing in the petition.

‌



She said: “It is devastating to see that after all these years, water companies are still putting children’s lives at risk by polluting, and that the government is not doing enough to stop it. No one should have to live through what our family has. Andy Burnham has the chance bring about real change that can end sewage pollution. The public is telling the Prime Minister to put an end to this.

“Children are getting sick, and families are worried about visiting the beach. All while water company bosses get rich. Andy, you have made some promising comments. Please listen to the public, and deliver the change we need."

A spokesperson for trade body Water UK said: “The latest data from the Environment Agency show 87% of bathing waters achieved a ‘good’ or ‘excellent’ rating. This is a stark contrast to the 1990s when less than a third of bathing waters would have met today’s standards.

Article continues below

"No sewage spill is ever acceptable, and we are working to end them as fast as we physically can. That’s why we are tripling investment to halve spills from storm overflows by 2030 and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works.”

A Defra spokesperson said: "We know the water industry hasn’t been working in the public interest for far too long and it’s totally unacceptable to see the scale of discharges polluting our rivers, lakes, and seas. Storm overflows should only be used in very specific circumstances, and this government has already taken action against water companies who are failing to perform, making it a criminal offence to cover up illegal sewage spills.

"But we know the status quo isn’t working, and it’s why we’re driving forward the biggest overhaul of the water sector in a generation to deliver improved water quality for swimmers across the country and creating a powerful new regulator to hold companies to account."

News.title: What happens in Lindsay Clancy trial next explained as jury fails to reach verdict again
News.content:
What happens in Lindsay Clancy trial next explained as jury fails to reach verdict again

The trial of Lindsay Clancy, accused of murdering three of her children, has seen the jury force into a sixth fay of deliberations but what could happen next?

View 4 Images Lindsay Clancy in court over the alleged murder of her kids (Image: Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledge)

The jury in the case of a mother accused of killing her three children have failed to reach a unanimous verdict for the second time.

‌



Lindsay Clancy, 36, is charged with murder of the 2023 deaths of her children: Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months. The former labour and delivery nurse, from Massachusetts, has not denied that she killed her kids but argued that postpartum psychosis led to her actions. The case has gripped the US as the topics of mental health and pregnancy are debated across the country following the livestreamed trial.

‌



The jury in this case has deliberated for five days and still with no unanimous decision they were told by the judge to go back and try reach a decision again.

‌



PM pledges action over maternity closure after Mirror reveals women taught to give birth in car READ MORE :

View 4 Images Cora (L), Callan (C) and Dawson (L) (Image: Plymouth Superior Court)

Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility but prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing. The 36-year-old had been at home on maternity leave when her then-husband Patrick Clancy went to run errands and pick up dinner, on January 24, 2023.

When Patrick returned to their home, in Duxbury, Massachusetts, he found his three kids dead in the basement and his then-wife in their garden and injured from a suicide attempt.

‌



The jury will now reconvene on Thursday at 9am local time (2pm UK time) for a sixth day of deliberations. Below we've looked at what could happen and what the potential outcomes of the trial could be.

Not guilty or not guilty by reason of insanity

Clancy's defence argued throughout the trial that postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Postpartum psychosis is a serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, according to the NHS. Symptoms of this serious condition include hallucinations, delusions, mania, low mood and confusion.

View 4 Images Clancy with her three children (Image: Plymouth Superior Court)

‌



Massachusetts law does not put the burden on Clancy to prove her mental illness or that she lacked criminal responsibility. It is instead on the prosecution to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the mum was criminally responsible.

If a not guilty verdict is returned then Clancy could go free. A not guilty by reason of insanity verdict however could lead to the 36-year-old being detained in a hospital, according to the BBC.

Guilty of first-degree murder

Clancy is charged with three counts of first-degree murder and three counts of assault and battery. First-degree murder, the intentional and premeditated killing of a person, is the most severe outcome that could come out of the trial. In Massachusetts, this verdict results in a life in prison sentence, without the possibility of parole.

‌



View 4 Images Lindsay Clancy and her attorney Kevin Reddington in court (Image: Greg Derr/Pool The Patriot Ledge)

Mistrial

If the jury still cannot reach a unanimous verdict then a mistrial would be declared and the case would essentially go back to the same status as before the trial. The 36-year-old has been held at a psychiatric hospital since she was arrested back in 2023.

Criminal trials in the US must have the jury reach a unanimous decision to convict the defendant. This is different to the UK where a judge can allow a jury to reach a majority verdict if a unanimous one is not achieved.

Article continues below

Clancy could go back on trial

If there is a mistrial, prosecutors would have to decide whether they want to try again with a new jury. If they do, the jury selection process would begin again and a new trial would be scheduled.

A plea deal could also be offered to Clancy, according to Brad Bailey, a Boston defence attorney and former prosecutor who is not involved in the case. He said: "Any time the threat of a retrial with murder one hanging over the client is re-interjected, defence lawyers will, at the very least, explore whether or not there’s any interest in a resolution."

The district attorney's office however could decide to not retry the case. Bailey said: "Sometimes they decide not to, because of the sense that there may be the same result each time they try it, and because of the expenditures involved in trying the case to begin with, particularly when you have expert witnesses."

News.title: Newlywed wife's heartbreaking last words to Brit husband before vanishing in Nepal floods
News.content:
Newlywed wife's heartbreaking last words to Brit husband before vanishing in Nepal floods

A British man whose wife, mum, brother and uncle are missing following the horrific floods in Nepal has flown out to try and find his family

View 6 Images Pramod Poudel with his wife Sumitra

A British husband desperately searching for his newlywed wife who went missing in the deadly floods in Nepal shared her final words to him before she vanished.

‌



Pramod Poudel, 34, flew to disaster-zone to find his wife Sumitra, 25, who has been unaccounted for since last Wednesday. The husband revealed he spoke to his wife just hours before the catastrophic floods - believed to be caused by a glacial collapse in the Himalayas which sent rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods.

‌



Nepal-born Pramod said the last words he heard from his wife before the floods were: "I love you so much."

‌



Desperate search for British priest missing after horror Nepal floods while on spiritual tour READ MORE :

View 6 Images The couple married in June (Image: Family Handout)

Nepal's Foreign Ministry said 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries remain missing after the August 26 disaster that killed at least 1,118 people and left more than 3,900 missing. 36 Brits are thought to be missing in Nepal, with another 15 reported by the Chinese authorities in neighbouring Tibet, bringing the total to 48.

Pramod said he last spoke to his wife at 4.15pm UK time last Wednesday but said the call cut out and he was not able to reach her again. The husband said he called his aunt who revealed the horror floods had hit.

‌



View 6 Images Pramod (L) travelled to Nepal to search for his wife, mother, uncle and brother

He married Sumitra in June and she had moved to the Nepalese village of Sole to live with Pramod's family while he returned to the UK for work. Pramod, a British citizen who lives in Uckfield, East Sussex, was born and raised in Sole and moved to the UK when he was 18 years old. He revealed his wife, his mum, brother and uncle are also missing after the floods battered their village.

View 6 Images Homes damaged after the floods (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The heartbroken husband recalled his last call with his wife. He told The Sun: "When I last spoke to her, she said to me, 'How are you? I love you so much.'

"I have not had contact with her since then. It's devastating, I don't even know how to explain how I'm feeling right now. I'm so worried about her, and all my family. I work so hard for them and they are my whole world. I'm very hopeful of finding them but I'm also praying to God."

View 6 Images Grieving relatives mourn during symbolic Hindu cremation rites at Pashupatinath Temple, in Kathmandu (Image: Amit Shukla/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

‌



He flew out to Nepal on Friday and started his trek to his village, after the floods destroyed a bridge that led to Sole. Pramod, before flying to Nepal, spoke to the BBC and said: "It's a very, very difficult time for me and for my family and my country at this moment, but obviously I have to go and see what's happening there."

Under-Secretary of State at the Foreign Office Lord Wood of Anfield, on Tuesday, told the House of Lords that the number of British people missing due to the floods has risen to 36, up from 33.

View 6 Images Nepali rescue teams and the army searching for survivors inside mud-filled tunnels (Image: Nepalese Army/UPI/Shutterstock)

Article continues below

Some tourists previously reported missing in Nepal have made contact with authorities, officials said. Five Australians were confirmed safe overnight and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the number of Australians missing had fallen from 43 to 38.

Sunil Sharma, a spokesman for the Nepal Tourism Board, said at least five tourists who had been reported missing had contacted authorities by email or telephone in recent days.

News.title: School defends policy as pupils 'turned away after fortune spent on uniform'
News.content:
School defends policy as pupils 'turned away after fortune spent on uniform'

Denton Community Academy’s trust has defended its uniform rules after pupils were reportedly turned away on their first day back over skirt lengths.

View 4 Images Pupils were reportedly turned away on their first day back at Denton Community Academy over skirt lengths (Image: Sean Hansford | Manchester Evening News)

A secondary school has defended its uniform policy after pupils were reportedly turned away on their first day back for wearing skirts “a couple of inches” above the knee.

‌



One parent said his two daughters, who attend Denton Community Academy, were refused entry on Wednesday despite their skirts being bought through an official uniform provider.

‌



The father, who did not wish to be named, told Manchester Evening News he had spent a “fortune” on new uniforms for his children. He said: “They were ringing us saying they weren't allowed to enter the school.

‌



“The skirts they had on were not rolled at all and fell a couple of inches above the knee, if that.

View 4 Images Denton Community Academy’s trust has defended its uniform rules (Image: Denton Community Academy/Northern Education Trust)

Parents told sinister danger hiding behind a simple back-to-school photo READ MORE :

UK-wide police reminder as children return to school this week READ MORE :

“It was throwing it down with rain and there were 40 or 50 kids standing outside, not allowed in. They were soaking wet and some were crying.”

‌



The father said other parents also went to collect their children, while his two daughters spent the rest of the day at home and missed their first day back.

Northern Education Trust, which operates Denton Community Academy, said its uniform expectations had been shared with families several times before the start of the new academic year and insisted its policies were applied "consistently" and "fairly”.

The trust said: “Denton Community Academy is committed to maintaining the high standards that have driven significant improvements in our students' educational outcomes.

‌



View 4 Images One parent said his daughters were refused entry despite their skirts being bought through an official uniform provider (Image: Manchester Evening News)

“The academy is the most improved secondary school in Tameside and is now the highest-performing non-selective secondary school in the borough.

“We are incredibly proud of our students and the high expectations that have driven this improvement.”

‌



It said families had been told about the uniform expectations on May 6, May 18, July 16 and August 20. The trust added: “We cannot comment on individual cases, but we strongly encourage parents with any concerns to speak directly to the academy.

“We will always work with families to resolve issues, and believe that direct conversation with the school, rather than through the media, is the most constructive way to do that.”

The father said he had since returned to TopMarks Schoolwear in Ashton, where he claimed the longest skirts available were around 20 inches.

‌



He said his daughters were of average height for their age and claimed even the longest skirts available would not fall below their knees.

View 4 Images Denton Community Academy’s uniform policy on its website (Image: Denton Community Academy/Northern Education Trust)

The father also pointed to a photograph in the uniform section of the academy’s website which he said showed a female pupil wearing a skirt several inches above the knee.

‌



He said: “This is not an army camp. They're treating them like soldiers, but they are children, they need an education. It feels like punishment.”

Denton Community Academy’s website says its uniform policy is intended to “set an appropriate tone for education”. It says the uniform provides “a sense of belonging and identity for all students”, while also being “comfortable” and allowing pupils to be themselves.

The policy also prohibits make-up, hoodies and jewellery, as well as “writing on hands or arms for any reason”.

Article continues below

It states: “We do not exclude students for wearing jewellery, having mobile phones or any other breaches of this policy.

“We will however, always ask students to rectify the issue that we have raised. These are reasonable requests.”

News.title: Man killed pub-goer on Christmas Eve after learning he was his biological father
News.content:
Man killed pub-goer on Christmas Eve after learning he was his biological father

Martin Greensmith, 37, was convicted of manslaughter after pushing Steven Shevels, 61, in a pub garden on Christmas Eve - he learned Mr Shevels was his father just 'hours' earlier

View 3 Images Martin Greensmith was found guilty of manslaughter (Image: Durham Constabulary))

A man killed his biological father in a pub garden on Christmas Eve after learning that they were related.

‌



Martin Greensmith, 37, has now been convicted of the manslaughter of Steven Shevels, 61, in County Durham last year.

‌



Greensmith had admitted pushing his father, but denied manslaughter. He was convicted after a seven-day trial at Teesside Crown Court.

‌



The incident took place on Christmas Eve in the beer garden of the Queen's Head pub in Willington. Police were called to the scene at around 4.45pm, and it is understood Greensmith found out Mr Shevels was his father just "hours" earlier.

Durham Constabulary reported how "shortly after" hearing this news, Greensmith had been with Mr Shevels in the beer garden and ended up pushing him. This led to the 61-year-old hitting his head on the concrete floor, Chronicle Live reports.

View 3 Images Steven Shevels died in a pub garden on Christmas Eve (Image: Durham Constabulary))

‌



'Brave' police officers wade into sea to catch and arrest paedophile attempting to escape cops READ MORE :

Though Greensmith initially was among those who attempted to help Mr Shevels, he left the pub before emergency services arrived.

He was arrested the next day - Christmas Day - at home in Willington. Police said examination of his phone showed he had been researching "involuntary manslaughter" and solicitors.

Mr Shevels' sister Angela spoke after the trial. She said: "My brother Steven was the victim of an unprovoked act of violence that took his life far too soon. His passing has left a hole in all our hearts, and a future forever changed for all of his family, friends, and everyone who knew him."

‌



View 3 Images Police outside the Queen's Head pub in Willington (Image: Simon Greener/Newcastle Chronicle)

Det Ch Insp Alfie Keane, of Durham Constabulary, led the investigation. He said: "This is a truly devastating case. It shows how split-second decisions can have life-long consequences and an unimaginable impact on everyone around them. Our thoughts remain with Steven’s family and friends at this difficult time."

Previously, a family tribute to Mr Shevels read: "We are heartbroken to announce the tragic death of Steven, who was taken from us far too soon. He will be deeply missed by all of his family and friends."

Article continues below

Greensmith will be sentenced at Teesside Crown Court on October 21 this year.

News.title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
News.content:
Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of rising UK borrowing costs.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high on Wednesday.

He blamed the previous Tory government, saying the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".

Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July before Parliament's summer recess, meaning Wednesday was the first time he had faced Badenoch at PMQs.

Burnham sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.

He told MPs: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."

Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998.

This means it costs the government more to borrow over the long term and could constrain its spending choices as the 28 October Budget approaches.

Burnham's PMQs debut came after he used the summer recess to tour the UK, announcing a series of eye-catching policies mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.

On Wednesday, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill.

"The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said.

"He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.

"Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"

Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality.

"I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an earlier date for the Budget to reduce speculation.

In the Commons, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government.

Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.

Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict.

News.title: King hails 'unprecedented' Bayeux Tapestry exhibition in London
News.content:
The King and Queen, Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel were given the chance to see the historic embroidery in the atmospheric darkness of the British Museum.

It's displayed in a long glass illuminated cabinet, with the figures remarkably vivid for something almost a 1,000 years old, and visitors file along, following the story of the Norman invasion.

The royal visitors had a close look at key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.

It's filled with details of medieval life and the King commented on Normans pulling a cart with "an enormous amount of wine".

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the final scene, showing King Harold with an arrow in his eye, was what she found the most dramatic.

"We've just been talking to all the schoolchildren, and that's the bit that they really liked and really registered with them," she said.

"And it's amazing actually that a tapestry that is 1,000 years old can still inspire people to feel such emotion and capture such drama after all this time."

Nandy said she was inspired by the way this epic depiction of conflict had "come to symbolise probably the biggest act of friendship on behalf of the French nation".

Sending the tapestry to the British Museum was announced by Macron during a state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.

There had been fears that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said display conditions at the British Museum were "ideal".

The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry lying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres.

It also allows viewers to get a clearer view of all the animals, plants and often bawdy images sewn around the margins of the main narrative.

It is believed the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.

News.title: The overlooked factor driving the childhood obesity crisis
News.content:
"I loved school. I loved to learn."

Ibbie, 16, always struggled with her weight, but it was during the Covid-19 lockdowns that she started eating even more. She was bullied by classmates over her size, and in her first year of secondary school she stopped attending completely.

Away from the routine of the school day, her weight problems worsened.

"When you are at home 24/7 it is very easy to go into the kitchen to get a snack. It's not the same if you are at school," says Ibbie, from Doncaster.

By the age of 12 she weighed nearly 22 stone (140kg) and was diagnosed with liver damage. "I was told that I might need to have a liver transplant if I didn't lose weight. That was scary to hear."

Ibbie's experience is one of the more extreme examples of children living with obesity in the UK â but her story is not unique. She is one of more than 6,000 children who have been treated at a pioneering weight-loss service for the most obese children in the country. These Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics are a network of 39 specialist NHS hubs across England designed to treat severe obesity in children.

News.title: Uber launches UK's first robotaxis with a driver - here's what it's like to ride in one
News.content:
Londoners are able to hail the UK's first robotaxis - as Uber today becomes the first company to launch a self-driving minicab.

Initially, it only has 15 autonomous vehicles with a licence to operate in the city, and each one must have a human safety driver behind the wheel ready to take control if anything goes wrong.

Uber said it surveyed London-based customers via the app and more than 100,000 said they would choose a self-driving taxi if one was available, despite incidents of driverless rides malfunctioning in US cities where they already operate.

As I found out when I became the first UK journalist to hail one, it was mostly smooth but the safety driver did intervene on one occasion.

At the moment the UK fare for a robotaxi ride will be the same fare as a standard UberX, Uber Electric, or Uber Comfort journey, with upfront fares shown in the app.

Taking a self-driving ride will only appear as an option in the app after the journey has been booked, and if one of its cars is available nearby.

Uber's global head of autonomous mobility and delivery Sarfraz Maredia said the plan was to phase them in over a period of several years.

"We always want consumers to be able to request a human ride or an autonomous vehicle, and because the market's growing, we expect that there will be human drivers on Uber London for a long time to come," he said.

The Ford Mustang electric vehicles which make up Uber's current small fleet are fitted with the UK tech firm Wayve's driverless car technology, which uses AI to analyse data about what is going on around it in real time, gathered by sensors in a bar on the roof of the vehicle and elsewhere.

The vehicles are not pre-programmed - their actions are determined on the spot depending on what is going on.

Google's autonomous car company Waymo and the Chinese tech giant Baidu are also vying to launch services in the UK, and the competition is fierce.

Wayve chief executive Alex Kendall described developing the technology as "the space race for our generation" but added there were some "really hard problems to solve" along the way.

"What we've done over time is pioneer a completely new approach to autonomous driving, making it possible to bring this to a busy and complex city like London and scale it globally," he said.

News.title: B&Q and Five Guys among firms that paid staff below minimum wage
News.content:
DIY store B&Q and the fast food chain Five Guys are among hundreds of UK businesses named by the government for paying staff below the minimum wage.

More than 600 employers were ordered to pay affected workers the outstanding wages, with Â£4m returned to workers, according to the Department for Business and Trade.

The firms have also been issued penalties worth Â£7m.

B&Q said the underpayments were unintentional and the result of calculations involving geographical allowances, while Five Guys blamed "technical differences in how payroll regulations were applied".

The list of 658 businesses includes shops, restaurants, nurseries, social care providers and a handful of NHS trusts. The government did not say over what time period the underpayments spanned.

Minimum wage is Â£12.71 for staff aged 21 and over. For 18 to 20 year olds the rate is Â£10.85, and for under 18s and apprentices it is Â£8.

B&Q underpaid 4,530 workers a total of more than Â£456,000, according to the government.

B&Q said in response: "The shortfalls in payments were unintentional. They relate to calculations involving geographical allowances which are paid in addition to minimum hourly rates. All affected colleagues were quickly paid in full in July 2025."

Five Guys, named in the list as owing over Â£54,000 to 3,699 staff, said "technical differences in how payroll regulations were applied" led to its underpayments, which were identified in a review by the HMRC, the UK's revenue and tax authority.

"We worked closely and transparently with HMRC throughout the process and have made all required payments to affected current and former employees," the company said.

St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group failed to pay over Â£123,000 to 75 workers, according to the list, which also says St George's University Hospitals in Wandsworth, London, underpaid 55 workers.

A spokesman for the two hospital trusts said that "no colleagues were underpaid".

"This relates to a technical compliance issue where part of their salary for a non tax-deductable 'salary sacrifice' (for example, towards childcare) was not counted towards the national minimum wage, even though their gross salary was above the national minimum wage," he said.

A spokesperson said apprentices at Norfolk Community Health and Care NHS Trust were inadvertently underpaid between 2019 and 2023.

They said while their pay met the requirements for their contracted hours, meetings, handovers and time spent changing into uniform hadn't been accounted for, adding the trust has since changed policies and practices.

The other trust named has been contacted for comment.

There were also several nursing homes on the list, and multiple childcare providers.

Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the government was determined to stamp out the practice of "short-changing your staff".

"The best businesses know that looking after your workers isn't just the right thing to do, it's the smart thing to do," he said.

Kate Dearden, minister for the future of work, said: "Underpaying your staff is illegal, and we will not let workers foot the bill for their boss failing to follow the rules."

"Every employer should check their payroll now and reach out to Acas if they need further support," she added.

The first 10 employers on the government's list, which was sorted by the amount of wages not paid, are:

1. B&Q Ltd, failed to pay Â£456,934.72 to 4,530 workers.

2. Elysium Healthcare Holdings 3 Ltd, Borehamwood, failed to pay Â£330,048.81 to 1,095 workers.

3. St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group, failed to pay Â£123,331.97 to 75 workers.

4. Support Staff Services Limited, Slough, failed to pay Â£119,715.13 to 323 workers.

5. Forest Holidays Ltd, Moira, failed to pay Â£100,308.68 to 598 workers.

6. St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, London (Wandsworth), failed to pay Â£77,498.91 to 55 workers.

7. Lanes Group Limited, Leeds, failed to pay Â£67,893.34 to 297 workers.

8. UK Care Team Ltd, Leicester, LE19, failed to pay Â£67,082.76 to 99 workers.

9. Five Guys JV Limited, London (Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea), failed to pay Â£54,642.47 to 3,699 workers.

10. Merlin Cinemas Limited, Redruth, failed to pay Â£50,198.75 to 181 workers.

The list marks the first "naming round" since the Fair Work Agency was set up in April under the Employment Rights Act.

As well as enforcing the minimum wage, the agency also will soon tackle practices of denying workers holiday and sick pay.

Chair of the agency's advisory board, Matthew Taylor, said naming employers which underpay staff was an important reminder that "paying the minimum wage is not optional - it is the law".

He said: "Most employers want to do the right thing, and we will support them to comply, but those who fall short should expect robust enforcement to protect workers and maintain a fair playing field for responsible businesses."

News.title: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says
News.content:
Reform has been critical of measures contained in the bill and the impact they could have on funding the party receives from donors.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties and politicians.

Labour MP Stella Creasy said donations from individuals and companies giving Â£1m or more had "surged" in the last decade and gave examples for different political parties.

Among those she named was British billionaire Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman, who is one of Reform's biggest backers.

Last year he gave a single donation of Â£9m to Reform - the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person.

Creasy was among those who tabled amendments seeking to also impose a cap on UK-based donors.

One of her proposals called for an immediate Â£500,000 limit which would reduce to Â£100,000 in the second calendar year. Minsters would have been able to set a permanent cap.

The amendment, which was not moved to a vote, was signed by more than 60 MPs.

Creasy told the Commons: "Obscene wealth is increasingly dictating who is heard, whether we like it or not, what issues are being prioritised and whose interests shape policy decisions."

The Walthamstow MP added that there was a "need to act now to protect the next general election". Her proposals would have exempted trade unions from the donation cap, with the MP saying this is "already well regulated" and "clean money".

Kruger highlighted the millions of pounds donated by trade unions to the Labour Party as he criticised the proposals and the bill.

The MP for East Wiltshire said: "The claim is made that this bill will defend democracy, but actually it's a flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap Reform UK."

The former Conservative MP added: "The suggestion is made that this bill will restore trust in politics and that is exactly what is needed.

"But what they all mean is to restore trust in the class of politicians and in the political parties that have got us into the mess that we are in, including the party I'm afraid to say I was part of which is why I left it. We need change."

Responding for the government, Eshalomi said the bill "already contains a package of significant measures designed to strengthen the political finance regime whilst ensuring that legitimate donors can continue to fund election campaigns".

The communities minister added that the prime minister was among those "determined to tackle the UK-based issue of mega-donors in UK politics".

"That is why I'm happy to commit and announce the new cross-government task and finish team will be working at pace to find a solution without unintended consequences," Eshalomi said.

"I can reassure members that once these solutions have been found, we would want them in force as soon as possible."

Full details of the new team's remit have yet to be confirmed by the government.

It last month emerged that Burnham registered accepting Â£345,000 of donations over the past year, including Â£164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.

The Liberal Democrats proposed establishing a royal commission to make recommendations for a cap on political donations and the "effectiveness" of existing campaign expenditure limits.

This proposal was rejected in the Commons by 427 votes to 85, majority 342.

Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said Creasy had made a "clear case" for a cap on all donations, adding she would prefer it to be lower and suggested Â£50,000 a year.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said it was a "noble aim" to protect UK democracy from foreign influence but changes proposed by the government had not always been produced with "proper care and attention".

In March, the government said donations in cryptocurrency to UK political parties would be banned alongside the move to cap donations of British citizens living abroad at Â£100,000 annually.

Ministers later announced overseas voters moving to the UK would be prevented from giving more than Â£100,000 in political donations for a year after their arrival.

This was announced alongside tougher checks on company donations, which they believe will help stop foreign money from influencing UK elections.

The bill also contains measures to change the voting system, including extending the right to vote to 16- and 17-year-olds.

MPs approved the bill at third reading by 411 votes to 102, majority 309, and it will undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords at a later date.

News.title: Rocky Horror star Tim Curry's cause of death revealed
News.content:
British actor Tim Curry died of coronary artery disease, his spokesman has confirmed to the BBC.

The Rocky Horror Picture Show star died in his Los Angeles home on 25 August, aged 80.

In addition to the heart condition, Curry had a history of stroke and kidney cancer, which were significant conditions that contributed to his death, his spokesman said, citing a death certificate filed in Los Angeles County.

Stars of stage and screen paid tribute to the actor, who shot to fame as the lingerie-clad Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult 1975 film The Rocky Horror Show.

After having a near-fatal stroke in 2012, the actor used a wheelchair. He shifted his focus to voice acting exclusively, expressing gratitude that the stroke resulted in paralysis rather than taking away his ability to speak.

He continued to appear at film conventions and published his memoir, Vagabond, last year in which he opened up about the medical incident and his prolonged recovery.

"If there was anything impressed upon me in the aftermath, it was just how remarkable it was that I was still alive," Curry said, according to People, external.

News.title: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night
News.content:
The biggest factor pushing up rates is the credibility of the borrowing plans set out by major countries. The increase is not based on fears about countries "going bankrupt".

But it is based on the brutal market equation that if a country wants to borrow more, and to do so without a credible plan, especially if there are doubts over the stability of a given government, it should expect to pay a higher rate.

Influential economists lean on different factors. Mohamed el-Erian told me the AI competition in bond markets was the biggest new factor.

Lord Jim O'Neill, says the recent action has been caused by uncertainty about US policy, and in particular efforts by the US Government to try to manage down surging yields.

This brings us to the UK. The profound and rolling instability of multiple prime ministers, chancellors, policy U-turns and the seeming inability to push through major structural change in this country over the past decades, has attracted a premium.

It was part of Sir Keir Starmer's strategy to try to take on boring reforms and offer markets stability in a bid to lower borrowing costs.

It was a shock to many in the markets that despite a landslide majority, Labour could not push through plans to cut Britain's welfare bill. This added to the ups and downs in the gilt markets - the trade in British government debt.

Actually, there are signs of green shoots in the underlying economy. Economic growth has been faster than peers so far in 2026, despite the energy price spike.

Measures of consumer confidence have ticked back up again. The PM is hoping to build on these signs to help rebuild the economy.

But the ongoing rout in global bond markets raises serious questions about the coherence and detail of Burnham's broader plans.

"More public control" and more support for those struggling with the cost of living sounds like a plan for more spending, while the former could turn off potential investors looking at the country.

Burnham's former economic adviser, Lord O'Neill, told me yesterday that the PM's 10-year plan, expected in November, needs to set out how he will tackle "excessive spending".

Lord O'Neill believes showing investors he can be decisive on the state pension or the welfare bill will give him breathing room to focus on his favoured infrastructure investments.

As interest rates tick up, the trade offs facing the prime minister only get more difficult.

News.title: How Victoria Beckham turned her fashion firm around and made it profitable
News.content:
It has taken Lady Beckham 18 years to shift her business - where she is creative director - into the black.

The former popstar admitted in a Netflix documentary that the company had once been "tens of millions into the red", with "mind-blowing" waste including a flower budget of Â£70,000 a year.

Lady Beckham spoke of her "panic" as the debt piled-up.

"It's been a hell of a journey. I almost lost everything and that was a dark, dark time," she said. "I used to cry before I went to work every day, because I just felt like a firefighter."
