World.title: INTERVIEW: How we are reforming the SSS – DG, Oluwatosin Ajayi
World.content:
In this rare interview, the Director General of the State Security Service, Oluwatosin Ajayi, speaks on the agency’s institutional reforms, international cooperation and the fight against terrorism and other crimes.

EXCERPT:

PT: Thank you for finally honouring our request for an interview after several failed attempts.

DG SSS: You are welcome. I changed my mind to encourage the improved relationship between the media and security agencies in Nigeria. Moreso, it is not unusual with intelligence organisations globally to do this when the need arises. Our counterpart, the current Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), held a televised briefing on 16th September 2025, in which he spoke about the Agency’s fight against criminal cartels, terrorism, and drug traffickers. Traditionally, the MI6 Chief also makes annual public speech aimed at building public trust and explaining threats.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

PT: Your Service is 40 years now. That’s a huge milestone. We expected some fanfare, but you seem to be celebrating quietly. Can you walk us through your experience over the past decades? What has it been like and what has happened so far?

DG SSS: Intelligence organisations are not disposed to public fanfare; we hold most of our celebrations internally. Moreso, the mood of the nation does not warrant that now. The background is that I grew up in the Service. I started as a Cadet Officer, rose through the ranks, and, by God’s grace, I am here. So, I have been part of the system. I therefore acknowledge our challenges and problems. I also know the strengths and weaknesses of the system. Thus, what I have done over the last two years is not different from what I did at every level of leadership I held before now.

In summary, I am building on past managements’ successes, improving on our weaknesses, and developing our strengths. One result I think you can see is, firstly, strict law enforcement, which is one of the things that helps every society. The convictions of terror suspects and other criminal elements so far prove this. Secondly, and quite importantly, is the improvement of cooperation between sister agencies and our foreign allies. I’m sure you’ve also noticed that. And then improving the Service’s respect for Human Rights. Where we commit unavoidable errors, we proactively compensate victims without waiting for litigation. And in cases where the Court has issued an order, we ensure the compensation meets the highest standards of adequacy. For instance, in a N10 million compensation judgment, the person we mistakenly shot deserved more, so we added N10 million to it. We also provided him with fully covered medical treatment. And of course, we are also purging ourselves. We maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards unethical conduct. Such staff are not accommodated in our Service. We enforce a strict disciplinary process and keep the public duly informed. The idea is to be proactive in addressing misconduct, to ensure that ex-staff do not go on to commit crimes in our name. That’s a summary of what I have concentrated on in the past 2 years.

PT: Let me ask about some specific reforms?

DG SSS: The reforms fall into the five broad categories that I mentioned: law enforcement, synergy, accountability in what we do as a Service, respect for Human Rights, and infrastructural/administrative reforms to enhance operational efficiency.

PT: Before you came in as DG, the DSS was known for arbitrary arrests and extrajudicial treatment of suspects. Can you speak to the specific actions you took that led to the improvements we are seeing now?

DG SSS: We visibly separated civil matters from criminal matters. My experience through my career path showed that we conflated the two aspects. For instance, I must thank you in the media for the three awards I received from IPI, NUJ, and BON. You cannot apply the use of force in civil matters. Even some criminal matters don’t require force. Take, for example, the attempt to establish a shadow government, i.e., the Service versus Pat Utomi. Rather than arrest him, we sought judicial interpretation. And the Court ruled that his adventure was unconstitutional, illegal, and a threat to national security. So it was with SERAP, which wrongly accused two (2) DSS operatives of invading their premises. They approached the court, on my approval. Throughout the process, nobody was arrested, and the court awarded over N100 million in their favour. The case with the owner of Sahara Reporters, Sowore, is the same. Even from day one, when he went to court, the court asked whether we objected to his bail, and we said no because we hadn’t arrested him in the first place. He was granted bail on self-recognition. Whatever later transpired that he violated the court process is unrelated to the Service, and then the court revoked it, but eventually granted him bail with conditions.

PT: So, you now go to court for civil matters?

DG SSS: Yes. I have told my people that there should be no arrest in any civil case. And I’m sure you have found out that, even in cases involving journalists, we would rather approach the court because we do the same job. I call you guys our professional colleagues. The only difference is that, while you inform the public, we inform the Government. And because we inform the Government, our information is classified until we declassify it.

PT: Journalists will disagree when you call them your professional colleagues because, before you came, your agency was known for serial violation of press freedom.

DG SSS: You can attest to the fact that not a single journalist has been victimised under my watch. When any misgivings arose and I became aware of them, we responded immediately and offered an apology. Like the case of a journalist in Plateau State, I apologised for our staff’s error, and the NUJ President confirmed it. It was one of the reasons they cited for awarding me as NUJ MAN OF THE YEAR, 2026. If, for any reason, we need to question a journalist, we go through the IPI, the NUJ, or any other relevant body.

PT: What suddenly changed in the relationship between this Agency and the media? It was very frosty in the past, and in fact, your agency was known for being the biggest violator of press freedom, journalist safety, and independent journalism. So, what changed suddenly?

DG SSS: What changed is that I believe civil matters do not require the use of force. We also have a responsibility to protect journalists’ rights so they can do their job. Having been in the system, I have seen many things we could have handled better, and I am bringing those lessons to bear.

Journalists do similar work to what we do. In some cases, we even rely on them for information, so it makes no sense to use force against them. We can simply call the NUJ President, the IPI, or another relevant body, if there is an infraction, because they are known people, not criminals, terrorists, or people hiding in the forest. That is why I decided we must protect journalists and allow them to do their work. Our energy is focused on terrorists and other criminals, not on fighting our partners. Differences can be resolved through dialogue or judicial interpretation.

PT: People are wondering how an agency that was once seen as hostile to the media now enjoys a robust relationship with it, to the point where you are receiving several honours from media organisations.

DG SSS: As I said earlier, what has changed is our respect for people’s right to do their jobs without hindrance. Our responsibility is to protect those rights. If a journalist publishes an inaccurate report about the Service, my first step is to request a correction, not to make an arrest. We’ve done this on several occasions. For instance, when some media organisations reported that the DSS invaded the Lagos State House of Assembly, we demanded a retraction of the story within seven days. When they all complied, we took no further action because that’s the proper civil approach.

The same happened with the report from the Order Paper, which alleged that the DSS was involved in moves to impeach the Senate President. We clarified the facts and requested a retraction. Where there is a refusal, we seek redress through the Courts, not arrests. That is the same approach we adopted in cases involving SERAP and Sahara Reporters.

PT: So, where are you on SERAP? Is there no way to resolve the matter out of court?

DG SSS: We are very open to conversations if they apologise. We didn’t invade SERAP, and the Court has ruled in favour of the two operatives who sued for defamation. They chose to appeal the ruling, and we respect their right to do so.

Let me stress something on this. You see, if I, as the leader of this organisation, can tell my staff across the States to apologise when wrong, that must mean something. It is a sign of courage to admit errors, as we are doing, and to pay compensation when a mistake is made without waiting for the court to order us. So when you wrong us, should you grandstand instead of apologising, and turn it into a pity party or false claims of harassment?

PT: Let’s talk about your agency’s past reputation for arbitrary arrests and prolonged detention, then releasing those found innocent without any justice or redress. But lately you’ve been paying compensation in several cases. What informed this change in approach?

DG SSS: The simple reason is, you cannot do injury to someone, go on to admit that it was a mistake and then refuse to seek restitution. Even before God, there is room for restitution. Sometimes it is to heal the trauma, to provide the resources to help reintegrate, after we’ve disrupted a life. Most of the time, we follow up to see how to get the victim back in business. You see, what people hear is the initial compensation, like the Jos businessman; we actually went further by setting up a business for him, and he is now an employer of others.

PT: What happened to the Jos man really?

DG SSS: He was mistakenly shot, and in 2016, there was a court judgment for the Service to pay compensation of Ten million Naira.

PT: In 2016?

DG SSS: Yes, it happened in 2016. A court ordered the Service to pay him ₦10 million in compensation, but that wasn’t done. I take responsibility and won’t justify what happened then.

However, on assuming office as DG, I ordered a review of such cases because I believed we had to correct our past mistakes. As the Yoruba say, “when you wake up, that’s your morning.” It’s never too late to do the right thing. When I was appointed, the President’s only charge to me was that he expected me to do things differently, respect people’s rights, and uphold the reputation I had built. That guided my decision. Our review showed that, in some cases, we were clearly wrong.

Compensation for operational mistakes is not uncommon. Countries such as the UK have done the same in similar circumstances. After our medical team assessed his condition and found that his leg had deteriorated significantly, we offered him treatment in our hospital and eventually approved an additional ₦10 million to help him rebuild his livelihood. For me, it was about justice, accountability, and strengthening public confidence in the Service.

PT: You call this restorative justice, and we learned that your agency has so far paid about 300 million Naira in compensation. You’ve talked about the Jos man, so what are the other cases?

DG SSS: There are several others. In one case, an Abuja-based businesswoman was mistakenly arrested during an operation targeting suspected oil bunkerers. She was simply there to deliver goods. Once the investigation confirmed she was innocent, she was paid an initial ₦10 million in compensation, and I directed my officers to support her in rebuilding her business.

There was also the case of the Ifedi couple arrested before I became DG and detained in Wawa. It was later established that they were not terrorists. The woman’s only link was that IPOB members patronised her restaurant, and that was clearly not enough to label her a member. I ordered their release, compensated the professor, and we are discussing how to preserve his late wife’s memory by acquiring the restaurant’s premises and rebuilding it in her honour. Those are just a few examples. There are many other cases across the country in which people who were wrongfully detained have been released and compensated.

One case that received little media attention involved an operation in Cross River State. Our operatives were pursuing a notorious kidnapper who fled into a student area. During the operation, four female students had their phones damaged. When I was briefed, I directed that their phones be replaced immediately. The students insisted they only wanted the repair of the damaged devices, which spoke to their integrity. I also approved scholarships to support their education. For me, that’s the right way to respond when innocent people are affected during legitimate operations.

PT: Was this in addition to their telephones?

DG SSS: Yes. My three (3) children were in universities at some times in their lives, and I only imagined how they’d feel seeing people with guns destroying their phones. I know the trauma and decided to do something to ease it. I could list a lot more, but the amount is certainly higher than N300 million. Some don’t get to the press at all.

PT: What is the philosophy behind this restorative justice within an Intelligence agency?

DG SSS: The philosophy is that the Intelligence Community leverages humans as its greatest asset, not only technology. For Intelligence, you need the people. An Intelligence Service that is completely alienated from the people by its conduct might not get the credible information it needs. Much as our activities are not open, we do a lot to endear ourselves to the people. We try to conceal these activities, but some of them still leak. For instance, our humanitarian outreach across the LGAs targeting the indigent in these areas was not made public. Somehow, one Chairman put it out: “Look at what the DSS did for our people. We have offices across all 774 Local Governments and 37 states Commands. When people are hurting or aggrieved, even if they have information, they might not volunteer it, though they will be harming themselves unknowingly. And that’s why we correct any injustice against people.

PT: Following what you have just said, I am curious: is there a link between that and your recent recruitment drive targeting orphanages? How did that come about, because there were reports that you were hiring people from Orphanage homes.

DG SSS: It’s part of our philosophy that people are our greatest intelligence asset. Human intelligence is more valuable than any technology because people can provide context, answer questions, and be engaged repeatedly in ways machines cannot. That’s why I believe in treating people fairly and correcting injustices. When people trust you, they are more willing to work with you. In security, we summarise it this way: one of the most effective counterterrorism measures is “reducing areas of discontent”.

PT: So, are you saying those in orphanage homes are discontented, or is it because you see them as valuable human assets?

DG SSS: No. First and foremost, they are part of our society that can be easily forgotten if care isn’t taken, making them vulnerable. And then, as you rightly said, despite that, they can be very useful, but you can still forget. The ones we’ve had to recruit in the past have done very well for us. I have been doing this before I became DG in every State where I served as State Director. But I remember one of those I recruited; she remained in the orphanage and helped to groom and reorient others to become better citizens. So, they form part of human assets, but if there is no deliberate action to seek them out, they could easily be forgotten. Interestingly, from experience, some of our best brains are from there. It’s what I have done, and now doing at the National level. Again, I don’t know how that got out because I like to do it quietly, as I did for 14 years as State Director across 5 States.

PT: So, these people are graduates?

DG SSS: Graduates are recruited into the officer’s cadre, and others are recruited into our junior cadre with a First School Leaving Certificate. Afterwards, they train in the Service.

PT: You’ve been talking about Intelligence. Some people see your Agency as simply providing intelligence that makes government happy. What will you say to that?

DG SSS: Some people even say we only act after crimes are committed, but much of our intelligence work is classified, so the public never sees it. Our job is to provide Intelligence to the government and sister agencies, including advice on the security implications of policies. Our job is not to tell Government what it wants to hear. The Intelligence helps prevent attacks, rescue victims, identify perpetrators, and make arrests. While many of those successes cannot be disclosed, recent cases, including suspects arrested for planned terrorist attacks, show that preventive intelligence is at work.

PT: That was what I wanted to ask: if you gather all this intelligence, how come the Government does not do enough to stop these attacks from happening?

DG SSS: I want to anchor on the fact that we recognise that attacks are still happening, which tends to diminish our efforts. For instance, somebody whose child was kidnapped doesn’t care if you prevented 200 attacks. For that person, you haven’t achieved. On that basis, I acknowledge that we need to do more. The President keeps urging the protection of Nigerian lives; he doesn’t forget to caution that “Nigerians are in a hurry to celebrate peace.” That’s what is important, and we have to do more.

But talking specifically about sharing intelligence, what happened to the attacks that were carried out? I’ll first draw your attention to the fact that, all over the world, no one can completely root out crimes one hundred per cent. But we owe it to this generation and those unborn to reduce crimes to the barest minimum.

If we go by those who even started the intelligence business before us, here we are talking of 40 years, you can imagine the global threat levels and how even the most powerful nations on earth are currently grappling with various forms of internal insurgencies, heightened violent crimes, among others. Thus, intelligence worldwide can’t be perfect. I won’t tell you it’s 100%. Secondly, where we get a good percentage of it, there are issues such as capability, terrain, and the need for strategic decision-making. Hence, the presidential actions on State Police, forest guards, are strategic solutions to enable vulnerable communities to defend themselves.

Imagine our closeness to the Sahel and the difficult terrain around Lake Chad. Imagine the Niger Delta militancy and the challenge of navigating the creeks by regular forces. We have such peculiar problems that require strategic solutions. Take the example of a State with a difficult terrain with its own Police; they know how to deploy. The Federal authority cannot do it alone.

PT: Just a follow-up: will you say that those factors you’ve listed contribute to the inability to provide a swift response? I think that whenever these attacks are recorded, and security steps in, we are able to fight back against the terrorists. But people complain that the response isn’t swift enough. For instance, the Oriire attack in Oyo and the fact that the victims were held for weeks before eventually being rescued, the complaints are that the response wasn’t swift enough. Nigerians want swift responses. Are the above reasons why that has not been achieved?

DG SSS: What I’d tell you is that immediately the incident happened, based on credible intelligence, troops chased them immediately, and sadly, a vigilante and a policeman were killed. During the second raid, more were killed, making a total of nine (9) fatalities, four (4) civilians and five (5) security personnel. It was a complex operation involving a two-and-a-half-year-old infant who could not run much if we invaded the place.

As expected, the rescue operation attracted a lot of social media disinformation. You have to sieve the information there. I give you an example: while that incident lasted, they were posting deepfake videos of children beaten with lacerations on their bodies. They were actually footage from a particular country on witchcraft-related incidents passed off as real-time crude events here. Recall the victims recounted how well-treated they were by the criminals. So, one of the things I’d like you to do in the media is fact-finding and separating facts from fiction. Some patriotic Nigerians understood that a soldier was killed, and other lives were lost during the rescue operation, and they empathised, having learnt about the nature of the kidnap group- an international terrorist group with links to Al-Qaeda.

Citizens ought to know that the incarcerated leaders of the kidnap group who were requested in exchange for the victims were arrested last year by the Service; their arrest helped to prevent high-profile attacks. These are people found complicit in the Abuja/Kaduna train attack and were planning more kidnappings of foreigners, students, women and their children on a large scale. They wanted to demand state recognition and freedom to practice their religion somewhere, hence the arrest of their leaders. That proved proactiveness. The kingpins are the ones now sentenced to life imprisonment. The three other collaborators earned life imprisonment, and the Service will push for a stiffer penalty.

PT: How will you assess the working relationship between your agency and other sister agencies in Nigeria and with foreign intelligence partners? Where are the gaps, and where is cooperation strongest?

DG SSS: Locally, our information/intel sharing is great. Over the decades, we have collaborated with our allies in the US, the UK, France, and many other European countries. After we share our intelligence, we determine where we want joint boots on the ground. Don’t forget that, sometimes around 2000, US soldiers came to join us to deal with some threats. So, it’s very useful. One of our strengths is that we are very open with ourselves and get support when we need it. We also support our partners. So, it’s the openness and frankness that are our greatest strengths. Can it be better? Yes. We will achieve many more feats with the liaison we now share.

Our citizens often misunderstand it, and we must keep educating them.

PT: There is another side to my question, especially about inter-agency rivalry. So how are you navigating that?

DG SSS: For me, that has to do with leadership. Anytime you see it happen, it is because a leader encourages it. My operatives know I encourage collaboration and joint operations. I must commend the leadership of all the agencies; we have an excellent working relationship. In fact, it was demonstrated in Oriire, Oyo State. No single agency could claim supreme credit for it. It was jointly achieved, and you saw the GOC when he was giving his brief. He called out every other agency that participated- DSS, Navy, Air Force, Police, NSCDC, vigilante, everybody. When you see rivalry thrive, the leaders encourage that. This crop of leaders, no!

PT: You made a comment earlier about sentencing and obviously about the recent case that the Ansaru leaders were given life imprisonment, and that you are pushing for a death sentence. I think we’ve also had a few other capital sentences for terrorists in Owo, but I think the problem with capital sentencing is in the carrying out of the executions. We’ve not had one in close to 20 years. So, is there an effort to get Mr President to sign the execution of these death sentences?

DG SSS: A nation evolves with its realities. Years ago, when we did not face this level of violence and terrorism, hesitation over signing death warrants may have reflected a different context. Today, with terrorists attacking innocent people in public, the reality has changed. I doubt any responsible authority faced with that level of brutality would refuse to sign.

PT: Okay, so you’ve been getting a lot of convictions. Some life sentences and some death sentences. What are you doing differently to achieve that?

DG SSS: Diligent prosecution. It is not enough to allege that someone committed a crime; you must prove it. We are strengthening our investigations, evidence gathering, and understanding of offences because justice depends on the facts presented before the court. Even a strong case can fail without convincing facts.

PT: Thank you very much for this opportunity.

DG SSS: Thank you, too.

World.title: Igbo traditional rulers, others seek an end to ‘Osu caste’ practice
World.content:
The traditional rulers are Obi of Onitsha, Alfred Achebe; the Traditional Ruler of Nnewi, Kenneth Orizu, both in Anambra, and Samuel Asadu, the Enugu State Chairman, Traditional Rulers Council.

They made the call when the producer, directors and crew of the new Nollywood movie, “Properties of the Gods”, visited their palaces separately on Wednesday.

They described the practice as discriminatory and inconsistent with the equality of human beings. They said the visit was to seek their blessings ahead of the movie’s nationwide cinema premiere.

The movie – ‘Properties of the Gods’

The News Agency of Nigeria reports that the movie, produced by renowned Nollywood actor Joseph Okechukwu, addresses the Osu caste practice and its effects on people in Igboland.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The movie is scheduled to premiere in cinemas nationwide on 4 September.

Receiving the team at his palace, Mr Achebe said ignorance was responsible for many superstitious beliefs and practices that had persisted despite advances in knowledge and civilisation.

He said all human beings were equal before God and that no individual or group had the right to regard another person as an underclass.

“Ignorance drives superstition, which is anachronistic in the 21st century.

“All human beings are equal in the eyes of God, who created all of us. Whether you are black, yellow or white, tall or short, man or woman, we are all created in His own image,” he said.

The traditional ruler described the Osu caste system as a “disgrace” and urged communities where the practice still existed to abolish it, saying that “This discrimination must end forever”.

He said increased knowledge and education had helped society to overcome several superstitious beliefs, adding that the same approach should be applied to the Osu system.

More than legislation needed to end Osu caste – Achebe

Mr Achebe said legislation alone might not be sufficient to eradicate the practice, stressing the need for mass mobilisation and a change in people’s mindset.

He noted that Onitsha did not operate the Osu caste system in the conventional sense, explaining that the traditional institution had a different understanding of the term.

According to him, the abolition of discriminatory practices requires sustained advocacy and social acceptance.

‘Nnewi had abolished it’

Also speaking, Mr Orizu, who addressed the visitors through the Crown Prince of Nnewi, Obi Orizu, recalled the Nnewi traditional institution’s decision to abolish the Osu system.

He said the decision was driven by the question of why some people should continue to live in bondage and be denied freedom and opportunities to prosper.

“On his own initiative, and after consultations with the traditional authorities, he decided to abolish the system.

“The ban was significant because immediately after the pronouncement was made, he was put to the test,” Mr Orizu said.

Mr Orizu said the decision had continued to yield benefits and should serve as an example to other communities.

“We cannot say that our forefathers were enslaved and then turn around and enslave other people ourselves. That would be contradictory,” he said.

On his part, the Chairman of the Enugu State Council of Traditional Rulers, Samuel Asadu, endorsed the movie, describing it as a timely and welcome development.

A philanthropist and media personality, Emmanuel Oko, popularly known as Okwuluora Ndigbo, said the Osu issue was one of the factors hindering the progress and unity of Igbo people.

Mr Oko commended the filmmakers for using cinema as a tool to reshape people’s mindset and promote inclusion.

“I am from Nkanu, where the practice is worse. People still tell me to avoid those they call Osu, yet some of the people helping me most in Enugu are those they call Osu. I still do not understand it,” he said.

He urged people, particularly in communities where the practice remained prevalent, to watch “Properties of the Gods” and support the campaign against discrimination.

Why we visited traditional rulers – Producer

Earlier, Mr Okechukwu, the movie’s producer, said the team visited the traditional rulers to seek their blessings ahead of the film’s release.

Mr Okechukwu said the movie was not produced to create conflict or attack anybody, but to advance the conversation on the need for Igbo people to embrace one another.

“Our mission is to advance the conversation to a point where our people can easily understand that the time has come for us to embrace one another rather than scatter one another,” he said.

He said the position expressed by the royal fathers demonstrated the need for other traditional rulers in the South-east to embrace inclusion.

World.title: 2027: Ex-Lawmaker rejects zoning claim, backs Ugochinyere for second term in Imo constituency
World.content:
A former member of the House of Representatives, Rufus Omeire, has rejected claims that the Ideato Federal Constituency seat in Imo State is subject to a zoning arrangement between Ideato North and Ideato South.

Mr Omeire, who is the Action Peoples Party (APP) senatorial candidate for Imo West, said the latest agitation over the constituency’s 2027 representation was an attempt to undermine the incumbent lawmaker, Ikenga Ugochinyere (APP, Imo).

Mr Ugochinyere, who represents Ideato North/South Federal Constituency, is the Chairman of the House Committee on Petroleum Resources (Downstream).

In a statement issued in Abuja on Wednesday, Mr Omeire argued that Mr Ugochinyere did not emerge through zoning but through the decision of voters in the constituency.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Ikenga is not a product of zoning. He is a product of our people’s decision to elect a messenger they have confidence in, even while he was in exile,” he said.

Mr Omeire, who is from Ideato South, said the constituency had never operated a formal zoning arrangement for the federal House seat.

“We don’t have zoning, and he can’t be a product of what does not exist,” he said.

He cited Mr Ugochinyere’s victory in the 2023 election over the then incumbent, Paschal Obi, who is from Ideato South, as evidence that voters in the constituency had not been bound by a rotational arrangement.

“His closest challenger, who was the incumbent, was from Ideato South, went even up to the court, and Ikenga defeated him,” Omeire said.

Mr Omeire said he had personally attempted to secure a second term when he represented the constituency from Ideato South, but was not returned, which he cited as further evidence that there was no binding arrangement guaranteeing successive terms to a particular area.

According to him, voters should be allowed to determine who represents them based on performance rather than geographical rotation.

“The people love Ikenga because he is a light and a messenger who will one day host the Ideato flag at the centre of national and international politics,” he said.

Mr Omeire argued that repeatedly replacing representatives after a single term could undermine continuity and development in the constituency.

“We are short-changing ourselves in this quest to always change our Reps after one tenure. We can never achieve any meaningful development from the federal level like this. We have finally gotten it right with Ikenga, so he should continue the wonderful work he is doing,” he said.

The former lawmaker also defended Mr Ugochinyere’s record, particularly his role in attracting federal attention to infrastructure in Ideato.

He credited the incumbent with securing President Bola Tinubu’s approval for N26 billion for the Ideato Bridge, claiming the intervention was obtained before the Imo State Government subsequently approached the Ministry of Works to take over the project.

Mr Omeire challenged the Imo State Government to identify projects it had initiated independently in the federal constituency.

“Until they start the Amanator-Isiekenesi-Dikenafai Road and finish it, nobody can say they have done anything for us,” he said.

Mr Omeire, however, dismissed Mr Ugochinyere’s critics as “roadside clowns,” accusing them of mounting what he described as a “kindergarten attack” against the lawmaker.

He urged those behind the agitation to abandon what he called an attempt to create unnecessary tension and attract political attention.

“This desperate show of shame was only an act to beg for the extension of their tenure, which has already expired,” he said.

Backstory

Mr Ugochinyere was declared the winner of the 2023 election by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) after polling 13,026 votes. Mr Obi, who contested on the Labour Party platform, came second with 5,696 votes, while the All Progressives Congress candidate (APC), Chika Abazu, scored 2,368 votes.

The election was subsequently challenged at the tribunal. In September 2023, the Imo State National and State House of Assembly Election Petitions Tribunal ordered Mr Ugochinyere’s removal and a supplementary election after ruling on the validity of his nomination. However, the Court of Appeal later overturned the tribunal’s decision and affirmed Ugochinyere’s election.

The disagreement over zoning is not entirely new. While there is no evidence of a formal statutory or legally binding zoning arrangement for the federal constituency, available records show that the seat has historically alternated between politicians from the two LGAs, although not in a strict one-term-each pattern.

Records of the Fourth Republic show that ThankGod Ezeani and Patricia Udogu, both from Ideato North, represented the constituency between 1999 and 2007 before Mr Omeire, from Ideato South, took over from 2007 to 2011. The seat returned to Ideato North with Eddie Mbadiwe and was subsequently retained by Austin Chukwukere, both from Ideato North, between 2011 and 2019. Paschal Obi, from Ideato South, won in 2019 before losing to Mr Ugochinyere in 2023.

The zoning argument resurfaced in 2026 as political activity ahead of the 2027 elections intensified. In April, a group identified as the Ideato South Political Forum publicly adopted Mr Ugochinyere for another term, saying it had consulted communities, youths, elders and political actors before reaching the decision. The group expressly argued that Ideato South should not sacrifice what it described as quality representation for zoning.

World.title: 2027: Wike vows to deliver Rivers, FCT to Tinubu
World.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has declared that he remains in charge of the political structures in Rivers State and the FCT, vowing to deliver them to President Bola Tinubu in the 2027 presidential election.

Mr Wike made the declaration on Wednesday during a media chat in Port Harcourt, where he described himself as the “General Commander of the Political Infantry” and dismissed the suggestion that only a sitting governor could control a state’s political structure.

“You do not need to be governor before you can be in charge. I am the General Commander of the Political Infantry; therefore, I am in charge. So also in FCT. I owe the President to give these two,” he said.

Mr Wike, a former governor of Rivers State, has remained one of Mr Tinubu’s strongest political allies outside the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC), despite retaining his membership of the opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He has repeatedly pledged to mobilise support for Mr Tinubu in Rivers ahead of the 2027 election.

In February, Mr Wike said supporters of the president in Rivers did not need a sitting governor to mobilise votes for him, arguing that he and his allies had enough political structures across the state to deliver the president.

His latest declaration comes amid continuing questions over the balance of political influence in Rivers State, where Governor Siminalayi Fubara has returned to the political centre after last year’s crisis with Mr Wike.

Mr Wike, however, insisted that occupying the governorship was not the only route to political control.

‘I owe Tinubu Rivers, FCT’

Explaining his political role, Mr Wike said his objective was to ensure that Mr Tinubu wins both Rivers and the FCT.

He said he would not sit back and allow opposition politicians to take the territories from the president.

“Politics, of course, this is the time. You want me to fold my hand for Atiku to come and win the election?” he asked.

The minister also dismissed suggestions that he was relocating to Rivers State, saying his return was partly to reconnect with his political base and spend time with his family.

His comments come as politicians intensify preparations for the 2027 election.

Suspension of FCTA director

The minister also announced the suspension of an FCTA director for allegedly issuing unauthorised temporary approvals to commercial operators on designated green areas.

Mr Wike said the action was part of the administration’s response to violations of the Abuja master plan, particularly the encroachment of green areas and waterways.

“Beyond structural enforcement, the FCTA is also taking stern administrative action against officials within the administration who facilitate illegal encroachment into green areas and the waterways,” he said.

He said another official had faced disciplinary action for allegedly reallocating parkland under the guise of security clearing.

The sanctions followed recent flooding in parts of Abuja, particularly along the Airport Road corridor and in Lokogoma.

Mr Wike said the Executive Secretary of the Federal Capital Development Authority (FCDA) and the Director of Development Control had been dispatched to inspect affected communities.

“When I heard of the incident, the executive secretary of the FCDA and the director, development control had to go to the place, not only at the Airport Road but also in Lokogoma,” he said.

He blamed part of the flooding on years of violations of the Abuja master plan, particularly developments that blocked waterways and road corridors.

“From our studies, Lugbe has always violated the Abuja master plan. All over the years, you see people building without approval and blocking where there is supposed to be a roadway. As an administration, we are not taking it lightly,” he said.

Mr Wike vowed to remove structures found to be obstructing waterways and road corridors.

He also rejected claims that government approvals should protect structures built in prohibited areas.

“You got approval to do something wrong, sometimes, it’s under influence. government policy is that nobody should do anything on green areas,” he said.

“Now you go with the spirit that nothing will happen, and then when we come to enforce, you say you have approval. It is not going to be accepted.”

The FCTA has intensified enforcement against structures built on waterways and other prohibited areas following flooding in several parts of Abuja.

World.title: CAFWCLQ: Edo Queens thrash USFA to reach WAFU-B final
World.content:
Defending Nigeria Women’s Football League (NWFL) champions Edo Queens FC produced another statement performance in Ouagadougou on Wednesday, thrashing Burkina Faso’s USFA FC 5-1 to book their place in the final of the WAFU-B CAF Women’s Champions League qualifying tournament.

The Nigerian champions dominated proceedings at the Stade 4 Août, taking control of the semi-final from the early stages before completing a comprehensive drubbing of the Burkinabè hosts.

Atume Doosuur opened the scoring in the 17th minute, giving Edo Queens an early advantage and putting the 2024 WAFU-B champions on course for another final.

Edo Queens continued to pile pressure on USFA and were rewarded with two more goals shortly before half-time.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Chioma Moses doubled the advantage in the 43rd minute before Valentina Uroko struck just two minutes later to make it 3-0 and leave the Nigerian side firmly in command at the break.

There was no let-up after the restart as Edo Queens continued to dictate the contest, as Doshima Tarnum extended the lead to 4-0 just a minute into the second half when she converted from a corner kick.

Aminat Folorunsho then joined in the party, completing the rout in the 62nd minute, effectively putting the result beyond doubt and sending Edo Queens cruising into the final.

USFA managed to score a consolation goal in the first minute of stoppage time, but it did little to change the outcome as Edo Queens completed a dominant 5-1 victory.

The result caps an impressive campaign so far for Edo Queens, who had earlier navigated their way through Group B with two wins from three matches.

READ ALSO: Edo Queens clinch second NWFL Premiership title

They emphatically began their campaign with a 7-0 demolition of the Niger Republic’s AS Garde Nationale before following it up with a 3-1 victory over ASEC Mimosas of Côte d’Ivoire.

Their only setback came in their final group game against Ghanaian champions Ampem Darkoa Ladies, who edged them 2-1 on Sunday.

Despite that defeat, Edo Queens bounced back emphatically against USFA to move within one victory of securing the WAFU-B title and qualification for the CAF Women’s Champions League.

The Nigerian champions could now face Ampem Darkoa Ladies again in the final, setting up a potential rematch against the Ghanaian side with the WAFU-B crown and a place in the CAF Women’s Champions League at stake.

World.title: Akwa Ibom publishes Q2 budget report but fails to show where trillions went — BudgIT
World.content:
Akwa Ibom State Government has published its second-quarter 2026 budget implementation report, but the three-page document leaves major gaps in its account of public spending.

Missing details, the BudgIT Foundation says, make it difficult for citizens to determine where trillions of naira received by the government were spent.

The finding places Akwa Ibom in a peculiar position: while 34 states published their Q2 2026 Budget Implementation Reports, BudgIT singled out Akwa Ibom for publishing a report that, despite being publicly available, contains “significant data gaps” that limit meaningful scrutiny of government expenditure.

In its report, Half-Year BIR Status and Comparative Insights 2026/2025, BudgIT said publishing a budget implementation report should not be treated as transparency if the information disclosed is incomplete or unusable.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Publishing a BIR is not enough, but the data must be complete and usable,” BudgIT said.

“While Akwa Ibom State published its Q2 2026 BIR, the report contains significant data gaps that limit public scrutiny of government spending.”

The criticism raises fresh questions about fiscal transparency in Akwa Ibom, where Governor Umo Eno’s administration has received over ₦2.943 trillion in 38 months, according to revenue data previously reported by PREMIUM TIMES.

With detailed revenue and expenditure information missing from the state’s budget implementation reports, citizens are left with limited means to independently determine whether all the state’s revenue sources are remitted to the state coffers and where portions of the public funds received by the government have gone.

BudgIT said it had formally raised concerns with the Akwa Ibom State Government over the omissions but received no response.

“Transparency requires disclosure—not just publication,” the organisation said.

Report without enough answers

BudgIT said the Akwa Ibom case shows that publishing a fiscal document does not automatically constitute transparency.

“A published report can still leave out important information,” the foundation said.

“Take Akwa Ibom. The state published its Q2 BIR, but it didn’t give enough information to show where all the money went.”

The finding is consistent with PREMIUM TIMES’ reporting on the state’s declining fiscal disclosure under Mr Eno.

The newspaper has consistently reported that the state government stopped publishing detailed BIRs starting in the first quarter of 2025, replacing them with a three-page summary that was later increased to a five-page summary in the second quarter of 2026.

When Mr Eno was recently asked in a live interview for details on how the state’s accrued trillions are spent, he referenced the state’s audited financial statements for more comprehensive information.

However, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the audited financial statements also fail to provide sufficient details of capital expenditure, meaning the alternative source cited by the governor does not fully close the information gap.

An investigative report by PREMIUM TIMES in January found that Akwa Ibom had slipped deeper into fiscal secrecy under Mr Eno, despite his commitment to fiscal transparency in his manifesto and provisions of the state’s Fiscal Responsibility Law.

The latest BudgIT report now raises a similar concern from a national assessment of state-level fiscal disclosure.

National compliance falls

Across Nigeria, BudgIT found that 34 of the 36 states had published their Q2 2026 BIRs, representing 94.4 per cent compliance.

Osun and Rivers states accounted for the remaining 5.6 per cent, with no Q2 2026 BIR available for either state.

The 2026 figure indicates a decline from the second quarter of 2025, when 35 states, or 97.2 per cent, had published their BIRs.

“While compliance remained unchanged between Q1 and Q2 2026, the year-on-year decline suggests a setback in fiscal transparency,” BudgIT said.

Rivers State remained non-compliant throughout both years, while Osun was added to the list in Q2 2026.

While some states failed to publish their reports altogether, BudgIT’s assessment of Akwa Ibom reveals another aspect of the transparency issue: a report can be published and still prevent citizens from properly tracking their money.

World.title: 2027: We’ll remove you from office if APC loses in your area, governor threatens council chairmen
World.content:
Governor Francis Nwifuru of Ebonyi State has threatened to remove any chairman who fails to win his council area for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in the state during the 2027 general elections.

Mr Nwifuru spoke on Tuesday in Abakaliki, the state capital, when he inaugurated the new chairmen and vice chairmen of the 13 local government areas of the South-eastern state.

A video clip which showed the governor making the controversial remarks has gone viral on social media.

“As a local government chairman, if you like, go and sleep so that another person will take over your house.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“You will not stop us (APC) from winning. But when we win, we will remove you,” he told the newly inaugurated chairmen.

The governor maintained that he was not interested in hiding his stance on sacking the local government chairmen who failed to secure victory for the APC in their council areas in 2027.

“It is also not hidden. So let the front page of a newspaper show it tomorrow: we will remove a council chairman who did not win in his local government. We will use your councillors and remove you,” he reiterated.

He urged the chairmen not to allow the opposition to win in their areas because “charity begins at home”.

Mr Nwifuru was first elected governor of Ebonyi State in 2023 under the APC platform. His first four-year tenure will elapse by 29 May 2027. He is seeking re-election in 2027.

Independence of LGs and executive influence

Mr Nwifuru’s remarks have raised many fundamental questions, including the independence of local government areas and their chairmen, as well as the influence of governors in Nigeria.

A turning point in the attempt to achieve the independence of local government came in July 2024 when the Supreme Court delivered a ruling, upholding a federal government suit seeking to enforce financial independence for local governments.

In a unanimous decision, a seven-member panel declared it unconstitutional for state governments to retain or manage funds meant for local councils.

The court ordered that allocations from the Federation Account be paid directly to local governments, as provided under Section 162 (5–8) of the Nigerian Constitution.

Despite the ruling, many state governments have continued to channel local government funds through joint accounts, a practice the court deemed unlawful.

For instance, in October of 2024, Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State signed the Anambra State Local Government Administration Bill into law.

The law compels local governments in the state to remit a portion of their federal allocations into a consolidated account controlled by the state government.

Observers said the law was at variance with the Supreme Court ruling, which affirmed the financial autonomy of the country’s local governments.

Beyond the independence of council areas and their chairmen, the Ebonyi governor’s remarks also raised another question: whether governors have the unilateral power to remove an elected local government chairman.

Obioma Ezenwobodo, an Abuja-based legal practitioner, told PREMIUM TIMES that Mr Nwifuru has no power to remove any local government chairman.

Mr Ezenwobodo stressed that Ebonyi State has a local law that governs the operations of its local government areas.

“The councillors can impeach the local government chairmen. So, the governor doesn’t have the power to remove an elected local government chairman,” he said.

The lawyer also cited the Supreme Court ruling, which affirmed the autonomy of the country’s local governments.

He further cited another Supreme Court ruling that held that local governments are not under the state’s control.
