“The attempt to forcibly disappear Alex Kiprotich, three days after President William Ruto railed against The Standard Group, reflects the growing dangers that journalists face in Kenya, despite the president’s earlier promise to allow the press to work freely,” Quintal said.

The New York-based press freedom organisation further expressed concern over what it described as an escalation in cases of abductions and enforced disappearances in Kenya.

World.title: Trumpets of reforms blow louder as Kenya marks 16 years under 2010 Constitution
World.content:
The Constitution, Kenyan flag and the National anthem. [PCS]

On Thursday, August 27, a group of people largely composed of the youth gathered under some trees at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, carrying Kenyans flag, and banners and placards inscribed with "implement the constitution. Kenyans first" words.

These were in protests against what they believed is deliberate failure of those in authority to fully implement the 2010 Constitution.

World.title: Ruto allies hit back at Gachagua over IEBC tender concerns
World.content:
The Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kit. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto’s allies led by National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula have launched a scathing attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and the Opposition over their criticism of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), citing blackmail by the Opposition.

The leaders warned that attempts by politicians to dictate how the electoral agency procures technology and other election materials could undermine public confidence in the 2027 General Election.

World.title: IEBC rejects Gachagua's claims, defends 2027 polls preparations
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

IEBC dismissed Gachagua's claims of political interference, graft and voter suppression in 2027 polls.

The Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) has dismissed allegations of political interference, corruption and voter suppression surrounding preparations for the 2027 General Election, terming the claims false, unsubstantiated and aimed at undermining public confidence in the electoral body.

In a statement issued on Thursday, IEBC Chairperson Erastus Edung Ethekon said the allegations followed statements made by Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua during a press briefing on Wednesday.

The commission specifically rejected claims that politicians had purchased a house for its chairperson to influence him, saying the allegation had changed from an alleged Sh80 million property to one worth Sh200 million.

"The allegations that a house has been purchased for the Chairperson of IEBC by some politicians for purposes of influencing him are unfortunate, unfair and unsubstantiated to date," Ethekon stated.

The commission also challenged Gachagua to provide evidence, including the location of the property, sale and transfer documents, payment receipts and details of the parties involved, and submit them to the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission for investigation.

The electoral body also dismissed claims of improper staff changes, saying deployment and redeployment of employees was part of its normal administrative functions and was guided by its human resource policies and public service regulations.

"The Commission complies with its Human Resource policies, guidelines and other relevant instruments under the larger public service when engaging employees," the statement read in part.

It further denied allegations of malpractice against the chairperson and vice-chairperson, describing them as fabricated claims intended to damage the reputation of the commissioners and the commission.

Magarini by-election

On the Magarini by-election, IEBC said the poll was conducted in a free, fair and credible manner and was not challenged through an election petition. The commission added that it had successfully conducted several by-elections and was prepared to oversee the 2027 General Election.

At the same time, IEBC also defended its procurement process for election technology and ballot papers, saying all tenders were being conducted in accordance with Chapter 12 of the Constitution and the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act, 2015.

"Two key tenders, one for the Integrated Elections Management System, hardware and accessories, and another for ballot papers and other election materials, have temporarily been halted following a request for review filed before the Public Procurement Administrative Review Board," IEBC stated.

According to IEBC, documents for the technology tender were uploaded on its website and the Public Procurement Information Portal on August 11, 2026.

The commission said the technical specifications were generic and performance-based and open to all qualified suppliers. It stressed that the procurement process was still at its initial stages and that no company had been awarded the tender.

Voter register protected

The commission also dismissed claims that voter registration data could be manipulated or shared with external parties, insisting that the Register of Voters remained under its exclusive custody.

"Voter registration involves several stages, including in-person registration, verification of identity, collection of biometric and biographical data, transmission to a central database and automated biometric deduplication," IEBC added.

Flagged records are subjected to data cleaning, validation and adjudication before valid records are incorporated into the register.

The register will subsequently undergo a 30-day biometric verification exercise, followed by an independent audit before it is finalised and certified for use in an election.

IEBC said allegations of bribery, predetermined tender awards and voter suppression were false and potentially harmful to public confidence in the electoral process.

World.title: Ruto hands Sh2.6bn to Mau Forest evictees
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto also announced the lifting pf the caveat that had been placed on land bordering the Mau Forest. [PCS]

President William Ruto has announced the payment of Sh2.6 billion to 13,000 families evicted from the Mau Forest in Narok six years ago, marking what he described as the closure of a long chapter.

Each beneficiary received Sh200,000 through M-Pesa to help them resettle and rebuild their lives away from the water tower.

Speaking at Sogoo in Narok South Constituency on Wednesday, during the final day of his two-day tour of Narok County, Ruto said the Government had taken steps to address the longstanding Mau Forest resettlement problem.

He noted that in 2023, the Government gave Sh300,000 each to 2,000 families living in tents in the Mau Forest to enable them to leave the water tower and purchase land elsewhere.

“We are today officially closing the long and painful chapter of people who were removed from the Mau Forest, which the County Government of Narok will now manage,” Ruto said.

The President criticised politicians who, he said, had continued to politicise the Mau Forest issue without providing lasting solutions.

“Many politicians have talked of the Mau question, but I talked of the Mau answer. This is why we are here today closing this chapter,” he said.

Ruto also announced that the Government had purchased 5,800 acres of land to settle families who have been living as squatters on property previously owned by the family of former Provincial Commissioner Isaiah Cheluget.

“We are processing title deeds of the people living on the land after buying the Cheluget farm,” he said.

Construction of Johanna Ng'eno University

The President also announced the allocation of Sh1.2 billion for the construction of Johanna Ng’eno University in Emurua Dikirr Constituency.

Speaking during the laying of the foundation stone, Ruto said the institution would fulfil a pledge to residents while expanding access to higher education for students from across the country.

“You told me, as residents of Emurua Dikirr, that you want a university. Today, I have brought KSh1.2 billion to construct the university that will be named after our brother Johana Ng'eno,” he said.

He said the university would create employment opportunities and attract new investments to the region.

At the same time, Ruto maintained that his administration had fulfilled at least 80 per cent of the pledges contained in its 2022 campaign manifesto.

“Kenyans will elect leaders based on their development record. Sloganeering will not make Kenyans vote for them. They have a long way to go,” he said.

The President further launched the construction of the 18-kilometre Mogondo-Cheramgoi-Mogor-Soit road in Emurua Dikirr, saying the project would improve connectivity and unlock economic opportunities in the region.

“This new road will strengthen connectivity and unlock greater economic opportunities in the region,” Ruto said.

World.title: Gachagua to Duale: You don't own pastoralists
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

DCP leader Rigathi Gachagua and delegates from Isiolo and Marsabit at Wamunyoro, Nyeri County on August 25, 2026. [Ali Abdi, Standard]

Democracy for Citizen Party (DCP) Leader Rigathi Gachagua has accused Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale of allegedly doing nothing for pastoralist communities in the country.

Mr Gachagua said Duale, while being the only CS from northern Kenya and claiming to be the spokesperson of the group, had instead been a liability to pastoralists.

“You, the Borana who are here, along with the Turkana and Somali, are all complaining like other Kenyans. You suffer from runaway insecurity and widespread underdevelopment. We must join hands to vote out this rogue government (in next year's general election),” the former Deputy President told a delegation of grassroots leaders and residents from Isiolo and Marsabit who paid him a courtesy call at his Wamunyoro rural home in Nyeri.

“Duale thinks that the pastoralists are his property, his children or servants. What has he done for the people of Isiolo and Marsabit? (He has) only rhetoric, shouting pastoralists everywhere, every day,” he said.

Gachagua questioned how Duale would be able to marshal ‘millions’ of votes for President Ruto in the 2027 General Elections while he (Duale) could only raise 7,000 votes for the UDA presidential candidate in the 2022 polls in his Garissa Township Constituency backyard.

Despite his little contribution to the Kenya Kwanza administration's victory, Gachagua said Duale was appointed as the only CS from northern Kenya but had ended up doing nothing for the region and pastoralist communities.

“He only gave him (Ruto) 7,000 votes in Garissa Township. It's Central Kenya that propelled this government,” Gachagua told the gathering.

“Duale was appointed CS and he has nothing to show apart from empty words, going round shouting (the name of) pastoralists, and you (the pastoralists) are suffering. If you love them, then why are their livestock stolen every day?” He asked the CS.

“These pastoralists are killed every day and their cows and goats stolen. What have you done for them and you are in the government?” Gachagua posed.

The Opposition leader claimed that the government was ill-prepared for the heavily forecasted El Niño rainfall, pointing out that those living in flood-prone areas like the Tana Delta and Garissa are exposed to danger.

“Now, going into El Niño, what plan has been put in place to save people from death as a result of floods and how livestock will survive?” he asked the State.

During the event, Gachagua revealed that Yusuf Huka Jillo from Isiolo would represent Upper Eastern at the DCP secretariat and serve as a member of the National Executive Committee (NEC) in an acting capacity.

Gachagua said the mountain was now complete, with Isiolo and Marsabit forming Mt Kenya North.

The locals alleged that the Health CS was interfering in Isiolo County politics, with elder Hussein Jama claiming that Duale and the Office of the DCI were shielding a section of leaders accused of corruption and criminal activities.

Speakers claimed that there was massive corruption at the local lands registry office, while Mr Jillo faulted the State for the slow pace of registration of community land in Isiolo.

Jama said Isiolo International Airport, which was constructed during the administration of President Kibaki to help in the export of miraa and horticultural goods from the Mt Kenya region and livestock products, mainly meat and hides, lies idle because the expansion of the runway from 1.5 metres to 3 metres had not been done.

In response, Gachagua said the airport was meant to create employment and wealth, but the Kenya Kwanza administration had instead left it in ruin deliberately, claiming the move was aimed at sabotaging the economy of Mt Kenya and pastoralists’ economies.

“What was the good about destroying the Imenti forest to construct an airstrip for an individual while there is an international airport meant partly to serve the entire region just a few kilometres from Meru town?” Asked the DCP leader.

World.title: Relief for schools as government releases Sh18.5b capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Education CS Julius Ogamba. [File, Standard]

The government has released Sh18.5 billion in capitation to support operations in public basic education institutions during the third term of 2026, as schools reopened across the country on Monday.

Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba said the funds have already been released and will support learners in pre-primary, primary, junior and senior schools.

The allocation is intended to facilitate smooth school operations and ensure learning activities continue without disruption.

The Sh18.5 billion has been distributed across three major capitation programmes, with Free Day Secondary Education (FDSE) allocated Sh10.963 billion, accounting for the biggest portion of the Term Three capitation.

The money will support operations in public day and secondary schools and comes as institutions prepare learners for a busy academic term.

Free Day Junior School Education has received Sh6.1 billion, to support learners in the second tier of basic education and help institutions meet operational requirements as the Competency-Based Education system continues to expand.

Meanwhile, Free Primary Education has been allocated Sh1.4 billion to support learning in public primary schools.

The funds come as a relief to school heads who had raised concerns on the insufficient funds disbursed to schools this year.

However, Ogamba said the disbursement demonstrates the Government's commitment to ensuring that learners have access to free and compulsory basic education as provided for under Article 53(1)(b) of the Constitution.

“The Government affirms its commitment to fulfil its duty to learners and educational institutions,” said the CS.

Ogamba also warned school heads and principals against misuse of the funds, directing them to ensure the money is spent prudently and for the benefit of learners.

School administrators have further been cautioned against imposing unauthorised levies on parents and learners.

Ogamba said the Ministry would take firm action against institutions found to have misappropriated public resources or imposed illegal charges.

“We will deal firmly with any verified cases of misappropriation of resources and the imposition of unauthorised levies,” he said.

The warning comes as schools reopen for the third term, a period that is expected to be particularly demanding for institutions and learners because of the academic activities and assessments scheduled for the school calendar.

The Ministry has maintained that capitation is meant to ease the financial burden on families and enable schools to provide essential services without passing prohibited costs to parents.

Ogamba reiterated that school administrators must remain accountable for the public funds entrusted to them, warning that verified cases of misuse will attract action from the Ministry.

The Government has also reaffirmed that every child is entitled to free and compulsory basic education, placing the responsibility on education officials and school managers to ensure capitation achieves its intended purpose.

World.title: After King Harald V’s death, what comes next for Norway’s scandal-prone royals?
World.content:
The death of a monarch can boost national unity, and support for the crown.

Norway’s new King Haakon VIII will be hoping that sentiment rings true following the death of his father, King Harald who died Friday after 35 years on the throne, marking the latest blow for a family reeling from scandal.

The royal clan was thrust into the global spotlight earlier this year, when Queen Consort Mette-Marit, Haakon’s wife of 25 years, made headlines for her past association with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, while her non-royal son from a previous relationship stood trial for rape.

The succession of scandals sparked an open discussion in the country about her suitability to the role of Queen, with some experts even laying out possible options for her withdrawal from royal duties.

But past criticism seems to have softened of late. Instead, the death of Harald V, who was Europe’s oldest reigning monarch, could potentially mobilize a fresh wave of support and empathy for the clan, experts now suggest.

An official portrait of King Haakon VIII of Norway, who thanked the Norwegian public on Friday for their compassion following the death of his father. The Royal House of Norway

“Maybe people will remember the Epstein scandal, but I think maybe the worst will fade away,” Kjetil Alstadheim, the political editor at Norway’s influential newspaper Aftenposten, told CNN.

The late King’s death could also contribute to “helping the new King and Queen into their roles and their positions because of how people will gather around the institution and the family,” Alstadheim said.

Or as Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre put it on Friday after the news broke, “a whole nation is in mourning.”

Harald’s death was officially announced at an extraordinary Council of State meeting at Norway’s Royal Palace on Friday, as the full title of the new King was formally presented. Haakon chose to keep the personal motto “All for Norway.”

In his first comments following the death of his father, Haakon thanked the Norwegian people for their “support and compassion for the Royal Family during this time.”

People gather to pay their respects outside the Royal Palace in Oslo on Friday following Harald’s death, as the government declares a period of national mourning. Dylan Martinez/Reuters

Haakon, 53, previously reflected on the power of succession to boost a sense of unity when speaking about the death of his grandfather.

“It made an impression on me,” Haakon told NRK, Norway’s public broadcaster, in 2023. “It did something, with the understanding of how this was going to be for me, and it was also a clear expression that people were happy with my grandfather and the institution.”

“There was a change in my life” at that moment, he said.

Controversial union

Haakon met Mette-Marit in the late 1990s, and the pair married in 2001 at Oslo Cathedral in front of 800 guests and a TV audience of millions.

At the time, Mette-Marit’s openness about what she described as a “wild life” in her youth was well-received, particularly among younger Norwegians.

“It mobilized the younger generations who felt this was a modern monarchy, and they could identify with that,” Alstadheim previously told CNN. “She managed to build trust and be respected.”

Then-Crown Prince Haakon and Crown Princess Mette-Marit wave at well-wishers from the balcony of the Royal Palace after their wedding in Oslo in 2001. Jerry Lampen/Reuters

But others felt she was an unconventional addition to one of Europe’s oldest royal houses as a single mother and given her reputation for partying.

Speaking about the early days of their relationship, Haakon described Mette-Marit as “confident and worldly.”

“You notice when Mette enters a room,” Haakon told NRK. “The fact that she had a young child really only told me that she wasn’t afraid to take on commitment and responsibility.”

A troubled stepson

That young child would years later spark a major PR crisis for the royal family. In June, Marius Borg Høiby, 29, was sentenced to four years in prison after being found guilty of rape and domestic violence after a seven-week trial that further tarnished the family’s reputation.

Høiby pleaded not guilty to the most severe accusations against him, including those of rape, while admitting to some lesser charges. He is currently under house arrest at Norway’s Skaugum royal estate as he awaits a court decision about whether an appeal will be considered, his lawyer Petar Sekulic told CNN.

Around the same time as Høiby’s trial began, a second scandal erupted, this time implicating Mette-Marit herself.

Marius Borg Høiby, the son of Norway’s new Queen Consort Mette-Marit who was found guilty of rape earlier this year, in Oslo, Norway in 2022. Hakon Mosvold Larsen/NTB/AFP/Getty Images

The Epstein files revealed that she had maintained extensive correspondence with the disgraced financier years after he had pleaded guilty to soliciting sex from a minor. She later expressed regret over the association, saying it did not “represent the person I want to be.”

Royal historian Ed Owens said that as a result, the royal house had no doubt been brought into a “degree of disrepute,” with the family facing a “difficult moment ahead of them in terms of the succession.”

One concern was the family’s “reduced capacity” due to a “lack of manpower,” Alstadheim said, referring to its severe shortage of working royals.

It was announced earlier this year that Mette-Marit would temporarily step back from royal duties to undergo a lung transplant after she was diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, a chronic progressive lung disease with a poor prognosis, in 2018.

But her absence has “put things into perspective for many people,” said Tove Taalesen, a royal correspondent for news outlet Nettavisen.

“It doesn’t erase what happened, and it shouldn’t. But I believe there is more sympathy for her now,” she told CNN. “I am more interested now in who Mette-Marit will be, after everything she has been through, than in continuing to punish her for mistakes she has already acknowledged.”

Despite the challenges ahead, the royal commentators agree this moment could be unifying for the country, and its support for the monarchy, with Owens calling it a “re-energising of national identity.”

‘A solid foundation’

Haakon, a more energetic King than most European royal houses can lay claim to with a passion for the outdoors, takes the helm of a monarchy that still enjoys substantial support among the public, even if the latest scandals have taken their toll.

A poll in February, during Høiby’s trial, showed its popularity dropped to a record low, but has since recovered. Debates over abolishing or scaling back the institution, which occasionally flare up in the United Kingdom and other nations, are rare in Norway.

It is Haakon’s natural ability to, as Alstadheim puts it, be “close to the people” that brings hope for the monarchy’s future, and its ability to modernize with the times.

King Harald and Queen Sonja together with then-Crown Prince Haakon, Princess Ingrid Alexandra and then-Crown Princess Mette-Marit pose for a Christmas photo in Oslo, Norway, in December, 2024. Stian Lysberg Solum/NTB/Reuters

In 2023, Haakon said he often gets asked what he would have done if he wasn’t a royal. “I say I would have been a pro surfer on the World Tour,” he told NRK.

The new King also holds a bachelor’s degree in political science from the University of California at Berkeley, and credits his experience there with introducing him to people from different backgrounds.

“The Norwegian royal family has managed to modernize gradually,” Alstadheim said. “Building on the popularity of King Harald, Haakon will have a solid foundation for his reign.”

Taalesen agreed. “I believe in him. And I believe the Norwegian monarchy will survive King Harald. That is, after all, the whole idea of a monarchy: the person changes, but the institution continues,” she added.

The new King and Queen Consort have two children together, and the elder – Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, 22 – now becomes heir to Norway’s throne.

World.title: Save the Children plans for rebuilding lost infrastructure in Nepal
World.content:
Save the Children is focusing on basic needs as it serves Nepal’s badly-hit Nuwakot district — distributing food, water, diapers and toothbrushes.

“Everywhere pretty much in the affected area, the water sources are contaminated,” said Amy Lefevre of Save the Children, who is in Nepal. “Nobody should really be bathing in that water, let alone drinking that water.”

The aid group is viewing their work as a long-haul relief operation, planning for the rebuilding process, she said.

“Once the story’s over, everybody’s going to fly out,” said Lefevre. “The people who are left here are the communities whose homes have been washed away.”

“The next step will be, ‘I need a job, I need to rebuild my life, I need a livelihood,’” Lefevre said.

The organization has already begun speaking with local authorities.

“Children need to be back in school,” she said. “They need to be in education again.”

As survivors still process the disaster, psychosocial counselors have been assigned to child-friendly spaces in the organization’s temporary shelters.

“I think it’s really hard to comprehend how children are going to process this trauma and this event that they’ve lived through,” she reflected.

World.title: This university built an AI curriculum before ChatGPT. Now it wants to help other schools do the same
World.content:
Ethan Pecora has a team of 15 specialized artificial intelligence agents assisting him with his work. That includes helping to manage his calendar and various tasks related to the mental wellness app he’s building.

Also, his schoolwork.

Pecora’s setup may sound like that of a tech startup. But he’s actually a senior at the University of Florida, studying business and communications.

“Some people call it a second brain,” he told CNN about his swarm of AI agents, but he said he doesn’t like that term because “it seems a little dystopian.”

The University of Florida has been incorporating AI into its curriculum since 2022, before ChatGPT’s arrival, thanks in part to investments from chipmaking giant Nvidia.

The university said it aims to teach students how to apply the tech across all disciplines professionally and in their coursework, not just technical ones. Students have used AI to train chatbots to assist them on exams and catalogue dance moves to help the dancers protect their intellectual property.

The school now offers more than 200 AI courses, such as on AI basics and ethics, for any student or faculty member regardless of their technical knowledge. It also has AI certificates for specific disciplines, like hospitality and public health.

Ethan Pecora at the University of Florida’s AI2 Center in August 2026. Courtesy University of Florida

“We don’t think it’s appropriate or useful to relegate (AI education) to the computer science department or the College of Engineering,” said Joseph Glover, provost of the University of Florida. “Because then whenever you want to do something (with AI), you have to have an engineer sitting next to you.”

There is a nuanced and polarizing debate over AI’s impact on education and early-stage careers. Students and faculty grapple with a world in which jobs could look fundamentally different because of a rapidly evolving technology. Those concerns exist at the University of Florida, too, where some students have pushed back on the technology despite the school’s AI-forward approach, and reports of academic misconduct involving AI are starting to emerge.

One way the school hopes to address those concerns is through an international summit, where it hosts panels about AI’s role in education and shares its blueprint with other schools. Nearly 500 people from 10 countries and 40 US states attended the conference in 2026.

“Pretty soon AI is going to become such as the internet. It’s just a technology,” said Andrea Ramirez Salgado, a professor in the department of engineering who helped develop the university’s AI curriculum. “But if you really want to lead and drive that innovation, you need to be able to understand what is under the hood.”

A boost from the world’s most valuable company

The University of Florida had an early advantage: its close ties to Chris Malachowsky, cofounder of Nvidia, the $5 trillion juggernaut that’s been at the center of the AI boom.

Malachowsky graduated from the university in 1980 and sits on its Foundation Board, which supports the school through various investment and advocacy efforts.

Back in 2018, he told the University of Florida’s Board of Trustees that the school should start building a strategy around AI. Then in 2019, a meeting between Malachowsky and Glover set the stage for the program’s founding.

University of Florida provost Joseph Glover (left) and Nvidia cofounder Chris Malachowsky (right) discuss AI’s impact on education at the university’s A12 Summit on March 30, 2026. Courtesy University of Florida

The school wanted Malachowsky to invest in a new engineering program. But the Nvidia cofounder had another idea: He asked the provost what the school would do with an AI supercomputer – a high-performance computer often used for research purposes.

“And his response, and I’m telling you with almost no hesitation was, ‘I don’t know, I think I’ll teach AI across the curriculum,’” Malachowsky told CNN.

In addition to the supercomputer, called the HiPerGator, the school hired 100 new faculty members to help incorporate AI across all of its 16 colleges. A total of $95 million was invested to start the program from Nvidia, Malachowsky, the University of Florida and the state.

A student uses AI for research in the athletics department on June 10, 2025. Courtesy University of Florida

Employers are increasingly looking for AI experience. More than one third of entry-level jobs listed AI skills as a requirement, the National Association of Colleges and Employers said in a spring 2026 report. That’s up almost three-fold compared to last year.

Even if they didn’t widely incorporate AI into their curriculum, academic institutions have long paid attention to the technology. Carnegie Mellon University started offering an AI undergraduate degree in 2018. And the Milwaukee School of Engineering announced a new academic center aimed at boosting AI education in 2017.

Unlike the University of Florida, “there are more institutions that are just trying to educate their faculty about, ‘What is AI?’ and how to use it,” said Kelvin Bentley, director of community practice on micro credentials at the National Association of Higher Education Systems.

‘Easier to get a ‘C,’ harder to get an AI’

Emma MacKie, an assistant professor in the University of Florida’s department of geological sciences, was one of the faculty members hired to jumpstart its efforts.

She and her students use AI and other tools to simulate a landscape by crunching huge amounts of data and physical models. This past year, they mapped the topography beneath sheets of ice in Antarctica.

One challenge is keeping up with tech that is always evolving. In one instance, a lab activity MacKie prepared was dysfunctional by the time she taught it in class, she said.

Professor Emma MacKie conducting field work in Antarctica in March 2022. Courtesy University of Florida

“It was definitely an ‘oh crap’ moment,” she said. “I’m in front of my class, and my code doesn’t work.”

Pecora also said not all classes are as useful as they could be. A class about AI in business that he took in 2024 taught students how to automate some tasks by writing code. But he said it felt more like a crash course on the coding language Python than how to apply AI.

AI can also change how assignments are evaluated. MacKie allows her students to use AI freely but now grades term papers based on factors like originality and “the maturity of the ideas.”

“It’s easier to get a ‘C’ on that assignment, but more difficult to get an ‘A,’” she said.

Student worries about AI

Early concerns about AI in education mostly focused on how it could be used for cheating. But more existential worries have since surfaced, such as whether students are being adequately prepared and the tech’s impact on career opportunities.

Graduates at the University of Arizona and University of Central Florida booed mentions of AI during commencement speeches last spring. Forty percent of the more than 1,000 students from 203 institutions surveyed by education news website Inside Higher Education in May said they were worried that AI is reducing their ability to think independently.

Only 7% of students said they were “all in” and “genuinely excited” about AI’s potential.

“I think there are a lot of students who… they feel very unsettled by AI,” said MacKie. “They don’t like what it’s doing to their career prospects and have very little faith in the outputs, which I think is healthy.”

Malachowsky Hall, named after University of Florida alumnus and co-founder of Nvidia Corp. Chris Malachowsky, at the University of Florida in Gainesville, Florida, on February 20, 2024. Michelle Bruzzese/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Even at the University of Florida, there are concerns. One professor stopped assigning homework altogether and based grades solely on in-class exams to prevent AI usage, said Tristan Robbins, a rising senior studying sports management, statistics and economics at the University of Florida.

Academic misconduct reports mentioning AI increased from zero in fall 2021 to 66 as of April 2025, according to public records reported by The Independent Florida Alligator this year. (A spokesperson for the university said that it promotes the responsible use of AI and that students must “strictly comply with the instructions of their course instructor, faculty advisor or other academic supervisor” when using AI for academic purposes).

Additionally, Salgado said students are worried about AI’s environmental impact and say they feel less ownership over their work.

Nvidia’s Malachowsky acknowledged that these questions are difficult to solve. But turning away from the technology, he said, is a bigger mistake.

“I can’t promise that AI literacy and adopting this broadly is the answer,” he said. “But I do feel really strongly that doing nothing, or ignoring it, or trying to put it back in the can, is a kiss of death. There is no positive outcome that comes from that.”

World.title: Trump officials are losing the troll war, too
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, who walked away from US trade talks last week due to what he said was American intransigence, now wants to get negotiations started again.

But he suggested Tuesday the Americans are too busy trolling.

“When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said, lamenting “It’s not constructive. But that’s their democracy.”

What Carney means is that rather than making any visible efforts to end the trade war with Canada, American leaders are trying — and sometimes failing — to own the Canucks. Meanwhile, the 50% tariffs the US imposed on a host of Canadian goods and dollar-for-dollar response tariffs from Canada continue.

Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks to journalists as he arrives at the Office of the Prime Minister and Privy Council in Ottawa, Canada, on Tuesday. Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/AP

Carney didn’t mention that Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also trolled Trump, and a Canadian city council is considering renaming a street currently named for Trump with a deliberately taunting moniker. But much of the new material from top officials is coming from the US.

When the White House posted an image of a bald eagle appearing to hold down a Canada goose — something it has posted before — Canadians pointed out photos showing the same goose getting the better end of the fight.

After Trump renamed Lake Ontario, he then called Apple to make sure the change showed up on maps. It does in the US, but not in Canada. And interest surged in Mapquest in App stores after it refused to change the name of Lake Ontario for US users.

While Trump has focused on nomenclature, his aides have been belittling the Canadian military.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada is “a country that doesn’t have a military.” That’s not true, obviously. Canadians have fought and died alongside American allies in multiple wars.

Insults do not seem to come as naturally to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who does not have a background in reality TV or at Fox News. But Bessent tried to land one on the neighbors to the North.

“I mean, we’re not at war with Canada. How are we going to be at war with Canada? They’re going to take their two set submarines from the Edmonton Mall and sic them on us,” Bessent said Monday during an interview on CNBC ahead of a G20 finance meeting he is hosting in Asheville, North Carolina.

Apparently there used to be a submarine attraction at a mall in Edmonton. Sick burn, Scott!

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks during a fireside chat during the 2026 G20 Financial meetings in Asheville, North Carolina, on Tuesday. Melissa Sue Gerrits/Getty Images

But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who prefers to be called secretary of war, was clearly trying to be mean Monday on X, when he posted a photo of two women in Canadian military uniforms.

He included a Canadian flag emoji and added, “(this is real).”

Maybe he was trying to say something about how the Canadian military is not as macho as he’s tried to make the US military.

In any event, at least one of the women in the photo may have been part of a cadet program for young Canadians. It is arguably poor form for a high-ranking US official to be trying to make fun of a young Canadian, particularly one who may be considering a move into public service. Canadians remain American military allies. They responded when the US was attacked after 9/11.

Hegseth has sometimes been on the other side of internet trolling, for example, his form doing pull-ups and bench presses in the workout videos he frequently posts have been mocked online. That’s also rather harsh, since a man deep in his 40s who can do any number of pull-ups should be celebrated.

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth participates in morning physical training with US service members in Coronado Beach, California, on October 18, 2025. Staff Sgt. Madelyn Keech/Department of Defense

But Hegseth doing pull-ups won’t help to end the war in Iran, which has gone months longer than Trump initially promised and warped the world economy.

Pull-ups also aren’t going to help rebuild the upper ranks of the Army. The same day Hegseth was trolling the Canadian youth, Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, just before resigning, apparently went to the White House and told Trump that Hegseth’s leadership had left the Army with key leadership positions unfilled. Some of Hegseth’s picks for top generals may not have the bipartisan support to get confirmed.

And he should also know better than to criticize cadets interested in the military. The US has been able to meet recruiting goals the past two years in part because of pre-enlistment programs meant to get American recruits in shape to pass fitness tests.

But Hegseth isn’t about to sanitize his insults. He leans into criticism of diversity efforts. Appearing at an event in support of a Republican Congressman at the Iowa State Fair over the weekend, Hegseth used an epithet for transgender people, whom he has tried to boot from the military.

And yes, when a partisan US official makes an appearance at the Iowa State Fair it often means they’re considering a run for president. Hegseth says he’s not.

All of these men have arguably better things to do than troll Canada. Hegseth has a war the US has yet to win. Bessent could spend some more time on the squirrely bond market, Duffy could be focused on gas prices, say.

If the trolling was meant to help build support for the US in the trade war, they have so far failed.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found a majority of Americans oppose both renaming Lake Ontario and the imposition of tariffs on Canada.

This headline has been updated.

World.title: Egypt’s exports to China see 199.8% jump
World.content:
The Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics (CAPMAS) revealed a significant surge in Egyptian exports to China, reaching 199.8 percent during the first half of 2026.

This brought bilateral trade between the two countries to US$11.3 billion, despite the continued widening trade deficit in favor of China, whose imports were primarily concentrated in the electrical machinery and automotive sectors.

Whopping 199.8 Percent Jump

CAPMAS issued a report reviewing economic relations between Egypt and China, revealing that the value of Egyptian exports to China rose to $ 840.8 million during the first half of 2026, compared to $ 280.5 million during the same period in 2025, representing a 199.8 percent increase.

The value of Egyptian imports from China reached $ 10.4 billion during the first half of 2026, compared to $ 9.1 billion during the same period in 2025, reflecting a 14.3 percent increase.

This indicates that the value of trade exchange between the two countries will increase to $ 11.3 billion during the first half of 2026, compared to $9.3 billion during the same period in 2025, an increase of 21.5 percent.

Egypt’s Top Exports

The most important commodity groups exported by Egypt to China during the first half of 2026 were:

Fuels, mineral oils, and their distillation products, valued at $ 494 million

Vegetables and fruits ($150.6 million)

Cotton and vegetable textile fibers ($ 76.4 million)

Natural calcium phosphate ($ 31 million) organic and inorganic chemical products ($ 21 million).

Cars Lead Imports

The most important commodity groups imported by Egypt from China during the first half of 2026 were:

Machinery and electrical and mechanical appliances ($4.1 billion)

Cars, tractors, and bicycles ($1.2 billion)

Iron and steel and their products ($930.7 million)

Plastics and their products ($524 million)

Organic and inorganic chemical products ($423.7 million).

Remittances from Egyptian in China

Remittances from Egyptians working in China reached $23.3 million during the 2024/2025 fiscal year, compared to $19.5 million during the 2023/2024 fiscal year. Meanwhile, remittances from Chinese workers in Egypt amounted to $3.5 million during the 2024/2025 fiscal year, compared to $3.1 million during the 2023/2024 fiscal year.

Egypt’s population was recorded at 109.4 million in August 2026, while China’s population was 1.4 billion during the same period.

The number of Egyptians residing in the People’s Republic of China, according to the embassy’s estimates, reached 8,000 by the end of 2024.

World.title: Tehran still seeks negotiated solution with Washington, says Iranian President
World.content:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian announced Monday that Tehran still seeks a negotiated solution to the conflict with the US, following renewed strikes between both countries.

Pezeshkian added, during his meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit Kyrgyzstan that “the continuation of the war is not in anyone’s interest.

“Dialogue and cooperation are the way to resolve the existing problems,” he emphasized.

This comes after Pezeshkian said, before departing Tehran for Kyrgyzstan, that “Iran is not seeking war, and this is a clear message we have made to the world until now.”

“But we will not stand idly by in the face of any aggression, and we will respond decisively to the aggressors,” considering that “instability and turmoil in the region are not in the interest of any country and will present challenges for everyone.”

In the first direct military escalation between Washington and Tehran in weeks, Iran announced it had targeted US forces in Jordan and the UAE in retaliation for US airstrikes targeting the Iranian island of Larak.

World.title: US Federal Trade Commission to sue Amazon for deceiving advertisers: Wall Street Journal
World.content:
The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday – citing officials at the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) – that the FTC plans to file a lawsuit against Amazon, accusing it of manipulating advertising prices on its e-commerce platform.

Amazon shares fell 2.8 percent on Monday following the Wall Street Journal report.

According to the report, the commission plans to file a lawsuit in federal court in Seattle, alleging that Amazon manipulated the prices companies paid for advertising on its platform over a seven-year period.

More than 20 state attorneys general from both parties are expected to join the case.

World.title: Sisi: Egypt-China relations become model of partnership
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi sent a welcoming message to the event held in Cairo on Tuesday, September 1, 2026, to mark the 70th anniversary of the establishment of Egyptian-Chinese diplomatic relations.

The event was jointly organized by the State Ministry of Information and China Media Group.In his message, read by Minister of State for Information Diaa Rashwan at the opening of the ceremony, al-Sisi warmly welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to Egypt, describing him as a dear guest and a close friend of the Egyptian people.

Sisi greeted the Egyptian and Chinese peoples on the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the diplomatic relations between the two countries.

He said that he and President Xi have been working for more than 12 years to strengthen the bonds of friendship between Egypt and China, with their joint efforts helping elevate bilateral relations to the level of a comprehensive strategic partnership.He noted that the partnership has contributed to increased trade, investment, tourism flows and people-to-people exchanges, as well as scientific and cultural missions, particularly among Egyptian and Chinese youths.

Sisi said that over seven decades, Egypt-China relations have developed into a model of partnership based on mutual respect, solidarity and shared interests.

The two countries also promote cooperation among nations; uphold the principles of truth, justice and equality; and work toward comprehensive development and a just peace, he added.

Welcoming Xi to his second home Egypt, Sisi expressed hope for a new phase of more advanced relations, with the two countries working together in a wider range of fields to achieve mutual benefit and greater prosperity and progress for their peoples, as well as development and peace for the world.

World.title: BREAKING:Tweh Out as Justice Minister Amid Drug Scandal Fallout, Reassigned to Undisclosed Government Post
World.content:
Monrovia — September 2, 2026

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. has removed Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh as Minister of Justice and Attorney General, replacing him with Cllr. Betty M. Lamin-Blamo, according to a release issued Wednesday by the Executive Mansion’s Office of the Presidential Press Secretary. Outgoing Solicitor General Augustine Fayiah is also being moved, alongside Tweh, to other levels of government, the statement said. Cllr. Abrahim Boimah Sillah, Sr. has been named the new Solicitor General.

The Mansion’s announcement gave no reason for the shake-up, describing it only as part of a broader round of appointments touching the Ministries of Justice, Gender, Children and Social Protection, and Local Government, along with the PPCC and the National Transit Authority. But the reassignment lands at the end of a turbulent stretch for Tweh, whose tenure atop the Justice Ministry became entangled in Liberia’s sprawling narcotics-trafficking investigations.

Background: A Minister Under Pressure

Tweh spent much of 2026 as the government’s public face in the fight against drug trafficking, overseeing a period that produced some of Liberia’s largest-ever narcotics seizures — including roughly 237 kilograms of cocaine intercepted at Roberts International Airport and a nearly four-ton cocaine find in Duazon, Margibi County, which authorities called the largest in the country’s history. He repeatedly pledged that no one — regardless of wealth or political connection — would be shielded from prosecution if credible evidence existed.

But as the investigations widened to touch senior political figures, including a case alleging former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor’s connection to a $317 million drug case, scrutiny increasingly turned on Tweh himself.

In late August, reports emerged that Tweh had “voluntarily” appeared before the Senate Committee on Defense, Security, Intelligence and Veterans Affairs over questions about a vehicle he received from Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman — a vehicle critics alleged was traceable to drug-cartel money tied to the same trafficking networks under investigation.

The Justice Ministry pushed back, framing the vehicle as an official assignment rather than a personal gift from Coleman.

Journalist Aaron Kollie had characterized Tweh’s Senate remarks as effectively a confession that Coleman gave him the car, a characterization the Ministry disputed.

Days later, as recently as Wednesday, allegations resurfaced directly linking Tweh to individuals connected with the $317 million case, with some accusing him of accepting gifts from suspected traffickers.

His special assistant, Atty. Siafa Bahn Kemokai, publicly defended Tweh’s character and integrity, arguing that unproven claims of wrongdoing should not be conflated with ordinary political disagreement.

Separately, civil society and press figures — including CENTAL’s Anderson Miamen and Senator Amara Konneh — had pressed for an independent panel to probe the broader drug crisis, a call Tweh resisted, arguing that ongoing prosecutions, backed by cooperation with the U.S. DEA, Homeland Security and FBI, should not be interrupted.

Whether Wednesday’s reassignment is connected to the vehicle controversy, the trafficking-linked allegations, or is part of a routine cabinet reshuffle has not been confirmed by the Executive Mansion.

The appointments, the Mansion said, are part of the President’s “ongoing efforts to strengthen key institutions of Government,” and nominees requiring Senate confirmation will go through that process.

World.title: Liberia: Rep. Fahnbulleh Hails Pres. Boakai’s Support After Talks on Bong’s District Seven Development Priorities
World.content:
MONROVIA — Bong County District Seven Representative Foday Fahnbulleh has expressed excitement following a meeting Tuesday with President Joseph Nyuma Boakai at the Executive Mansion.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Rep. Fahnbulleh said the meeting provided him an opportunity to engage the President directly on issues he considers critical to the welfare of residents, particularly the participation of local contractors in development activities, the impact of concession operations on host communities and the need to protect the interests of citizens living in areas where major economic activities are taking place.

The lawmaker described the discussion as frank and productive, stressing that he went into the meeting with the concerns of his constituents at the center of his engagement with the President.

According to Rep. Fahnbulleh, one of the major issues he placed before President Boakai was the situation confronting local contractors in Fuamah and Sanoyea, where he said Liberian businesses should have greater opportunities to participate in development activities.

He argued that the presence of concessionaires and major development projects should result in opportunities for local businesses rather than leaving communities and Liberian entrepreneurs on the sidelines.

For Rep. Fahnbulleh, the question of local participation is directly connected to whether communities hosting major economic activities are actually benefiting from the resources and investments taking place within their areas.

He told the President that development must go beyond infrastructure and investment figures and translate into practical economic benefits for ordinary Liberians, including employment, business opportunities and improved livelihoods.

The Bong lawmaker also raised concerns about the relationship between concession operations and host communities, emphasizing the need for citizens’ rights to be protected while ensuring that communities receive meaningful benefits from activities carried out on their land and within their areas.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said he was encouraged by President Boakai’s response to the concerns, particularly the President’s acknowledgment of the issues raised and his stated willingness to support efforts aimed at protecting the rights and interests of affected communities.

The response, according to the representative, gave him renewed confidence that the concerns of Fuamah and Sanoyea could receive greater attention through continued engagement with the Executive Branch.

The meeting also provided an opportunity for Rep. Fahnbulleh to discuss an initiative he considers particularly important to the future of Bong County’s young population — the recently passed Bong Mines Vocational Training Institute Act.

The legislation, which was passed by the House of Representatives, seeks to establish a vocational training institution designed to provide young people with practical and marketable skills that can improve their chances of securing employment and becoming economically independent.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said he was particularly pleased with President Boakai’s expressed support for the initiative, describing the President’s position as an encouraging development for the county and its young people.

He said the President commended Bong County lawmakers for demonstrating leadership by supporting legislation intended to address the needs of citizens and complement the administration’s broader development agenda.

The representative said the President’s support was significant because the vocational training initiative could provide a direct response to the challenges of youth unemployment and the shortage of skilled workers.

Rep. Fahnbulleh believes the proposed institution could eventually help create a pool of trained Liberians capable of taking advantage of employment opportunities generated by mining, construction, agriculture, infrastructure and other economic activities.

He said the initiative could also create an avenue through which young people could acquire skills for self-employment, rather than depending exclusively on limited formal-sector jobs.

The lawmaker’s excitement following the meeting appeared to be tied not only to the President’s support for the vocational training legislation but also to what he described as a willingness by the Executive to work with Bong County lawmakers in addressing the concerns of their constituents.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said lawmakers have a responsibility to maintain direct communication with the Executive while remaining committed to representing the interests of their people.

He stressed that elected representatives must continue to raise citizens’ concerns, demand accountability and work with the government whenever such collaboration can produce concrete benefits for their constituents.

The District Seven representative said his engagement with President Boakai demonstrated the importance of constructive dialogue between the Legislature and Executive, particularly when national development policies intersect with local concerns.

He said he welcomed the President’s commitment to working with lawmakers and viewed the meeting as an opportunity to strengthen collaboration around development initiatives affecting Bong County.

Fahnbulleh also emphasized that his advocacy for local contractors is part of a broader effort to ensure that Liberians benefit directly from economic activities taking place in their communities.

He said local businesses should not merely observe development projects from the sidelines but should be positioned to participate in contracts, supply chains and other opportunities created by government and concession investments.

The lawmaker further maintained that host communities should have a meaningful stake in development taking place within their jurisdictions.

His position reflects a broader concern among communities across Liberia over the distribution of benefits associated with concession agreements and large-scale investments, particularly where local residents expect employment, contracts, infrastructure and other economic opportunities in return for hosting such operations.

Fahnbulleh said the concerns he presented to President Boakai were therefore aimed at ensuring that development reaches the grassroots and that communities such as those in Fuamah and Sanoyea are not excluded from the economic opportunities generated within their own areas.

He expressed optimism that the President’s acknowledgment of the concerns and support for the vocational training initiative could lead to further engagement and concrete action.

The lawmaker said he remains committed to working with the administration while continuing to serve as an advocate for the people of District Seven and the wider Bong County.

For Fahnbulleh, the meeting represented more than a routine engagement between a lawmaker and the President. He said it offered an opportunity to place local concerns directly before the national leadership and secure commitments around issues affecting communities, businesses and young people.

He welcomed what he described as the President’s readiness to partner with Bong County lawmakers, saying such cooperation could help advance development priorities while ensuring that the voices of local communities remain part of national decision-making.

Rep. Fahnbulleh said he left the engagement encouraged by the President’s response and determined to continue pushing for initiatives that create opportunities for young people, strengthen local businesses, protect citizens’ rights and ensure that development produces tangible benefits for the people of Bong County.

He said his commitment remains to keep the concerns of Fuamah, Sanoyea and the wider county at the center of his legislative advocacy while working with the Executive to turn those concerns into meaningful development outcomes.

World.title: Liberia Wraps Up Rwanda Study Mission on Proposed Peace and Reconciliation Museum
World.content:
KIGALI, RWANDA — Liberia has concluded the Rwanda phase of a high-level study mission designed to gather practical lessons for the establishment of the proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum.

The initiative is intended to preserve Liberia’s history, promote national healing and ensure that lessons from the country’s civil conflict are passed on to future generations.

The delegation, headed by Minister of State without Portfolio, Hon. Hadja Mamaka Bility, engaged with Rwandan institutions involved in reconciliation, historical preservation, archives, education and post-conflict recovery.

Supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the mission forms part of efforts to translate President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s vision for reconciliation and historical preservation into a lasting national institution.

Minister Bility said Liberia’s objective is to move reconciliation beyond speeches and discussions by establishing institutions capable of preserving the country’s experiences and helping future generations understand its past.

“This study tour is part of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s vision for national reconciliation, with the support of UNDP. We want to move Liberia beyond simply talking about reconciliation to building strong institutions that can preserve our experiences, tell our story, and pass the lessons of our past on to future generations,” Minister Bility said.

The initiative comes amid President Boakai’s broader reconciliation efforts, including his July 2025 public apology on behalf of the Liberian State to victims and families affected by the country’s civil conflict.

During the Rwanda phase, the Liberian delegation studied the country’s approaches to unity, reconciliation, citizenship education, community resilience and the preservation of historical memory.

The team visited and examined the Gacaca archives and their digitization, Rwanda’s National Archives, the Campaign Against Genocide Museum, the University of Rwanda’s Centre for Conflict Management, the Rwanda Peace Academy and the Mutobo Demobilisation and Reintegration Centre.

The engagements provided lessons on how Liberia could collect, authenticate, digitize and preserve photographs, films, documents, testimonies and other historical materials currently scattered across government institutions, private collections and archives within and outside the country.

The mission also underscored the need for a credible memorial institution to go beyond the construction of a museum building, with education, research, documentation, reconciliation and community engagement forming key components of its mandate.

UNDP Liberia Resident Representative, Amb. Aliou Mamadou Dia, said the initiative forms part of a broader effort to strengthen peacebuilding, reconciliation and national unity.

“UNDP is working with the Government of Liberia to support the establishment of a Peace and Reconciliation Museum as part of the President’s broader reconciliation agenda.

“This study mission gives us an opportunity to learn from the experiences of other countries, document lessons that can be adapted to Liberia, and engage partners who can support the Government in moving this vision forward,” Amb. Dia said.

Amb. Dia stressed that lasting peace requires Liberia to confront difficult issues from its past, pursue genuine reconciliation and strengthen accountability, while building an institution that preserves history, promotes healing and educates future generations.

As the Rwanda phase concluded, the leadership of Rwanda Cooperation emphasized experience-sharing and the prospects for continued technical partnership with Liberia.

The discussions identified potential areas of cooperation, including museum development and management, training for Liberian heritage professionals, preservation and digitization of historical records and testimonies, peace education and technical exchanges, including potential collaboration with Aegis Trust Rwanda.

The Liberian delegation will now proceed to South Africa to continue studying African experiences in national healing, peacebuilding, reconciliation and memorialization.

A central lesson emerging from the Rwanda experience is that Liberia cannot simply replicate another country’s model. Instead, it must develop an institution rooted in its own history and informed by the voices, photographs, documents and experiences of Liberians.

Such an institution, the mission emphasized, would help acknowledge the country’s past, educate new generations and contribute to preventing Liberia from returning to conflict.

World.title: Liberia: Security Tightens at RIA as Weah Returns Today
World.content:
Airport Restricts Access, Regulates Traffic as CDC Mobilizes Supporters for Former President

Monrovia — Security has been heightened at Roberts International Airport (RIA) ahead of the arrival of former President George Manneh Weah on Wednesday, with the Liberia Airport Authority (LAA) introducing special measures to manage the anticipated movement of passengers, supporters and dignitaries.

The LAA Aviation Security Department (ASD) said all well-wishers intending to welcome Weah must gather at the RIA Public School, while only designated supporters appointed by the former president’s organizing committee will be permitted beyond the designated point.

The measures are part of arrangements to ensure what airport authorities described as a smooth, secure and orderly arrival of the former president, who is expected to touch down at RIA later today.

In a public safety announcement issued for September 2, the Aviation Security Department advised passengers traveling through the airport to arrive earlier than their usual scheduled time to avoid delays.

The announcement also warned that vehicular and pedestrian traffic around the airport would be regulated by the Joint Security, with members of the public instructed to follow directions from security officers deployed to the area.

Despite the special arrangements, the LAA said normal airport operations would continue.

The heightened security follows a September 1 communication from LAA Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer Ernest R. Hughes to CDC National Chairman Janga Augustus Kowo, formally notifying the party of Weah’s scheduled arrival through RIA.

Hughes said stakeholders had been provided with Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to ensure the efficient coordination of operational, security, protocol, safety and facilitation arrangements associated with the former president’s arrival.

He urged all relevant agencies and service providers to take the necessary measures within their respective mandates to ensure a seamless and secure reception in line with established airport procedures and applicable regulations.

CDC Mobilizes for Weah

Meanwhile, the Coalition for Democratic Change (CDC) is mobilizing partisans and supporters to turn out in large numbers to welcome Weah, who remains the party’s political leader.

A special steering committee established to coordinate activities surrounding his arrival has also submitted a list of 20 persons to the Liberia Airport Authority for access to the airport to participate in his official reception.

The committee, chaired by former House Speaker Dr. Bhofal Chambers, said the designated individuals would help coordinate the reception, subject to all airport security and operational protocols.

The former president’s return comes after a series of engagements outside Liberia, including stops in Ghana and Nigeria.

In Ghana, Weah participated in a charity football match, while in Nigeria he served as keynote speaker at an annual event of the Nigerian Bar Association.

Return Amid Drug Case Fallout

Weah’s return also comes against the backdrop of a major drug trafficking and money laundering case involving his former Vice President, Jewel Howard Taylor.

Taylor, who served as vice president during Weah’s 2018–2024 administration, is facing prosecution in connection with the government’s investigation into the seizure of a cocaine consignment valued at approximately US$317 million.

Weah has publicly rejected the allegations against his former vice president, describing the charges as bogus and pledging his support for Taylor.

Her prosecution has generated intense political debate, with the CDC and other political actors raising questions about the government’s handling of the narcotics investigation.

With supporters expected to converge around the airport area, authorities are urging the public to comply with security instructions as they seek to balance the anticipated welcome with normal airport operations.

The LAA has appealed for the cooperation and understanding of passengers, well-wishers and other stakeholders, saying the measures are intended to ensure safety, security and an orderly reception.

World.title: One Woman, half a Billion Dollars: The Question Liberia’s Drug Investigation hasn’t Answered
World.content:
As former President George Weah touches down in Monrovia, the two record-breaking drug busts that started this saga — nearly half a billion dollars combined — have quietly gone still. A vessel authorities once chased across Liberian waters was recently brought ashore, and nobody in government has said a word about it since. Somewhere in that silence sits a question this newspaper thinks Liberia must ask out loud: is one former Vice President really the whole story?

By Rodney D. Sieh | [email protected]

Monrovia — As former President George Manneh Weah touches down in Monrovia Wednesday, the fate of his former Vice President, Jewel Howard-Taylor, lingers in a state of uncertainty, as the ruling Unity Party-led government worked through an audio recording and what it calls mountains of evidence tying the former First Lady to a litany of charges in the ongoing investigation into cartel-driven drug trafficking in Liberia. Weah’s arrival, months after he pledged from abroad to return home and “rally the CDC along with all well-meaning Liberians” against what he called a politically motivated prosecution, adds a charged political backdrop to a week already centered on his former running mate’s fate.

But there is a version of this story Liberians could be forgiven for believing, if all they did was follow the headlines of the last two weeks: that a former Vice President ran a cocaine empire more or less by herself, that she has been caught, and that the case is now simply a matter of scheduling hearings and arguing over a recorded phone call. It is a tidy version of events. It also happens to leave out most of what happened this summer, and nearly everyone else who was standing in the room when it did.

A Summer That Started with Two Busts, Not One

Long before anyone in Liberia was arguing about a Dubai hotel meeting or a foundation called Jewel Star Fish, the story began with customs officers and a number nobody wanted to believe: US$19.2 million in cocaine, seized at Roberts International Airport in June. It should have been the year’s biggest story on its own. Instead, it was a preview. Weeks later, authorities raided a stash house in Paynesville and pulled out somewhere between US$317 million and US$319 million in narcotics — an estimated 238 kilograms to nearly 4 metric tons, the largest seizure in Liberia’s history, and enough to make the June bust look, in hindsight, like a warning shot nobody heeded in time.

Add the two figures together, and Liberia is sitting on almost half a billion dollars in drugs that moved through, or nearly through, its ports and airport in the space of a single summer. That is the number that should anchor every conversation about this case. Instead, it has quietly receded behind a single name.

The Ship Nobody Talks About Anymore

Somewhere in between the two seizures sits a vessel that, for a few uncomfortable days in June, became the most-watched ship in West Africa: the IB Atlantic IV, which sat off Liberia’s coast for the better part of a week while the government worked out what to do about it, before slipping away from patrol boats that were, by multiple accounts, too small to catch it. This newspaper has since learned that a vessel matching that description — or one very much like it, caught up in the same broader case — was eventually brought ashore in Liberia. What was aboard it, what has been done with it, and whether anyone has been charged in connection with it has not been made public. A ship that once dominated the national conversation has become, in the span of a few months, a footnote nobody in government seems eager to revisit.

How the Story Narrowed to One Name

The path from those two seizures to a former Vice President in prison runs through a 2022 meeting in Dubai, arranged, prosecutors say, by a middleman named Sheikh Bassirou Kante, who later became a cooperating witness after running into his own legal trouble in the United States. A wiretapped phone call in which Kante told Jewel Howard-Taylor that the “investors” she met in Dubai had sent her a “gift” became, by the government’s own account, the piece of evidence that turned years of quiet financial ties into a formal arrest. She was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19, charged five days later with nine felony counts spanning trafficking, importation, conspiracy, money laundering and abuse of office, and has remained in custody since, her preliminary hearing delayed once already and now set to resume in the coming days. It is, by any measure, a serious and detailed case. It is also, notably, the only piece of this entire saga that has moved with anything resembling urgency.

The Arrests So Far: A Short List for Such a Big Number

Set the charge sheet against Jewel Howard-Taylor next to everyone else this investigation has touched, and the list gets uncomfortably short, uncomfortably fast. Beyond Howard-Taylor herself, only two people connected to this saga have been charged and sent toward trial: LDEA officer Moses Jallah and Paynesville bar owner George Harris, both swept up months ago in the early stages of the case. That is the entire list of people Liberia has formally accused of a crime in connection with nearly half a billion dollars in narcotics.

Everyone else occupies some quieter, murkier status. Mark Egon Kuiah, the former operations chief at Roberts International Airport, was named in a writ of arrest back in June and fired from his job in late July — but two months later, he has not been charged with anything a judge could rule on and is reportedly cooperating with investigators rather than facing them. Jonathan Momolu, a security officer at the airport tied to both this year’s case and a 2023 methamphetamine shipment disguised as tea leaves, was questioned once and sent home. Fitzgerald Biago, the Officer-in-Charge of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, recused himself months ago over an unresolved allegation involving vehicles, and that recusal has never been followed by a public resolution one way or the other. Two currently serving Liberia National Police officers, alleged to have physically escorted the drug shipment at the center of the Paynesville case, remain unnamed by the government to this day. Gerald Smith, a former NSA deputy director, was called in for questioning and, as far as the public record shows, nothing more. And the five-person European network this newspaper has identified as the operational core of the entire scheme — Croatians Nikola Ivancic and Mihovil Vrovac, Ukrainian Taras Zadereiko, and a Serbian national and a Spanish national charged earlier in the same case — have all been charged in absentia, and all remain free, spread across Dubai, Ghana and destinations unknown, precisely because a network built to survive the loss of any single member was never going to be dismantled by one arrest in Monrovia.

Is She the Only One Responsible?

Put plainly, because the question deserves a plain answer: no. Nothing in the public record supports the idea that Jewel Howard-Taylor single-handedly moved nearly half a billion dollars in cocaine through Liberia. The government’s own charging documents describe a five-person foreign network with a financier in Dubai, an operator running logistics from Ghana, and a technician structuring the money laundering — a structure that, by design, requires local facilitation at multiple levels to function inside Liberia’s ports, airport and government circles. Names tied to that facilitation — an airport operations chief, an airport security officer, a drug enforcement chief, unnamed police officers — have all surfaced in this newspaper’s reporting over the past two months. Only one of those threads has produced a former official sitting in a prison cell facing trial. The rest have produced recusals, questionings, and silence.

That is not necessarily evidence of a cover-up. Some of it may simply reflect where the evidence is strongest, or where a cooperating witness has made a prosecutor’s job easier. But intent matters less here than pattern, and the pattern is now impossible to miss: the case that moved fastest, hardest and most publicly is also the case attached to the most politically recognizable name. Every other thread — including two seizures worth, combined, more money than the charge against Howard-Taylor alone — has moved slowly enough that most Liberians could be forgiven for forgetting it was ever a separate story.

Where the Silence Is Loudest

Ask the Ministry of Justice today for an update on the broader investigation into the June airport seizure, separate from the Howard-Taylor case, and there is no recent public answer. Ask what happened to the vessel recently brought ashore, and there is no public answer. Ask whether Liberia has made any real progress toward extraditing the five foreign nationals charged in absentia, and there is no public answer beyond a general promise of cooperation with Interpol. Each of these silences might have an innocent, procedural explanation. Together, they describe an investigation whose public face has narrowed to a single defendant, while the machinery that moved nearly half a billion dollars in narcotics through this country continues to operate largely out of view.

President Boakai has pledged “no sacred cows” in this fight, and this newspaper has held him to that standard before. The test of that pledge was never going to be how thoroughly Liberia prosecutes the one defendant whose arrest generated the most headlines. It was always going to be whether the government keeps chasing the money, the network and the local facilitators after the cameras move on to the next hearing date. Right now, on the evidence available to the public, that chase looks like it has largely stopped at one name — and nearly half a billion dollars in drugs says that cannot be where the story ends.

World.title: Liberia: They Were Found Guilty in Liberia’s Biggest Human Trafficking Trial But No one Has Been Charged Over a Death in the Case. Now the Family Wants Justice
World.content:
Ophelia Melway, 32, who victims say died after ill treatment at a compound where as many as 150 trafficking victims were detained. Credit: Ophelia Melway’s family.

Summary:

The family of Ophelia Melway, a trafficking victim whose death helped expose Liberia’s largest human trafficking case, wants the investigation into her death fast-tracked.

Prosecutors are investigating whether her death warrants homicide charges.

Melway’s family, survivors and anti-trafficking advocates are demanding a swift and transparent investigation.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

It was Liberia’s biggest human trafficking trial to date. At the end of 22 days of hearings in June and July, a jury took just 23 minutes to decide eleven defendants were guilty of a range of crimes against 57 victims who were trafficked, starved, forced to work and deceived into handing over more than US$100,000 in total in the belief they would travel to jobs in Canada.

Eleven traffickers are now serving sentences as long as 50 years and have been ordered to pay US$131,500 in restitution and fines. (15 defendants have yet to face trial because they have not been apprehended.)

But victims say there is one major crime for which no one has faced justice: the death of Ophelia Melway, one of the victims, who fell seriously ill and was finally released by the traffickers only to die soon after.

Melway’s family has been joined by survivors of the trafficking ring who say determining whether anyone bears criminal responsibility for Melway’s death is essential to delivering full justice.
