World.title: Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull
World.content:
Iran fires on its Gulf neighbors, retaliating for U.S. strikes after a monthlong lull

toggle caption Masoud Mohammadi/Tasnim News Agency via AP

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — Iran fired on U.S. allies in the Gulf early Wednesday following a night of American bombardment that Iranian officials say included a deadly strike on a wedding party.

The latest violence came after a monthlong lull in fighting. The six-month war has led to a spike in oil prices, roiled the global economy and posed increasing political problems for U.S. President Donald Trump's Republican Party ahead of November midterm elections.

Sponsor Message

Fighting has escalated since the American military hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, saying Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at American bases in Jordan that were intercepted.

American military resources are stretched and political pressure in Washington is mounting, while Iran's economy falters. Iran's currency hit another record low on Wednesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging 2.20 million rials for one U.S. dollar, a 10% hike from last week's record.

Neither side can continue indefinitely between full-scale war and a truce, said Hamidreza Azizi, senior Iran analyst at the Crisis Group, an international think tank.

"At some point, one of the sides may see a need to escalate in order to break this cycle," he cautioned. "So that could bring the two sides to a point that they have been trying to avoid until now, which is a full-scale war."

The struggle is focused on the Strait of Hormuz and oil prices

The latest flare-up in violence came as the standoff seemed to be shifting slightly more in the U.S.' favor, with the price of oil around $80 a barrel and Iranian leaders talking about growing economic hardships, said Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst with the International Institute for Strategic Studies' Middle East office in Bahrain.

toggle caption Razieh Poudat/ISNA via AP

Last week, U.S. Central Command's Adm. Brad Cooper said the strait had been secretly cleared of mines and that the U.S. Navy had helped nearly 1,500 commercial vessels carrying some 750 million barrels of oil pass through in recent months — still far below prewar levels.

Sponsor Message

"He basically told the world oil is flowing out and Iran is not capable of restricting the U.S.'s approach," Bruchmann said. "The U.S. is trying to reinstall some kind of confidence into the global oil markets … and the Iranians had to respond to that by reinserting insecurity and doubt."

Since the fighting resumed, the price of Brent crude oil, the international standard, has climbed to around $95, up more than 30% from the start of the war.

U.S. allies in the region fend off Iranian attacks

Following the strikes at Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain said they had also come under attack, without reporting any casualties.

"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy, and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," the recently appointed head of Iran's powerful Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, said on X.

In Iraq, where Iranian-backed forces are active, Kurdish authorities said they had intercepted 10 drones laden with explosives in the Irbil area. Iranian television reported that American bases in Irbil had been targeted.

Israel's military also said that Iran-backed Hezbollah fired two explosive drones at its soldiers in southern Lebanon, without causing casualties.

The U.S. Central Command said Tuesday's strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defense sites, radar systems and maritime assets.

Casualties in Iran include people at a wedding party

One U.S. strike hit a home hosting a wedding in Kuhestak, a small coastal town overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian media.

Four people were killed — two women and two children, aged 4 and 16 — and at least 68 were wounded, the state news agency IRNA and state TV said Wednesday. Just after the strike, Ahmad Nafisi, the province's deputy governor, had told Iranian state television that five people were killed. There was no explanation for the change.

toggle caption Vahid Salemi/AP

Several heavy explosions shook Kuhestak, with fireballs that lit up the night sky, according to security camera footage carried by the semiofficial Fars news agency.

Sponsor Message

Images from Iran's semiofficial Tasnim news agency showed several hospitalized children being treated for injuries at a hospital in the nearby town of Minab, where a U.S. missile strike on the opening day of the war hit a primary school, killing more than 100 children.

Footage from the Iranian Red Crescent showed rescue workers entering a damaged home in the wake of the strike. It showed a hole in the roof of one house in a neighborhood of densely packed homes.

Experts say a "very precise" weapon appears to have been used

Two weapons experts told The Associated Press that images of fragments of a missile, which Iranian media said was used in the strike, were from a U.S.-made SLAM-ER cruise missile.

Trevor Ball, conflict researcher at the investigative group Bellingcat, said the SLAM-ER was "developed as a very precise weapon" that can be retargeted in flight by a human operator watching by infrared camera.

N.R. Jenzen-Jones, director of Armament Research Services, said the air-launched missile is also used by the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. Neither has reported carrying out any recent strikes on Iran.

"Make no mistake: these crimes will not go unpunished," Ebrahim Azizi, chairperson of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X.

U.S. Central Command spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said the U.S. military was "aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media, and we are looking into them." He would not say if CENTCOM had launched a formal investigation.

Separately, Iran has said four members of its paramilitary Revolutionary Guard and 10 members of the Guard's volunteer Basij forces died in the U.S. attacks.

The Strait of Hormuz remains largely shut down

During last month's lull in fighting, the U.S. ramped up economic pressure on Iran as Washington sought to fully open the Strait of Hormuz.

Sponsor Message

About a fifth of the world's traded oil was shipped through the key waterway before Israel and the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28 and Iran largely shut it down in response. Despite many pronouncements from Washington that the strait is open, only a handful of ships are making the passage each day and Iran has regularly attacked vessels.

On Wednesday, Saudi shipping company Bahri said two Filipino sailors were killed in an attack late Monday as their vessel transited the strait.

A ceasefire deal reached in June quickly fell apart amid exchanges of strikes that same month. Mediator Pakistan has been working to restart talks.

Late Tuesday, Trump said he would not force Iran to the bargaining table.

"I couldn't care less if they sign a worthless, to them, agreement. I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?" Trump wrote on social media.

World.title: Greetings from the Royal Pavilion, a stunning reminder of India in southern England
World.content:
Greetings from the Royal Pavilion, a stunning reminder of India in southern England

Lauren Frayer/NPR

Mughal arches, onion domes, chhatri-topped towers. Living in India for five years, I'd Instagram my way through a maharaja's palace, Sikh temple or sultan's fort every weekend. I got used to strolling through scalloped arches. How I miss them!

Which is why I froze in my tracks last winter when I spotted this building in Brighton, on England's south coast. The day was drizzly gray, I'd gone for a bracing swim in the English Channel, and was walking back to the train station, shivering, when I was flooded with warm memories from India.

It's the Royal Pavilion, built in the late 18th century by British royals fascinated by South Asian architecture, as they commandeered the subcontinent. It's funny: In Mumbai, I'd marvel at how many buildings look Victorian, in the same stone and style of my husband's hometown in northern England. Looking up at this pavilion, I realized the British didn't just impose their style on India. They also took India's style home.

Sponsor Message

Queen Victoria herself — who also went by "Empress of India" — lodged in the Royal Pavilion in the 1830s and '40s, before the construction of railways brought the working-class masses to Brighton — spoiling, she complained, her private seaside oasis. She decamped to Buckingham Palace and took the pavilion's lotus-flower chandeliers with her.

During World War I, the building became a military hospital, treating thousands of Indian soldiers fighting for the British. Separate kitchens catered to different castes. Muslim soldiers prayed to Mecca from the east lawn.

Nowadays, the gardens designed for King George IV are being restored, a green lung for the city. They hosted some of the first weddings after the United Kingdom legalized same-sex marriage in 2014. And having survived centuries of royal caprice, and at least one arson attack, the pavilion is now a museum, open to the masses.

I wonder what Queen Victoria would think of that.

World.title: Republicans back Trump in his trade war with Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Republican members of Congress are publicly backing U.S. President Donald Trump in his trade war with Canada and blaming Prime Minister Mark Carney's government for walking away from negotiations.

Dozens of GOP House members gathered on Capitol Hill on Wednesday for a closed-door meeting with Trump's point man on tariffs, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

While some Republicans are quietly concerned that an escalation of costly tariffs could worsen their re-election prospects in the midterms in November, those who spoke with CBC News after meeting Greer generally expressed support for the president's trade strategy.

WATCH | How the trade war could impact Republicans ahead of midterms: Trade war a campaign hurdle for some Republicans ahead of U.S. midterms | Duration 2:09 As Ontario’s premier and the U.S. president traded jabs online, Republican candidates in some border states are up against the real consequences of the revitalized trade war on their economies — which analysts say could prove to be a challenge in the upcoming U.S. midterms.



Texas Republican August Pfluger praised Trump for bringing manufacturing jobs back to the U.S. and pinned blame for the trade war on Ottawa.

"It's a war that is perpetuated by Canada," Pfluger told CBC News. "The Canadians need to get reasonable. They've taken advantage of the United States for a long time."

Brian Mast, a five-term Congressman from Florida, also criticized Canada for the breakdown in trade talks.

"They were given the best possible deal, more generous than anybody else across the globe, and it's something that they turned their back on," Mast told CBC News.

When Greer emerged from the meeting, he did not respond to reporters' questions about the state of negotiations with Canada.

Republicans lawmakers who spoke to reporters on Capitol Hill on Wednesday largely backed U.S. President Donald Trump on his approach to the trade war with Canada. (Mariam Zuhaib/The Associated Press)

Trump criticizes Canada's banking policy

Meanwhile at the White House, Trump gave no sign of shifting his position that Canada has long taken advantage of the U.S. on trade.

Trump told reporters that one of his biggest grievances against Canada is the limits it puts on U.S. bank operations north of the border.

"They basically don't allow banks of America to be in Canada, that's sort of emblematic of the way they treat us," Trump said in the Oval Office on Wednesday afternoon.

"Canada has all of its major banks here, and we're their biggest source of income, far bigger than they are in Canada," he said.

WATCH | Why Trump uses rage bait as a political weapon: How Trump mastered the art of the distraction | Duration 3:29 From renaming Lake Ontario to outlandish memes, Donald Trump has rewritten the rules of political communication. For The National, CBC’s Ashley Fraser breaks down how the U.S. president used distraction to dominate the attention economy — and asks: is the strategy deliberate?

On Capitol Hill, the sole Republican who raised concerns about the impact of the trade war on voters was Ralph Norman, who represents a South Carolina district.

"What I hear in South Carolina is affordability," said Norman. "It all goes into affordability, whether it's this [trade war with Canada], whether it's tariffs, whether it's housing, gas."

He says Greer expressed willingness to address how tariffs are affecting each state.

"The concerns, they were real," Norman said. "I think the White House will be listening."

Although polling suggests Trump's tariffs are deeply unpopular, other Congressional Republicans lined up to defend the president's trade war with Canada, in some cases repeating his arguments almost word-for-word.

Missouri Congressman Eric Burlison said it would not be a smart move for Canada to levy counter-tariffs on U.S. exports, as Carney has threatened to do next week.

"We're the economic powerhouse obviously compared to [Canada]," Burlison said. "I think Canada needs the United States more than we need them."

World.title: Environment Canada lifts weather alerts caused by 'extremely dangerous' thunderstorm in Toronto
World.content:
Severe thunderstorm damages buildings, closes roads in Toronto area | Duration 3:51

An intense weather system brought torrential rain, large hail and the risk of a tornado to parts of southern Ontario on Wednesday. That included the Greater Toronto Area, where a heavy thunderstorm caused widespread power outages and localized flooding and led to the Canadian National Exhibition (CNE) closing early for the evening.

World.title: Canadian missing after Nepal flooding found safe, Anand says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says one of the 30 Canadian citizens and permanent residents missing after catastrophic flooding in Nepal's border region with China has been found safe.

She says the individual was unreachable due to communication outages and was able to establish contact Tuesday.

The flash flooding struck one week ago after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China.

WATCH | A glimpse of flood devastation: Drone video reveals flood devastation in Devighat, Nepal | Duration 0:54 Drone footage from Wednesday shows skeletal remains of homes and mud-caked debris in the Nepalese town of Devighat, which sits on the banks of the Trishuli river, after deadly flash floods tore through the region last week.

More than 1,100 people were killed and more than 3,900 are missing.

Nepal's Foreign Ministry says about 590 foreign nationals from 39 countries remain unaccounted for.

Anand says Canada will be sending more than 18,000 emergency items from Canadian Red Cross stockpiles to the area in addition to the $5 million Ottawa has already pledged in humanitarian aid.

World.title: 'My students should be here': Tumbler Ridge teacher shares toll of deadly B.C. school shooting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One of the teachers caught in the deadly school shooting at Tumbler Ridge Secondary has shared her story publicly for the first time, describing a "dark cloud" lingering over her hometown in the weeks and months following the tragedy.

Deidre Rushlow is one of the plaintiffs in a series of lawsuits filed this week in California against OpenAI, alleging the company's ChatGPT platform was used to help plan the shooting, which left eight victims, including five students and an educator at the school, dead.

Along with the lawsuit, Rushlow issued a written statement through the Canadian lawyers representing her in the case. In it, she says she is "haunted by the memory" of the day, calling it "a wound that sears with unending pain for my entire community."

Her letter is a rare insight into what people who were at Tumbler Ridge Secondary experienced, with the town's leaders asking for privacy as they recover from the tragedy.

"My name is Deidre Rushlow. Up until February 10, 2026, I was the English and Humanities teacher at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School. My students were in the library when the shooting happened. I did not know, nor could I know, that when I sent them to the library with my educational assistant, they were living their final moments," the statement begins.

Youth in Tumbler Ridge memorialize the victims of February's mass shooting, writing names and messages on a wall in the community's downtown. (Tom Summer/CBC)

Rushlow says she was in her first year of full-time teaching, having previously attended and graduated from the school before becoming a substitute.

"When I finally got the keys to my very own classroom last summer, I scrubbed each corner clean, added personal touches to brighten it up, and spent days organizing it until every last detail was perfect for my students," she writes.

"That same classroom has now been reduced to a pile of dust, all of my supplies and decorations packed into boxes and stored somewhere unknown to me. The career that once brought me such joy now terrifies me in ways I never imagined possible. How can I ever be responsible for another parent’s child again?"

WATCH | Remembering the victims of the Tumbler Ridge shooting: RCMP identify all 8 victims of shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C. | Duration 4:37





"My students should be here getting ready for the next school year," she says. "Instead, their families, friends and classmates are left behind to suffocate in limitless grief and trauma."

Investigation ongoing as new school year begins

As the school year begins, students at Tumbler Ridge Secondary will be back in portable classrooms that were set up in the wake of the shooting.

The school itself, which housed students from grades 7 to 12, is being demolished and replaced by a new facility funded by the provincial and federal governments.

The first wing of the former Tumbler Ridge Secondary School is seen here being dismantled on Monday, Aug. 17. (Tom Summer/CBC)

The municipality is also working with those higher levels of government to develop a recovery plan and to continue offering supports to those who need it.

The police investigation into the deadly day is also ongoing, RCMP say, with a coroner's inquest planned once that is complete.

'We will not forgive, we will not forget,' teacher says

Recent scrutiny has been centred on OpenAI after it was revealed that the shooter's ChatGPT account had been flagged internally, without warning Canadian officials or law enforcement.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has since apologized and says new policies are in place to offer better protections.

WATCH | Edelson explains what's in the new lawsuits: Lawyer for Tumbler Ridge victims says OpenAI should be held accountable | Duration 9:00 Jay Edelson is the CEO of Edelson PC, the law firm representing victims and survivors of the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., shooting in a lawsuit against ChatGPT. He says one of his chief aims is to have chat-logs between the shooter and ChatGPT released.



But as part of the lawsuits filed this week though U.S. class-action firm Edelson PC, it is claimed OpenAI's leadership "ignored its own safety staff and refused to alert police," instead "choosing profit over the lives of the children of Tumbler Ridge" as it prepares to become a publicly-traded company. "

Jason Kwon, chief strategy officer at OpenAI, said in a response posted on X that those claims are false and that his team works " hard to define standards and processes for when to report cases to law enforcement and to apply those standards to really difficult and complex situations."

The lawsuits and their claims will be tested in court in California, where OpenAI is headquartered.

In her statement, Rushlow writes she wants accountability for the company.

"We will not forgive, we will not forget, and we certainly will not rest until every last individual at OpenAI who was complicit in the Tumbler Ridge shooting has been brought to justice," she says.

World.title: Dancing With The Stars announces Season 35 cast: Julia Stiles, Jenna Dewan and more to hit the ballroom floor
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The stars have been picked. Now they just need to learn the steps.

The cast of Season 35 of Dancing With The Stars was officially announced on Wednesday, with a fresh lineup of familiar faces trading their famous day jobs for sequins, choreography and a shot at the mirror-ball trophy.

Before Wednesday's announcement on Good Morning America, Maura Higgins, Ciara Miller, Jackson Olson and Guillermo Rodriguez had already been confirmed as part of the cast.

Twelve more stars were then named to the roster on the ABC morning show — including Julia Stiles, trading in her Save The Last Dance flats and 10 Things I Hate About You acting chops for the cha-cha-cha, and The Rookie star Jenna Dewan.

With Hollywood heavyweights, social-media personalities, an Olympian, a Paralympian and even a banana stepping onto the dance floor (Savannah Bananas exhibition baseball player Jackson Olson), it's shaping up to be one very busy ballroom.

The show, which airs in Canada on Disney+, will have a double premiere on Sept. 15 and 16.

Here's the full cast and the professional dancers they've been paired with:

Tatyana Ali (Fresh Prince of Bel Air) and Jan Ravnik

Jan Ravnik and Tatyana Ali. (Disney/Andrew Eccles)

Tyler Cameron (The Bachelorette) and Sharna Burgess

Tyler Cameron and Sharna Burgess. (Andrew Eccles/Disney)

Giada De Laurentiis (celebrity chef and Food Network host) and Alan Bersten

Giada De Laurentiis and Alan Bersten. (Andrew Eccles/Disney)

Jenna Dewan (The Rookie, Step Up) and Val Chmerkovskiy

Val Chmerkovskiy and Jenna Dewan. (Andrew Eccles/Disney)

World.title: Air Canada Express flight attendants vote on strike mandate as contract talks stall
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Flight attendants who work on Air Canada Express flights are voting on whether to authorize strike action as their union says bargaining talks have stalled.

The Canadian Flight Attendant Union, which represents around 1,000 flight attendants, says it's seeking a strike mandate after being unable to reach an agreement with Jazz Aviation on "the most critical issues" despite nine months of negotiations and enlisting the services of a mediator.

"The CFAU believes a strong strike mandate from its membership is necessary to ensure Jazz Aviation understands the seriousness of the outstanding issues and the resolve of its members," the news release said.

A spokesperson for Jazz Aviation said the company remains committed to reaching an agreement at the bargaining table "without disruption to its operations."

The company is seeking out the appointment of a conciliation officer as negotiations with the Canadian Flight Attendant Union have reached an impasse, the spokesperson said in an email.

Jazz Aviation serves as the primary operator for Air Canada Express flights. It is not owned by Air Canada but by a holding company called Chorus.

Union says pay among key issues

Chris Schliep, the union's vice-president, said the parties have made progress on some items over the past few months but that significant issues remain unresolved.

The main outstanding issues for the union include wages, compensation for work performed on the ground and "improvements that recognize the impact this job has on our members' lives," Schliep said in an email.

"Jazz flight attendants have not kept pace with comparable flight attendants at other Canadian airlines, particularly in light of the recent agreements reached across the industry.

"We believe these are reasonable issues that need to be addressed. Our members are asking for an agreement that properly recognizes the work they actually do and the responsibility they carry."

The union also wants its members recognized as safety professionals for the work they perform completing checks, attending briefings and boarding passengers, he said.

The importance of safety was highlighted in March after the fatal accident involving Air Canada Express Flight AC8646 at LaGuardia Airport, which killed both pilots, the news release says.

"Safety does not begin at takeoff, nor does it end at landing," said Marsha Walters, president of the Canadian Flight Attendant Union, in the news release.

"It begins with fair working conditions, proper rest, and respect for the flight attendants who are responsible for the safety and care of passengers every day."

WATCH | Former WestJet flight attendant on why she left industry: Former flight attendant on why she quit the industry | Duration 5:10 Calleigh Gingras is a former flight attendant who has been a vocal critic on social media about issues within the airline industry. She says she is not shocked by news of a possible strike by WestJet flight attendants and that despite loving the job, the pay for the working conditions, including many hours of unpaid work, was 'not sustainable' for her.

Voting closes on Friday at noon. The vote comes just weeks after WestJet flight attendants went on strike and a little over a year after more than 10,000 Air Canada flight attendants did the same.

It's unclear when Air Canada Express flight attendants could walk off the job if they vote in favour of a strike mandate.

World.title: Pentagon makes testosterone screening mandatory for U.S. service members effective immediately
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The ​U.S. Pentagon issued detailed guidance on Wednesday for a new, mandatory testosterone deficiency screening policy for active-duty and reserve service members age 30 and older, ‌a follow-up to a July announcement from U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

The guidance, which is effective immediately, establishes standardized screening and treatment pathways for men and women that ​the Pentagon says are aimed at ​improving military readiness by identifying and managing hormonal and energy-availability issues.

Hegseth, who has promoted the use of ​testosterone, announced the mandate last month, raising questions ⁠among experts about whether ⁠there was a ‌scientific basis for such a policy. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration plans to hold a meeting of experts to discuss medical use of testosterone in ⁠mid-September.

According to the guidance, men age 30 and older will receive mandatory testosterone blood tests, while younger men will be tested ‌only on request or if clinicians identify warning signs.

For women, the guidance does not mandate routine testosterone blood tests, but it calls for screening for ​fatigue and disrupted menstrual cycles that can be associated with hormonal dysregulation and ⁠conditions called low-energy availability and relative energy deficiency in sport.

The ⁠document lays out guidelines for when it is appropriate to ⁠prescribe ⁠off-label testosterone in ​women, namely for postmenopausal women with unusually low sexual desire.

Doctors have ​raised concerns ⁠that broad testosterone testing could lead to unnecessary, or potentially harmful, treatment, saying there is little evidence that universal screening for low testosterone among military personnel would improve U.S. combat readiness.
