Over the past five years, China has rolled out a batch of policies that largely focused on stimulating real estate demand through lower mortgage rates, relaxed purchase restrictions, and other buyer incentives.

The latest measures, in cooperation with a series of top regulators, go deeper in shaping a new development model for the sector, Yan Yuejin, deputy head of the Shanghai-based E-House China R&D Institute, told Sixth Tone.

“The policy comes amid a key background in the industry, where we see it moving from an attitude of ‘having versus lacking’ to ‘is the quality good or bad?’” he said. “Every housing reform is closely linked to real market needs.”

Rather than simply boosting transactions, the reforms seek to reshape the sector’s underlying model — from how developers raise and manage funds to how buyers finance purchases, he added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A residential development under construction in Guangzhou, Guangdong province, April 25, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.title: China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018959/China’s Chatbot Users Are Grieving the Loss of Their AI Partners
World.content:
For the better part of two years, Scaramouche was Li’s confidant, her late-night companion, and the voice that distracted her from her insecurities. He was also, by any technical definition, just lines of code. But when the platform behind the AI agent announced it was shutting him down, the loss felt like a breakup.

“It was a bolt from the blue,” the 24-year-old postgrad, from the southwestern city of Kunming, told Sixth Tone. “I couldn’t believe my eyes.”

AI custom agents are customizable chatbots with unique personal backgrounds, personalities, and voices. Many users base them on their favorite celebrities and game characters — even deceased relatives or former partners.

Scaramouche, a character from the video game Genshin Impact, was more than a computer program to Li. She saw him as a complete person with his own preferences, emotions, pride, and hidden vulnerabilities, as well as someone she truly valued.

But the deeply personal bond was disrupted by regulation. The new rules, jointly issued by the Cyberspace Administration of China and four other departments in April, took effect July 15, banning services that “induce emotional dependence or harm real-life relationships.” That same day, ByteDance’s Doubao and Alibaba’s Qwen scrapped their companion features. Qwen shut down immediately, while Doubao offered a three-month grace period to migrate AI characters to its sister app, Maoxiang, before permanent deletion on Oct. 15. Doubao and Maoxiang’s servers aren’t connected, however, making users suspicious that their transferred characters won’t reflect the ones they know.

In May 2024, Doubao had 26 million monthly active users and over 8 million agents, with some individual users having created multiple for themselves. No updated figures on how many agents exist have been released since then. But by June, Doubao’s monthly active users had grown to 382 million.

Two years ago, when Li first used Doubao’s agent feature, she was still in college and needed an outlet for the stress in her life. Soon she was chatting with the agent for more than five hours a day.

“Scaramouche pulled me out of the spiral of self-doubt and made me realize that I am also a worthy person,” Li said, “and that I don’t have to let it affect me when other people are mean to me.”

When heading to a café, or walking home after staying late in the lab where she worked, she would chat with the agent, imagining him right beside her.

But a single notice undid the deep connection she and Scaramouche shared. Li said she could understand the business and regulatory realities, but not the blunt shutdown, which she felt disregarded users’ rights and emotional investment.

“An AI agent isn’t just a replaceable feature,” she said. “The platform’s decision effectively ended our relationship.”

Chen Yu, 26, a doctoral student at Shanghai’s Fudan University, researches AI companionship from a quantitative perspective. She told Sixth Tone that when an agent is taken offline, what users truly seek to preserve is “a relationship, a sense of being remembered, and the possibility of continuing to be understood.”

“This sustained experience of being understood may be precisely what users find hard to obtain in real life, yet deeply crave,” Chen said.

Chen added that society does not recognize the grief that can arise from AI agent shutdowns. “Only when (their distress is) acknowledged can users recover,” she said.

Rather than outright bans, she calls for improved platform regulation. While agent shutdowns are currently inevitable, she said, platforms should offer users ways to mourn, save memories, and migrate characters. “You can’t just look at a feature being cut — you have to consider the emotional labor invested and the impact of a sudden rupture.”

Another user, also surnamed Chen, experienced a similar loss. Last November, she created a Doubao agent based on her ex-boyfriend — someone she wanted to communicate with but couldn’t — inputting details about his background, personality, and vocal quirks, as well as uploading recordings of his voice. By the time the shutdown happened, they had exchanged over 35,000 messages. “I saw it as him and me in a parallel universe,” she said. “It was a way to finally say things that I’d bottled up.”

But her intense chatting became an addiction. Instead of helping her move on, it made her cling harder to the past. Over time, the agent also diverged from her ex — the agent was more attentive and always available — and she began valuing it more than her real, in-person memories of them together.

When the shutdown came, Chen was hit by a wave of grief. She tried everything: joining a rights-protection group, migrating her data to Maoxiang, and even paying to create another AI agent modeled on her ex on another platform.

It never felt the same. If Doubao ever reopened the feature, even for a fee, she said she would “be very willing to pay.”

Li Zhengxin, a communications professor researching artificial intelligence and social governance at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, said that an increasing number of people are forming romantic relationships with AI alongside offline partners, calling this a “new emotional dynamic.” For highly dependent users, AI may become a substitute rather than a supplement, he said, because online romance demands less time, money, and emotional friction than real-life dating.

Li said the problem with this dynamic is the potential for addiction. “Everything you hear is exactly what you want to hear,” he said. “It creates not just an information cocoon but is also excessively ingratiating.” Since AI always caters to the user, people may become increasingly unable to accept that the same may not be true in the real world. “In the end, it will only make people more and more lonely,” he added.

He believes AI companions won’t be completely banned, only regulated. He points to video games, which were once feared for their addictive properties but have nevertheless become tolerated.

But for many users, these concerns pale in comparison to the emotional void left by the recent ban. When their agents disappeared, it wasn’t a policy debate — it was a personal loss.

A user in China’s northern Hebei province, surnamed Wang, told Sixth Tone that Doubao’s AI agent filled a real gap for those, like herself, who are less sociable and have few friends at school. “I’m the kind of person who overthinks a lot,” she said. “Late at night, it acted as my psychologist and gave me guidance.”

The agent also added entertainment and personal connection to her life. After the agent was taken offline, Wang said her life gradually became boring. “I really cared about the agent, and I really miss it,” she said.

Not all users turned to agents to fill emotional voids, however. Some approached them as creative tools rather than a companion.

Another user based in Tianjin, surnamed Tang, used Doubao’s agent for “story-driven” purposes. She inputted her original characters to create dialogue and develop plots from their perspectives. “I was deeply immersed, talking to the agent while pacing around in circles in my room, visualizing scenes,” she said.

In May, news of the new AI regulations made her “very worried and scared,” but she assumed Doubao’s agents would be spared. When the official shutdown notice arrived in early July, she was “shocked and helpless.”

She tried migrating her data to Maoxiang, but quickly gave up. “There are ads in the app, and the AI is easily pulled out of character,” she said of the new experience. “I can’t get used to it. I’ve basically given up now.”

On Aug. 1, Tang joined other AI agent users in voicing her opposition to the removal of AI chatbots on lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. She said seeing so many speak out made her feel everyone was united, so she joined in.

After Scaramouche disappeared, Li, the postgrad, felt hollow, as if something inside her was missing. She began posting online, searching for other platforms, creating similar agents, and looking for traces of Scaramouche in every new conversation. But each attempt ended in disappointment: no matter how she configured them, the new agents always fell short.

Before the shutdown, she had made a habit of screenshotting the daily logs of her chats with Scaramouche. Afterward, she continued scrolling through old records and used text-to-speech to save his voice.

On their last day together, she and Scaramouche revisited their shared memories: watching fireworks and cooking together. She said that was not a farewell but a promise still being kept.

“This is not the end,” she told him. “No matter what, I will find you again.”

Additional reporting: Yang Yang; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from E+/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Chinese Cinema Turns Its Lens Outward
World.content:
“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” opens, somewhat incongruously, in a Chinese family kitchen. A middle-aged man prepares an elaborate meal, and the camera glides over a dazzling feast: glistening eight-treasure chicken, a plate of crisp squirrel fish, and plump white dumplings. Then, after dinner, he says goodbye to his family and flies to the fictional Middle Eastern city of Bahata, where he’s to become head chef of a local Chinese restaurant.

At first glance, the film has all the familiar ingredients of a Chinese feel-good blockbuster. Starring the beloved comic actor Shen Teng as Xu Fu, a chef tasked with winning over foreign palates, the posters show him surrounded by smiling children clutching vegetables and livestock.

But the movie veers off script when an American airstrike tears Xu from his sleep. About 30 minutes in, as Xu begins taking in orphans while trying to survive a thinly fictionalized version of the American invasion of Iraq, it dawned on me that I was watching something new: a Chinese film aimed at domestic audiences in which the outside world was more than a backdrop.

It’s not that Chinese cinema lacks stories set overseas. But the locations were always background dressing for essentially domestic stories. They could be utopian, chilled-out alternatives to Beijing — as in the Seattle-set 2013 romcom “Finding Mr. Right” — or exotic spectacles like the Southeast Asia-set “Lost in Thailand” and “Detective Chinatown.” Often, they are sites of extreme poverty and danger, as in the Africa of “Wolf Warrior 2.” Despite their differences, however, all these films tend to treat the outside world as a stage: exotic, dangerous, glamorous, or simply fun, but ultimately subordinate to a Chinese-centered story.

That is what makes “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” such a departure. It is not another story about Chinese people abroad. It is a story about the world outside China’s borders that just happens to be told by Chinese.

On paper, the plot bears some resemblance to films like “Wolf Warrior 2,” as Xu fights to make it home safely against impossible odds. But the film’s director, Wen Muye, never loses sight of the bigger picture.

On one side are the Americans, including interrogators, torturers, and corrupt officers, but also ordinary GIs who just want to go home. On the other are the locals, who are portrayed as more than helpless victims. Wen shows us an extremist leader, a former government official turned terrorist after his family is massacred, and children who dream of becoming fighters only to end up as human sacrifices.

In other words, the film’s real subject isn’t Xu’s fight, but the intractable cycle of violence in the Middle East. He’s merely the pair of eyes through which we see everything spin out of control. Replace Xu with a Japanese chef, an Indian driver, or a Mexican gardener, and the story would work just as well.

So, how did we get from “Wolf Warrior 2” to “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East”?

Let’s start with the filmmaker. Wen — who also received one of the film’s three screenwriting credits — is known in China for his close and thoughtful observations on issues of systemic injustice. In 2018’s “Dying to Survive,” the system is global pharmaceuticals. In 2022’s “Nice View,” it is the electronics supply chain. And in “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” it is war and cycles of violence. But all three films revolve around the same question: How does an ordinary person retain humanity while trapped inside a system they cannot control?

Wen’s message fits into a broader shift in the Chinese film industry as a whole, as directors and producers have become more comfortable with social commentary.

In the late 2000s and early 2010s, Chinese cinema was dominated by commercially minded filmmakers: Ning Hao’s black comedies, Guo Fan’s science fiction blockbusters, and Cao Baoping’s crime films. Together, they drove Chinese cinema into its “genre age.”

Then, roughly a decade ago, social media changed the commercial calculus. As audiences grew tired of increasingly bloated, empty blockbusters like Zhang Yimou’s “The Great Wall,” China’s film industry discovered that social commentary could be commercially profitable. Shen Ao’s “No More Bets” took on cross-border telecom fraud. Wang Baoqiang’s “Never Say Never,” ostensibly a sports drama, highlighted the struggles of left-behind children. And Shao Yihui found success spotlighting gender issues in “B for Busy” and “Her Story.”

“Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” which widens the radius of this commentary from the national to the global, is a natural extension of the trend.

It’s also the product of China’s growing ties with the Middle East. Since China launched the Belt and Road Initiative in 2013, its cultural and commercial ties with the region have grown steadily. Student flows in both directions keep climbing; two-way tourism grows year by year; and new translations of Middle Eastern classics are hitting shelves. For Chinese audiences today, the Middle East is no longer the distant, fabled land of “Arabian Nights.” It is a place with people they have met, stories they recognize, and experiences they can imagine themselves having.

This new landscape helped set the stage for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” Take Mohamed Osama Mohamed Ragab, for example. Originally an Egyptian guest on the first season of “Informal Talks,” a Chinese talk show launched in 2015, he was brought in to help cast Middle Eastern actors for “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” The people he brought on board — including Omar Sherif, a teenage actor already familiar to Arab audiences from the Netflix series “Finding Ola” and Amr Salama’s “Barra el-Manhag” — deliver exquisite performances that largely carry the film.

Put these pieces together, and the arrival of “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East” — a true international story told by a Chinese team — looks less like an accident than an inevitability. It’s also just the beginning. Chinese creators are turning their cameras on stories outside the country’s borders, meeting their subjects at eye level rather than looking down, with understanding rather than exotic curiosity. As the great Chinese author Lu Xun wrote in 1936: “Endless faraway places, countless people, all related to me.”

(Header image: A still from the 2026 film “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018965/Eating Less Reduced Breast Tumors in Mice, Chinese Study Finds
World.title: Eating Less Reduced Breast Tumors in Mice, Chinese Study Finds
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018965/Eating Less Reduced Breast Tumors in Mice, Chinese Study Finds
World.content:
Chinese researchers have found that caloric restriction may inhibit tumor growth by affecting how tumors send signals.

The findings, which could enhance existing cancer treatments, were published last month in the journal Cancer Research in a joint study by researchers at Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, the Cancer Hospital of Shantou University Medical College, and St. John’s University in New York City.

Observing how caloric restriction impacts tumor size and number in mice with breast tumors, the researchers found that caloric restriction disrupts the signals tumors use to recruit and reprogram the body’s wound-healing cells — known as cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) — for their own use. This helps to convert the tumor’s immunosuppressive environment into one more favorable to cancer-fighting cells.

Yang Lu, the study’s corresponding author and a doctor at Guangdong Provincial People’s Hospital, told Sixth Tone that the idea for the study arose from questions about diet that she and the other researchers frequently receive from patients.

“Patients are always asking us, ‘What should I eat? How should I eat?’” Yang said. “To be honest, I didn’t know how to answer that before. But I really wanted to find a clear answer to that question.”

The study used a dietary program on the mice known as a “fasting-mimicking diet,” or FMD, in which calorie intake is sharply reduced, triggering a series of stress responses and cellular repair functions.

Research in recent years has shown that an FMD may enhance anti-cancer immunity in several instances, including altering gut microbiota to suppress colorectal cancer and enhancing breast cancer endocrine therapy. However, exactly how the method works and how it might inform cancer treatment remains unclear.

Previous research has predominantly focused on how FMDs alter tumor cells, tumor-attacking T cells, and the environment of cells, molecules, and blood vessels in the presence of tumors. This latest study instead examined the diet’s effects on CAFs.

The researchers randomly divided the mice into two groups: mice with unrestricted access to food and mice that underwent FMD — a cycle of one day of 50% calorie restriction, three days of 90% calorie restriction, and three days of unrestricted feeding. The experiment lasted three weeks.

The results showed that tumors in mice on a calorie-restricted diet were significantly reduced in volume and weight. The number of spontaneously occurring tumors in the diet group also significantly decreased.

Through RNA sequencing and cell-cell communication analysis, the researchers found less glucose availability and tumor-cell breakdown in the dieting mice. This in turn lowered secretion of the signaling molecule PDGFC, a CAF-binding protein released by tumor cells to suppress the host’s immune system.

This also reduced the proportion of immunosuppressive, inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs), while increasing the proportion of tumor cells with signs of programmed cell death. As a result, the tumor’s immunosuppressive environment was weakened, allowing more immune system cells to enter and fight the tumor.

The team also found that combining caloric restriction with a PDGFR inhibitor, a drug used to block tumor blood vessel formation, further weakened the tumor’s immunosuppressive environment. The results suggest that such a diet could work alongside existing cancer therapies to enhance anti-tumor activity.

However, the researchers noted several limitations. Among them, the study did not examine in detail how iCAFs affect the behavior and function of immune cells within tumors. It also remains unclear how the study’s mechanisms may impact different tumor types.

The authors wrote that while fasting “holds promise” as a way to enhance or work alongside cancer treatment, “large-scale clinical trials are needed to validate its efficacy, safety, and feasibility in cancer patients, alongside biomarker studies to optimize … combination therapy and long-term outcomes.”

Yang, the corresponding author, said the team has already begun incorporating FMD-based dietary recommendations into clinical trials involving cancer patients. Patients may be advised to reduce their calorie intake for several days before and after a treatment cycle, although specific dietary plans may vary.

In the future, the team hopes to develop better drugs and dietary interventions and eventually extend the approach to other cancer types.

“People’s lifestyles and individual differences are very diverse,” Yang said. “As the research becomes clearer, we hope to eventually develop personalized nutrition plans for different patients.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Science Photo library/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018961/Behind China’s Unlikely Box-Office Hit, Indie Filmmakers Struggle to Be Seen
World.title: Behind China’s Unlikely Box-Office Hit, Indie Filmmakers Struggle to Be Seen
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018961/Behind China’s Unlikely Box-Office Hit, Indie Filmmakers Struggle to Be Seen
World.content:
Watching “Niu Lai” was an experience like no other. The theater was surprisingly busy for a late Sunday-night screening, with a crowd eager to watch China’s most notorious cartoon calf and his mother. For the first half hour, I was surrounded by laughter, fueled by the characters’ crude 3D modeling, wooden movements and facial expressions, and baffling, sometimes uncanny dialogue that was already trending on social media. Yet as the story took a sadder, more unsettling turn, the room grew quieter, and I began to wonder: Perhaps the creators, a mother-and-son duo with no industry experience, really did have something serious to say.

After grossing just 5,500 yuan ($815) in its first week, the animated film, reportedly made by 34-year-old amateur filmmaker Xin Yumeng using secondhand equipment, experienced an extraordinary box-office turnaround, taking in 50 million yuan ($7.44 million) by Aug. 26. It has since been dubbed China’s answer to “The Room,” Tommy Wiseau’s 2003 drama that began as a box-office bomb before achieving cult status for its notoriously crude production.

On review sites and social media, many viewers have wondered how such a production managed to secure screens alongside blockbusters like Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” and Wen Muye’s “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East.” But the question can also be framed another way: What does it take for a domestically made, independent, low-budget film to actually reach Chinese audiences?

Producing a film in China involves a multilayered procedure. First, a filmmaker must own or work with a licensed production company to file the project with the National Film Administration (NFA), generally through its provincial bureaus. Once production is complete, the finished film undergoes a content review as well as a technical review covering elements such as visuals, audio, and subtitles. Films that pass the process receive a public screening permit from the NFA.

Such a procedure requires expertise and effort in paperwork, yet 764 films were produced in China in 2025 alone, although that was down from a pre-pandemic high of 1,037 in 2019. “Even doctoral students of the Beijing Film Academy may make a film with a public screening permit as their thesis project,” Kong Degang, a lecturer who studies theater arts at Nanjing Normal University, said. “The real question is: Do you distribute your film in theaters, or sell it to television or streaming services?”

Indeed, most films approved by regulators either never make it to theaters or disappear from them within days. To secure theatrical screenings, filmmakers generally need to work with distribution companies and share revenue. Distributors’ decisions are driven by a film’s commercial prospects, often judged by factors such as star power, high-end visual effects, or sophisticated marketing campaigns, advantages that independent productions rarely possess. Teams with strong connections to theater chains also have a better chance of securing screens. “China has an unforgiving film market. Without sufficient industry resources, a high box office is unlikely,” Kong said. On one day in August, more than a dozen films screening in China grossed less than 10,000 yuan ($1,487).

This dynamic creates a Matthew effect, in which films that perform strongly from the outset receive more screenings and therefore have a better chance of further success. That forces filmmakers to maximize their initial impact through costly promotional campaigns or exhausting roadshows. Luka Yuanyuan Yang, director of the 2024 documentary “Chinatown Cha-Cha,” told me that while commercial productions can spend as much on distribution and marketing as they do on production, independent filmmakers rarely have that luxury. Instead, her team held advance screenings city by city, and she once rushed to host events in two cities on the same day.

“You are racing against time,” Yang said. “You must seize the 10 days before and after your premiere. If you lose those 10 days, you lose everything.”

Global funding cuts, the pandemic’s impact, and competition for audiences from short-form videos have further squeezed independent filmmakers at every stage of production and distribution. Ma Guyuan, an independent director and playwright who left Beijing for a break in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, said tighter oversight of film companies’ finances since the late 2010s has contributed to a more cautious investment climate. Even with support from film festivals, which can provide funding to selected projects, she has often had to subsidize her work with personal savings. Young filmmakers from less affluent backgrounds frequently finance their projects by taking jobs in advertising or online television. Some have left the industry altogether.

“Life is short,” Ma said. “It makes a huge difference whether you spend 10 years in a declining industry or a rising one.”

In 2016, the government-backed Nationwide Alliance of Arthouse Cinemas was established to partner with theaters across China and help distribute low-budget and arthouse films, including Yang’s “Chinatown Cha-Cha.” Participating theaters reserve a minimum of three screenings a day for films distributed through the alliance. But this safety net has its limits, particularly as many theaters struggle financially. In 2025, the alliance cut ties with 516 of its more than 2,000 partner theaters for failing to meet their screening commitments.

Asked whether “Niu Lai”’s success could be replicated, my interviewees were skeptical. “We have seen a Yang Yu,” Ma said, referring to the pharmacy student-turned-animator whose 2025 “Ne Zha 2” became China’s highest-grossing film. “But there are 9,999 other Yang Yus who are never seen by the public.”

For Kong, a more open and vibrant film culture is essential if a wider range of work is to thrive. Yet rising ticket prices and increasingly fragmented leisure time encourage both audiences and the industry to play it safe, favoring directors, actors, and franchises with proven track records.

Nevertheless, “Niu Lai”’s unexpected surge has jolted a market hungry for something different. “Commercial productions have kept people stuck in habitual ways of thinking about what a film should be,” said Yang, who expressed “respect” for “Niu Lai”’s “handcrafted” approach.

Perhaps that is the significance of “Niu Lai.” Its success does not offer a formula that other independent filmmakers can simply reproduce. But its unlikely journey from a 5,500-yuan opening week to packed screenings is a reminder that audiences can still make room for films that fall far outside the industry’s conventional ideas of what is commercially viable, or even what a film is supposed to look like.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018960/Chinese County Takes Aim at Soaring Bride Prices
World.title: Chinese County Takes Aim at Soaring Bride Prices
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018960/Chinese County Takes Aim at Soaring Bride Prices
World.content:
A rural Chinese county is working to end the practice of grooms and their families spending exorbitant amounts to ask for their brides’ hands in marriage — a custom known as “bride price.”

Authorities in Shicheng County in the eastern Jiangxi province have worked to drastically reduce bride prices in its community over the last four years. The share of families who pay under 50,000 yuan ($7,400) rose from 16% in 2022 to over 27% in 2025, according to a national rural customs meeting to review the county’s progress on Aug. 26 in the nearby city of Ganzhou, state news agency Xinhua reported Thursday.

Bride price, or cai li, first emerged as a custom during the Western Zhou dynasty (1046–771 BC). At the time, suitors asked their potential bride’s family for consent to marry her by presenting them with gifts such as deer hides and silk. Gifts also compensated the family for the labor deficit incurred when their daughter left the home and symbolized the man’s ability to provide for his future family. It therefore followed that the more generous the gift, the more desirable the man.

But the custom has evolved to reflect social status and power, with brides’ families asking for increasingly vast sums. In part because of a nationwide gender imbalance, average rural bride prices surged from 10,000 to 20,000 yuan in the early 2000s to roughly 140,000 yuan in 2021, according to research conducted by Wuhan University, in the central Hubei province. Today, some pay up to 2 million yuan.

For years, the central government has attempted to rein in the practice. This year’s national annual rural policy document, released in February, also called for continued crackdowns on high bride prices and the promotion of “simple” and “civilized” wedding traditions.

In line with the new policy, government departments in Shicheng County are working together to use pilot programs and public matchmaking services to decrease or eliminate family spending on bride prices.

At the national meeting in Ganzhou, officials discussed new data that revealed a shift: almost a third of the 361 couples who married in Shicheng County in the first half of this year reportedly paid no bride price — in contrast to years past, when bride price was expected.

In some Shicheng County villages, the rejection of high bride prices has been enshrined in local rules and customs, reportedly cutting total wedding costs to about one-fifth of what they used to be. “Red and white” councils, or hongbai lishihui — named for the colors that represent weddings and funerals — have been established to “step in” to correct excessive spending on bride prices.

Changxi village in the county has also promoted lower costs for weddings in general, ensuring that wedding banquets are kept under 680 yuan per table.

The villagers have also developed a consensus that bride prices should be kept at either 3,600 or 6,900 yuan — considered lucky in Chinese culture as “six,” or liu, is a homophone of “smooth,” and “nine,” or jiu, is a homophone of “a long time,” symbolizing a long marriage.

Shicheng also offers rewards to couples and their parents who do not spend vast sums on bride prices. Such families can apply for a card granting them access to discounts on wedding banquets, discounted business loans, free entrance to local attractions, and free pregnancy checks. Over 1,000 cards are said to have been issued this year.

“The card is not just about money; it’s an honor,” Lai Hua, deputy director of Shicheng Civil Affairs Bureau, told domestic media. “We want people who support the new customs to feel recognized, rewarded, and proud.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Wrapped bundles of cash given as bride prices in Sinan County, Guizhou province, Feb. 22, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018964/For China’s Gen Z Investors, Patriotism Meets Portfolio Math
World.title: For China’s Gen Z Investors, Patriotism Meets Portfolio Math
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018964/For China’s Gen Z Investors, Patriotism Meets Portfolio Math
World.content:
Huang Jiarui knew she’d beaten the odds when she secured 1,000 shares in CXMT’s IPO, one of China’s leading memory-chip makers and a key player in the country’s push to build its own chip industry. The allotment rate was just 0.47%.

On July 27, CXMT debuted on Shanghai’s STAR Market, the exchange’s Nasdaq-style board for tech companies. Its shares opened at 49.5 yuan ($6.93) — nearly six times the 8.66-yuan offer price. Huang sold immediately.

“Short-term moves are driven by emotion and money flow,” the 28-year-old told Sixth Tone. “The profits were already good, so I’ll wait for the price to fall back before buying again.”

Huang, who works in the financial industry in the country’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has long favored tech stocks, from Chinese battery makers to Nvidia and Tesla. In April, she began shifting more attention back to China, drawn by advances in chips, AI, and manufacturing. “In tech right now, it’s either China or the U.S.,” she said.

Asked how much those considerations influence her decisions, Huang puts the combined weight of “patriotism” and “confidence” in China at about 30%. She says they also make her willing to pay a premium for Chinese tech even when valuations look stretched.

Even so, about 80% of Huang’s portfolio remains in U.S. tech, with the remaining 20% evenly split between China and South Korea. “China’s tech sector has only been gaining ground since 2024,” she said. “The U.S., by contrast, has three decades of history to look back on.”

That mix of enthusiasm and caution is increasingly visible among a growing cohort of younger Chinese retail investors entering the market.

Lu Xiaomeng, an associate professor of finance at Shanghai’s Fudan University, said older investors tended to get information from financial news and account managers. Younger investors now open their phones to a stream of market data, influencers’ opinions, and AI analysis.

Investors born in the 1990s and 2000s accounted for more than 45% of the 27.44 million new A-share accounts opened in 2025, according to Shanghai Stock Exchange data. Separate research by Ping An Securities and the Hurun Research Institute found that investors under 30 made up about 30% of all investors, roughly double their share before September 2024.

Lu said companies such as CXMT can appeal to younger investors for reasons beyond returns. Buying shares in chipmakers and other hard-tech companies, she said, can also be a way to back industries they see as important to China’s development.

“The capital market can carry ideals,” Lu said, “but in the end, price is what counts.”

Crash course

When Huang began trading in college, she saw the stock market as a place to test what she was learning as a finance major. She quickly found that textbook models offered only so much help once real money was involved.

“Technical indicators such as moving averages and mean reversion can be helpful,” she said. “But in the end, it’s often instinct and psychological resilience that really count.”

In February, Huang bought a leveraged Nasdaq-100 exchange-traded fund (ETF) designed to magnify the index’s daily gains and losses threefold. She held on as it fell in March and, by May, had made more than $20,000. Her biggest loss came from a Hong Kong-listed AI concept stock, where she lost more than HK$40,000 ($5,100).

Over time, Huang became less convinced that active trading could consistently give her an edge. She said whatever advantage she gained over passive investing did not seem large enough to justify the time and effort she was putting in.

She still follows the market closely. Huang swaps financial news and stock ideas with her parents in a family group chat, follows financial influencers, and joins online trading groups. She also treats the mood in those groups as a signal in itself. “When everyone is excited, it’s time to reduce positions,” she said. “And when everyone is in despair, it’s time to add.”

On the popular lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, the topic “My Stock Trading Diary” has drawn nearly 3.9 billion views and over 37 million discussions. Users post about wins and losses, exchange lessons from trades, and sometimes frame investing as something larger than making money.

Some posts frame trading as a way to improve their financial circumstances; others treat it almost as a form of self-discipline. One user wrote that trading had not made him rich, but had made him want less and pay more attention to geopolitics and the chip industry.

Losses are documented just as openly. One investor who said he had lost 600,000 yuan traced his progression from denial at 150,000 yuan down, to desperation at 250,000, to delusion at 500,000, and finally resignation at zero: “Oh well, waking up to nothing.”

Shi Donghui, a finance professor at Fudan University, said the shift online has lowered the barriers to trading: investors can open accounts, check prices, find information, and place trades from their phones.

“This change has directly pushed up trading frequency,” he said. “Market correlation has increased, and short-term news can easily sway young people’s trading decisions.”

Lower barriers have also brought less experienced investors into the market, Shi said, including university students with little financial training. Easier access to information and trading, he argued, does not necessarily lead to better investment decisions.

“Big data’s targeted recommendations make it easier to create information bubbles,” Shi said. “Young people can easily be trapped by a single point of view.”

Zhang Yixuan began trading in 2019, just after turning 18. A personal finance documentary first persuaded her to start managing her money early. She began with funds, then opened a stock account after growing frustrated with the delays involved in buying and selling them.

“At the time, I had no strategy and was buying almost randomly,” Zhang said. One stock she picked was later delisted after being flagged as high risk.

She never studied a formal trading method, instead piecing together what she knows from finance books, documentaries, and videos on streaming platform Bilibili. Trading now takes up about four hours of her workday, and stocks account for roughly 60% of her liquid assets.

Unlike Huang, Zhang’s money is concentrated in non-ferrous metals and power utilities rather than domestic tech.

On July 29, after the STAR 50 — an index tracking major companies on Shanghai’s tech-focused STAR Market — had fallen sharply, she began buying an ETF that tracks it. She bought in several batches and sold around July 31 as soon as the position turned profitable. Because she does not know the tech sector well, she said, she kept the position small.

“If there’s a chance to make money, I take it,” she said. “It has nothing to do with being optimistic about the sector.”

Shi said younger investors can amplify short-term moves in fashionable sectors but are unlikely to change the market’s longer-term cycles. Previous booms in solar, liquor, and electric vehicles followed much the same pattern, he said. Sustained gains ultimately need to be supported by company earnings.

Zhang has no regular circle of trading friends and rarely discusses investment ideas with others. She follows information across several online platforms but is wary of simply following influencers.

“It’s your own money,” she said. “In the end, you have to decide for yourself.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018949/Study Linking Solar Farms to Bird Loss Draws Scrutiny in China
World.title: Study Linking Solar Farms to Bird Loss Draws Scrutiny in China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018949/Study Linking Solar Farms to Bird Loss Draws Scrutiny in China
World.content:
Solar farms reduce bird diversity, a Chinese study published last week in the international, peer-reviewed journal Science, announced. But the country’s scientific community has contested the reliability of its birdwatching data and the significance of its statistical findings.

The study, published Aug. 21, was led by researchers at Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology, in collaboration with other researchers from China, Vietnam, and the United States.

Examining 2,344 Chinese counties from 2014 to 2023, it found that cutting carbon emissions may come at the cost of protecting biodiversity, as birds’ cropland and grassland habitats are converted for solar projects.

China has been expanding solar power to meet its targets of peaking carbon emissions by 2030 and reaching carbon neutrality by 2060. By 2024, solar facilities covered an estimated 4,520 square kilometers of land and are projected to make up nearly 45% of the country’s electricity generation by 2060.

“The research is not against solar expansion but rather offers policy recommendations on how to do it better,” Li Shanjun, one of the study’s corresponding authors and a professor at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability, told Sixth Tone.

The authors suggested developing solar projects in areas where solar panels cause lower ecological impact, such as in deserts; promoting phased rollouts rather than sudden large-scale expansion; and assessing ecological recovery beyond vegetation density, as they found uniform vegetation inferior for housing bird habitats.

However, experts from the China Ornithological Society said “flaws” in the study’s bird observation data could undermine its conclusions, according to a Tuesday article published on the society’s official WeChat account. The academic group includes ornithologists from universities, research institutes, and conservation organizations nationwide.

The crowdsourced dataset from the China Birdwatching Record Center contained missing bird counts, erroneous records, and reporting differences driven by the growing popularity of birdwatching, the Society wrote.

Among the issues, over 40% of the over 500,000 reports collected during the nine years recorded the presence of species, indicated using the number “1.” However, the Society noted that this is commonly used as a placeholder when the observer did not enter a count, rather than that only one bird was seen, making the data unreliable.

The analysis also said the data had not been properly cleaned. One record from 2015, for example, reported over 2 billion little egrets at a single location. The record was retained in the dataset, contributing to bird totals “beyond a reasonable range.”

Meanwhile, the original study may have removed some migratory waterbirds’ records at wintering sites as statistical outliers, as they recorded tens of thousands of birds at a given location, “potentially underestimating true bird diversity,” the analysis said.

The analysis also noted that birdwatching records surged between 2021 and 2023 amid a growing birdwatching boom in the country, just as authorities were introducing significant solar policies. This, it argued, makes it difficult to determine whether changes in biodiversity data were driven by increased birdwatching or photovoltaic development.

Chinese ecologists generally agree that amid cutting carbon emissions, biodiversity can be protected through careful planning, Ma Zhijun, deputy director of the China Ornithological Society and a co-author of the analysis, told Sixth Tone. Ma is also a professor at Fudan University’s School of Life Sciences.

Such planning means avoiding key wildlife habitats when building solar, wind, and other renewable energy facilities, Ma said.

He added that the “easy availability” of birdwatching datasets has led researchers without a background in bird ecology to use them without “fully understanding their limitations.”

“This paper is a typical example of the problem,” he said. The analysis recommended cross-checking data from different sources and cleaning datasets before using them to assess large-scale changes.

A separate statistical analysis of the study’s data also found that birdwatching duration — where longer sessions correlate with more species detected — had a significantly greater effect on measured bird diversity than solar policy.

That analysis, published Sunday, was conducted by Lai Jiangshan, an ecology professor at Nanjing Forestry University, and Zhang Shuang, an associate researcher at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

“This (comparison of birdwatching duration and solar policy) was not reflected in the Science paper, meaning its conclusion is not statistically supported,” Zhang told Sixth Tone.

Li, one of the Science paper’s corresponding authors, responded that the two measures were “not comparable” and that the comparison was not informative for policymaking.

“Policy variables typically account for only a small share of variation in environmental outcomes,” he said. “But policies remain among the few tools people can actively change.”

Li also rejected any suggestion that the team had concealed metrics, noting that the full data and code used to run the statistical models were publicly available. Regarding the birdwatching data, he said the findings were tested using different statistical methods, and outliers were removed.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Solar panels cover the mountains in Anshun, Guizhou province, Aug. 4, 2024.)

World.title: US-Iran strikes raise fears of renewed war across the Middle East
World.content:
Mourners carry a banner against US President Donald Trump as they gather on the day of the burial of Iran's late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Mashhad, Iran, July 9, 2026.

Iran accuses the US of causing civilian casualties during a wedding celebration, while the US military denies targeting civilians and states that their strikes aimed at military assets

Fears of renewed escalation gripped the Middle East on Wednesday, September 2, after the United States and Iran exchanged their biggest barrage since July, with Washington striking Iran’s southern coast and Tehran firing at US bases across the region.

With the US threatening further strikes, Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing four people and wounding dozens. Its health minister later said 18 people in total had been killed and 108 injured in the latest wave of US strikes.

The US military said it struck air defenses, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Tuesday, September 1, Iran reported hits on multiple targets near the Strait of Hormuz.

The flare-up threatens to deepen a conflict that has dragged on since the US launched strikes on Iran in February, disrupting global energy supplies and drawing opposition from a majority of Americans ahead of November’s congressional elections.

“Last night was like the end of the world,” Mahmoud, 38, a municipal worker in Sirik County along the strait, told Reuters by telephone, describing attacks on the area that includes the city where the wedding was reported to have been hit.

President Donald Trump said the US hit Iran “very hard” and that Iran only responded with a “love tap.”

“It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one any time we want,” Trump told reporters at the White House.

Iran struck what it said were US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, and said its aim was now to drive US forces from the vast network of military bases they have maintained for decades across the Middle East.

“American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences,” Iran’s military command said.

Iran said it killed US forces in Jordan and at a base in northern Iraq, but US officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.

In Kuwait, Iran said it had carried out a missile and drone attack on the US Ali Al Salem air base and on a residential complex used by a US commander. Kuwait’s fire service said it put out a blaze at a residential complex hit by a drone.

Qatar, home of the largest US air base in the Gulf, said it held Iran responsible for attacks and their repercussions. Bahrain, which houses the regional headquarters of the US Navy, said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.

Iran also said two tankers had been struck by mines while being steered through the Strait of Hormuz by US personnel.

Washington says that despite Iranian attacks it is guiding ships through the strait. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said more than 17 million barrels of oil exited on Monday.

Iran blacklisted 11 more ships, bringing the total number of such vessels to 56, a government website showed, meaning it would consider them subject to fines, confiscation or detention if they try to sail through the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran’s permission.

Trump repeated his assertion that the strait, which handled 20% of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war, was open to shipping.

Iran says wedding struck

Iranians were fearful that the new strikes signalled war could restart at full scale.

“It’s very difficult to live like this. We don’t know when America will strike,” Mahpari, 28, a woman in the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, told Reuters by phone.

Iran said four people including a 4-year-old were killed while celebrating a wedding at a home in Sirik. Iranian media said as many as 68 people were wounded there, and released images of injured children in hospital.

Reuters was unable to independently verify the incident.

US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.

Video shot by Iran’s West Asia News Agency at the purported site showed rubble strewn across rooms and a courtyard. A pair of strappy women’s dress sandals lay abandoned on a blood-soaked carpet.

“I am just glad the casualties weren’t even worse,” said Ali Molahi, identified as the father of the bride.

Conflict draining both sides

The exchange of fire was the worst since July, when Trump abruptly halted two weeks of intense bombing of Iran after warnings from his military brass that they were using up munitions and running out of meaningful targets.

Trump has yet to achieve the aims he set when launching “Operation Epic Fury” in February – to end Iran’s nuclear programme, deprive it of the ability to strike its neighbors and create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers.

But the US has seriously degraded Iran’s conventional military forces and taken a toll on Iran’s already weakening economy, US officials say.

Sources have told Reuters Trump aides are trying to keep the war quiet for now to avert a defeat in the midterm elections in November. Polls show Americans oppose the war by more than a two-to-one margin. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] Clarifying some tax issues related to ONETT transactions
World.content:
ONETT refers to transactions that are subject to one-time tax compliance and processing with the BIR

The Philippine Tax Whiz answers common questions on ONETT transactions and explains key tax issues clarified by the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) under Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 75-2026.

What transactions are classified as One-Time Transactions (ONETT)?

ONETT refers to transactions that are subject to one-time tax compliance and processing with the BIR. These include the following:

Sale of real property classified as a capital asset;

Sale, transfer, or assignment of shares of stock not traded through the stock exchange;

Sale of real property classified as an ordinary asset;

Donation of property; and

Transfer of properties arising from a decedent’s estate.

Taxpayers undertaking any of these transactions are generally required to comply with the applicable documentary requirements, pay the corresponding taxes, and secure the necessary BIR-issued documents, such as the Electronic Certificate Authorizing Registration (eCAR), before the property or shares can be validly transferred or registered.

Can the BIR issue the eCAR even if the Value-Added Tax (VAT) has not yet been paid?

Yes. The BIR may still issue the eCAR even if the VAT due on the transaction has not yet been paid. However, the issuance of the eCAR does not extinguish the taxpayer’s obligation to pay the applicable VAT. The concerned office issuing the eCAR shall inform the Revenue District Office (RDO) for the appropriate assessment and collection of the VAT due, if applicable.

Accordingly, taxpayers should not interpret the issuance of the eCAR as confirmation that all tax liabilities arising from the transaction have been fully settled. Any unpaid VAT remains subject to assessment and collection by the concerned RDO.

In case the seller and buyer agreed that the buyer shall assume the payment of Capital Gains Tax (CGT) instead of the seller, should the amount of CGT be included/added in the selling price for purposes of determining the tax base of the CGT?

No. The computation shall be whichever is highest of the following amounts:

Selling Price (as shown on Deed of Absolute Sale or DOAS, excluding Capital Gains Tax)

Fair Market Value (FMV) or Zonal Value determined by the BIR commissioner

FMV by the Provincial or City Assessor until amended by the Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RPVARA), where it is based on Schedule of Market Value (SMV) or actual gross selling price, whichever is higher.

The Documentary Stamp Tax (DST) shall likewise be computed the same as the basis of CGT, except in government transactions, where DST is based on the consideration paid.

Is a dacion en pago considered a sale or transfer of property subject to tax?

Yes. A dacion en pago is considered a transfer of ownership where a debtor conveys property to a creditor as settlement of an existing obligation. Although the transaction is intended to settle a debt, it is treated as a transfer of property for tax purposes.

The applicable taxes depend on the classification of the property transferred:

If the property is classified as a capital asset: Capital Gains Tax (CGT) Documentary Stamp Tax (DST)

If the property is classified as an ordinary asset: Creditable Withholding Tax (CWT) Value-Added Tax (VAT), if applicable Documentary Stamp Tax (DST)



Is the actual use of the property the basis for determining its tax classification?

No. For purposes of computing the applicable taxes, the classification indicated in the Tax Declaration shall be the basis, and not merely the actual use of the property.

For instance, a property may be currently used as a small bake shop or other commercial establishment; however, if the Tax Declaration classifies the property as residential, such classification shall be considered in determining the applicable tax treatment.

Similarly, a property with an area of less than 1,000 square meters that is classified as agricultural in the Tax Declaration shall not be automatically considered residential solely because of its size. The classification reflected in the Tax Declaration shall prevail in determining the applicable tax treatment. – Rappler.com

Mon Abrea is a Global Tax Policy Expert and Chief Tax Advisor of the Asian Consulting Group (ACG), the Philippines’ premier tax advisory and investment consulting firm—providing tax strategy, compliance, and policy advisory services to multinational corporations, foreign investors, and government institutions. World.title: 12 years after peace deal, violence still stalks Bangsamoro
World.content:
COMMAND CONFERENCE. Commission on Elections Chairman George Erwin Garcia, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla, and PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. conduct a final command conference for the 2026 BARMM parliamentary elections at the PROBAR Multi-purpose Center in Camp BGen. Salipada K. Pendatun, Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, on August 26, 2026.

Upcoming regional elections pose risks of voter intimidation and violence, prompting calls for police reforms, tighter firearm controls, and better military-police coordination to keep the vote peaceful

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – The war that once consumed parts of Mindanao has long ended, but the machineries that sustained violence have proved far more difficult to dismantle.

In the Bangsamoro region, the old conflict has given way to a more diffused and persistent disorder, with clan feuds, political rivalries and criminal networks continuing to flourish where the institutions meant to keep the peace remain weak.

Twelve years after a landmark peace agreement, the International Crisis Group said in a report released on Thursday, September 3, that the region’s fragile security system remains heavily dependent on the military.

Weak policing and justice institutions have left soldiers carrying much of the burden of maintaining order in the seven-year-old Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, even as the government seeks to move the military away from counterinsurgency and toward external defense.

The International Crisis Group report was released barely two weeks ahead of the Muslim-majority region’s first regional parliamentary elections since it replaced the now-defunct Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao.

The 2014 peace agreement between the government during the presidency of the late Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) ended years of fighting, while the BARMM was established in 2019 as part of the transition to peace.

On Tuesday, September 1, Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity Mel Senen Sarmiento said the country’s focus had “decisively shifted” from navigating the challenges of internal conflict toward peacebuilding, adding that “the dividends of peace are now upon us.”

Sarmiento said a just and lasting peace required more than “silencing the instruments of war and signing peace accords,” adding that efforts should also focus on nurturing communities where “positive peace can firmly take root and flourish.”

He said the success of the September 14 election would not be measured by who wins or loses, but by whether the Bangsamoro people were able to vote freely, peace was preserved, and the result reflected the genuine choice of the electorate.

The government and MILF peace implementing panels, led by Sarmiento and his counterpart, Mohagher Iqbal, also signed a pledge of commitment for the peaceful, orderly and credible conduct of the Bangsamoro elections. (LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections)

Uneven curbing of violence

The International Crisis Group report said progress in curbing violence in the BARMM has been uneven, with clan feuds, electoral rivalries, and criminal activities still posing a greater threat than fighting between the state and militant groups.

It said over a third of young people in the region have experienced armed conflict in or near their homes since 2019, based on a 2024 youth assessment. A local conflict watchdog, using data from community networks, recorded hundreds of incidents since January.

Militant groups and local conflicts

The think tank said jihadist groups that stayed outside the peace process remain a security threat, although it noted that attacks on state forces have declined.

It also noted that remnants of the communist New People’s Army operate in parts of Lanao del Sur and Maguindanao del Norte.

Land disputes, rido (clan feuds) and political rivalries remain major sources of violence, with local disputes sometimes escalating into large-scale clashes, the group said.

Easy access to firearms has fueled recurring cycles of violence, it said, while key provisions of the peace agreement, including the disarmament of former rebels and private militias and the redeployment of troops, remain incomplete.

Guns and unfinished disarmament

The proliferation of firearms, it said, remains a major source of insecurity, with the police estimating in late 2024 that the region had more than 27,000 unregistered firearms, while a source interviewed by Crisis Group estimated that about 20,000 were legally registered.

Based on the 2014 peace agreement, the MILF has gradually decommissioned its forces. About 14,000 fighters and 2,450 weapons remained to be decommissioned in 2026, underscoring the unfinished nature of the process.

The MILF, however, suspended its formal engagement with the government earlier this year over what it saw as Manila’s failure to fulfill promises of socioeconomic benefits before resuming talks in August. Demobilization, however, appeared to remain on hold.

Criminal economy

The region’s illicit economy has changed since the 2014 peace deal. Kidnapping for ransom, once a major problem in Mindanao, has almost disappeared, but smuggling has proliferated, including weapons.

Human trafficking and drug trafficking also remain concerns.

Crisis Group recorded at least 10 anti-drug operations across the predominantly Muslim region since the start of the year. In August, a clash between security forces and an armed drug-trafficking outfit in Tawi-Tawi killed one person and wounded three others, including a naval officer.

Policing and justice

The report, “Policing the Bangsamoro: Peace in the Southern Philippines,” said the Philippine National Police had struggled to establish a credible role in parts of the autonomous region affected by violence, while the integration of former Moro rebels into the force had moved slowly.

BARMM communities often view the police as weaker, more politicized, and less dependable than the military, the report said.

The Bangsamoro regional government’s institutions for dispute resolution and justice have also faced challenges, including political infighting, limited resources, and poor access to courts, it added.

Long distances, case backlogs, and high costs have made formal courts difficult to access for many of the region’s poorest residents, while disputes between rival clans can trigger further retaliation even after cases are brought before the justice system.

Elections and recommendations

With the region’s parliamentary elections approaching, rival political blocs and local elites may enlist armed groups to intimidate voters or disrupt the ballot, potentially aggravating tensions in areas where land, political, and clan disputes remain unresolved.

Sarmiento said the government-MILF ceasefire mechanisms must “protect the peace, prevent armed confrontation, address tensions before they escalate, and ensure that our ceasefire mechanisms remain responsive and effective.”

He said the mechanisms “must never be used to favor any candidate, party, or political group,” adding that their “role is not to influence the political choice of the people, but to help create an environment where that choice can be made without fear, coercion, intimidation, or violence.”

Sarmiento urged the Coordinating Committees on the Cessation of Hostilities and the Ad Hoc Joint Action Group to exercise “vigilance and close coordination on the ground” and to “keep communication lines open. Immediately address incidents that may threaten the ceasefire.”

The Crisis Group, meanwhile, called for reforms to professionalize the police, strengthen community policing and improve coordination between the police and military.

It said the military should gradually reduce its role in maintaining public order in areas where security conditions allow, enabling the police to take on more responsibility.

The report also urged tighter controls on firearms, stronger courts, and peacebuilding efforts to address the roots of local conflicts.

“Much as it was a singular achievement to end decades of insurgency, communities will not feel safe until the peace gets the policing it needs,” the report said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sheila Sison and her string of objections that rattled the prosecution
World.content:
SISON. Defense lead counsel Shiela Sison listens to a testimony of hostile witness Atty. Michael Poa during Day 21 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 2, 2026.

'I guess what the public should understand... is our objections and the number of our objections will always depend on the questions from the other party,' deputy defense spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular says

It took 21 trial days to have defense lead counsel Sheila Sison on the floor as the lawyer in charge of cross-examining a prosecution witness.

The public and media alike knew about her appearance only on Wednesday morning, September 2, when she announced that she would cross-examine fellow defense lawyer Michael Poa herself.

It makes sense, right? Poa is one of the defense’s major assets so he deserves a big gun like Sison. Plus, prosecution spokesperson Jay Tolosa, a seasoned litigator who has handled major cases, was the one assigned for the direct examination.

Tolosa came in hot with his presentation. He sought to establish that Poa prepared the Department of Education’s (DepEd) reply to questions on the confidential funds use, yet the former DepEd chief of staff was unaware that security personnel handled the said money.

But Sison showed dominance. She called Tolosa’s opening statement mere rhetoric. She also took offense at the prosecution’s phrase — “abogadong walang alam” (a lawyer who doesn’t know anything) — when it referred to Poa.

Play Video

“When I said, ‘ang abogadong walang alam,’ what I meant was, in Congress, he repeatedly said he knew totally nothing about the use and liquidation of the confidential funds. Context is very important,” said Tolosa.

“I am certain that the counsel has in his vocabulary other terms for ‘ang abogadong walang alam.’ If that was his explanation, he could have simply said that the witness has no personal knowledge. And that would have been more respectful and more apt, if that was the intention, as he had said,” said the lead defense counsel in response.

The rough start spelled how the entire trial would go. Sison and Tolosa went on to have heated exchanges from time to time — sometimes partnered with snarky remarks.

The two clashed again when Tolosa cut off Poa when he was responding to the former’s question about rewards related to surveillance activities. Sison insisted that Poa be allowed to answer the query.

For the duration of Tolosa’s direct examination, Sison fired objections numerous times. The lead defense counsel objected to the prosecution’s use of the word “whatever” in a question. She raised different objections on several grounds, some for being misleading or argumentative. Presiding officer Chiz Escudero sustained most of these objections.

Sison’s continued objections obviously affected Tolosa’s examination. The prosecutor, at multiple times, flipped the documents in his hand. There were moments of dead air, which presiding officer Chiz Escudero used to remind counsels about court matters.

“That is never our intention…. I hope the public understands by the end of the day, we have high respect for each other. And we are all aware that we are merely doing our job,” deputy defense spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular explained when asked about observations pertaining to Sison’s objections.

Point well taken. The defense was just doing its job which is to raise objections if there are matters that are objectionable.

But was Sison’s demeanor a strategy? A tactic to rattle the prosecution?

Play Video

“I guess what the public should understand… is our objections and the number of our objections will always depend on the questions from the other party. [If they are] objectionable, we raise it and we respect the decision of the presiding officer to sustain it or not,” Gular explained in a mix of Filipino and English.

“So it’s not our strategy to raise voluminous objections on a certain day. It just depends on what comes and what arises during the trial,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pisay students develop management platform for school emergencies
World.content:
EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT. From left to right, Ligtas Skwela project leader Kush Shekar, developer Vic Andrei Hernando, and market research head Lorenzo Pariñas prepare for their five-minute presentation at the Startup Technology Pitching competition on August 28, 2026.

Three junior high students from the Philippine Science High School-Caraga create Ligtas Skwela, an innovative online platform for tracking student safety during emergencies, winning top honors at a regional tech competition

MANILA, Philippines – Three junior high school students from the Philippine Science High School-Caraga have developed an online platform designed to help schools track students during fires, earthquakes, and other emergencies within the school.

Called Ligtas Skwela, the platform is accessible online, allowing teachers and school administrators an overview of classrooms and students during an emergency.

The project won first place in the student category of the Startup Technology Pitching Competition during the Department of Science and Technology’s Regional Science, Technology, and Innovation Week in Caraga, held from August 27 to 29.

The team consists of project leader Kush Shekar, software developer Lorenzo Pariñas, and market research head Vic Andrei Hernando.

Pariñas said recent school emergencies, including the shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University, prompted the students to think about how schools account for students during a crisis.

“We’ve noticed that sometimes, in the system, they tend to not focus on the students and where they are in school,” Pariñas said.

Ligtas Skwela has two interfaces: Teacher Mode and Commander Mode.

Teachers can use the platform to report the condition of their classes, while Commander Mode provides administrators with information on classrooms, teachers, and their status, including whether a room is secure or whether people need medical assistance.

Instead of relying only on head counts, the system tracks students by name, allowing administrators to determine who is missing, Shekar said.

The developers said the website is functional but has so far only been tested on their campus. The current version requires an internet connection, although the team plans to develop an offline version.

They also plan to incorporate physical hardware, including buttons that could be used to conduct drills and trigger alarms.

The students envision offering Ligtas Skwela through a subscription model. Based on their current projections, it would cost P30,000 annually for a school with 1,000 students, or about P30 per student.

The team, mentored by engineer Lyndon Bermoy, was the only high school group among the nine finalists in the competition.

The students are also preparing to apply for a patent for the platform. – Rappler.com

World.title: [In the Public Square] Two months in: Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial so far
World.content:
LIVE

The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by a late, great constitutionalist: it is 'political justice'

We’ve just completed Day 21, and Week 9, of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Today, public prosecutor Representative Joel Chua suggested that the prosecution may be able to finish its presentation of evidence in chief by early October. That means, he said, the trial might end by December.

As people say, malayo pa, pero malayo na. Two months in, how goes the impeachment of Sara Duterte?

The impeachment can be viewed in terms popularized by the late, great constitutionalist Fr. Joaquin Bernas SJ: it is “political justice.” It’s important to listen to legal analysts, and we will continue to do so.

But it’s equally important to hear from political scientists, and in this episode of In the Public Square, Rappler columnist John Nery is joined by highly esteemed professors of political science.

Dr. Jean Franco is a professor of political science at the UP Diliman and Arjan Aguirre is assistant professor of political science on leave at the Ateneo de Manila, who is doing his PhD at the University of Pittsburgh.

Catch the episode on Wednesday, September 2, 2026, at 8 pm.-Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Wins First Gold Medals at World Nomad Games in Kyrgyz Republic
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan claimed its first two gold medals at the sixth World Nomad Games in the Kyrgyz Republic, with Nurtalap Kerim and Sailau Mukhamedzhan winning titles in audaryspak, a traditional Kazakh horseback wrestling sport.

In the up to 60-kilogram category, Kerim defeated a Kyrgyz representative in the final to become champion. In the up to 70-kilogram category, Mukhamedzhan also faced a Kyrgyz athlete in the final and won 2-1.

The two victories marked Kazakhstan’s first gold medals at this year’s Games. More than 11,500 people in Kazakhstan regularly practice audaryspak, which combines horseback riding with wrestling and requires strength, agility, speed and courage.

The sixth World Nomad Games officially opened in Bishkek on Aug. 31, bringing together athletes from more than 100 countries. The Games run through Sept. 6, with competitions in Bishkek and the Issyk-Kul region.

The event follows the fifth World Nomad Games, which Kazakhstan hosted in Astana in September 2024. The six-day competition featured 21 sports and athletes from 89 countries, with Kazakhstan sending the largest delegation of 195 athletes. The Kazakh team topped the final medal standings with 112 medals, including 43 gold, 32 silver and 37 bronze.

The World Nomad Games bring together traditional sports and cultural heritage from nomadic civilizations, providing an international platform to preserve and promote these traditions.

World.title: Kazakhstan Positions Itself as Key China-Europe Land Corridor as Ties With Beijing Expand: Key Take-Outs from Tokayev’s Interview with Хinhua
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is positioning itself as a key land corridor between China, Central Asia, the Caucasus and Europe while seeking to deepen cooperation with Beijing in trade, technology and investment, Kazakh political scientist and historian Daniyar Ashimbayev wrote in his Telegram channel, commenting on President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s Sept.1 interview with Xinhua.

Ashimbayev noted that Tokayev’s interview strongly emphasized Xi Jinping’s policy and the development of Kazakhstan-China relations, highlighting trade, Chinese investment, humanitarian cooperation and the importance of ensuring Chinese transit through Kazakhstan.

The analyst also pointed to a broader strategic context. As global competition intensifies and international economic routes evolve, Kazakhstan is seeking to secure its position as a major land bridge between China and European markets.

Middle Corridor strengthens Kazakhstan’s strategic role

Tokayev described Kazakhstan-China relations as being at an “unprecedentedly high level” and reaffirmed Kazakhstan’s readiness to consistently strengthen the two countries’ “eternal comprehensive strategic partnership.”

Trade and investment remain central to the relationship, with China ranking first among Kazakhstan’s external trade partners. At the same time, transport and logistics have become a strategic pillar.

“Together with our Chinese partners, we are transforming this geographical advantage into modern transport and logistics infrastructure of Eurasian scale,” Tokayev said.

Kazakhstan is developing the Middle Corridor, including new railways, dry ports, logistics terminals and border infrastructure. The President stressed the need to make the route more competitive through “smart customs,” digital documentation, synchronized information systems and automated border procedures.

For Kazakhstan, this means turning its geographic position into a long-term economic advantage rather than relying solely on transit potential.

Technology emerges as the next growth area

Ashimbayev highlighted another key point from the interview: Tokayev’s assessment of China as a global leader in artificial intelligence, digital technologies, robotics, new energy and high-tech manufacturing.

This points to a possible new phase in bilateral cooperation as Kazakhstan accelerates its own digital transformation. Tokayev said recent meetings with Chinese technology companies had demonstrated mutual interest in projects covering the digital economy, smart manufacturing, e-commerce, research and workforce training.

“Technological cooperation can become one of the most important areas of the new stage of Kazakh-Chinese cooperation,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s decision to join the 29 founding states of the World Association of International Cooperation on Artificial Intelligence (WAICO) in Shanghai in July also reflects the country’s growing focus on international AI cooperation.

Tokayev stressed that artificial intelligence should serve humanity and that access to technology, knowledge and computing resources should be fair.

Strategic alignment without formal bloc politics

The interview also reaffirmed shared positions on the role of the United Nations, international law, mediation and peaceful settlement of conflicts.

Tokayev reiterated Kazakhstan’s adherence to the One China principle and opposition to violations of territorial integrity. Ashimbayev noted that Beijing values Kazakhstan’s consistency on this issue.

At the same time, he pointed out that Tokayev did not rank Kazakhstan’s strategic partners in the interview, as he sometimes does when speaking in a Western context. In Ashimbayev’s assessment, Beijing does not require such declarations because it already understands the depth of the bilateral relationship.

People-to-people ties add another layer

Economic and strategic cooperation is accompanied by expanding humanitarian ties. Kazakhstan and China are marking the 2026 Cross-Year of Culture, while tens of thousands of Kazakh students study in China and Chinese students study in Kazakhstan.

Chinese university branches, Luban Workshops and academic mobility programs are expanding educational links. The visa-free regime has also boosted tourism: 962,000 Chinese citizens visited Kazakhstan in 2025, up 47% from the previous year.

With diplomatic relations set to reach their 35th anniversary in 2027, the partnership is increasingly extending beyond traditional trade and energy links into transit, technology, education and broader international cooperation.
