World.title: The moment a man is struck by lightning – then walks away unharmed
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaExtreme weather The moment a man is struck by lightning – then walks away unharmed Alexandra Snow September 3, 2026 — 11:11am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Thomas Fahmy stepped out his front door in New York’s Staten Island to head to the dentist, he was hit with a bolt from above. Footage from a home security camera shows the US Republican Party political staffer suddenly drop to the ground in a fiery flash – just metres from his car. “I didn’t even have a chance to step back, I just fell to the floor,” he said of the shock incident on August 27. Fahmy suffered no severe injuries and remained conscious the entire time, only reporting an intense burning sensation, tingling and pain in both of his feet.



Seconds later, he gathered himself, stood up and hobbled away, knocking on the nearest door for help. Stephanie Homan came to the front door with a young child in her arms, which Fahmy said reminded him of an image of the Madonna and child. Stephanie Homan came to the front door with a young child in her arms, which Fahmy said reminded him of an image of the Madonna and child. This image of Madonna and Christ Child is in St. Peter’s Basilica at the Vatican. AP Homan helped him inside her home, called 911 and within minutes emergency responders arrived. Fahmy was taken to Northwell Staten Island University Hospital, in Ocean Breeze, to be examined by doctors.



He did not suffer any visible burns from the lightning strike but was monitored overnight before being released the following day. After being discharged, he bought a Mega Millions lottery ticket and then attended church, where that day’s Bible reading was about the apocalypse, which he thought was particularly apt. The odds of winning the Mega Millions lottery jackpot are one in 300 million. Representative Nicole Malliotakis, a Republican from New York. Bloomberg Fahmy works in US representative Nicole Malliotakis’ Staten Island office. Malliotakis said: “We are grateful that Thomas, a member of my congressional staff, is alive and well after being struck by lightning last week.



“I thank the good Samaritan who ran to his aid and the medical staff at Staten Island University Hospital who treated him.” Fahmy gained a new perspective on life after finding himself on the ground following the lightning strike. He said: “In politics, you kind of forget sometimes that there’s something bigger than you. There is a power greater than you. “It all goes down the drain once you see life literally flash in front of your eyes.” In the US, there is roughly a one in 1.2 million chance of being struck by lightning in any given year.



While almost 90 per cent of all people struck by lightning survive, many are left with various degrees of disability, according to the US National Weather Service. Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

It comes a week later than expected, but Nash Rawiller believes his return aboard Lindermann could prove perfect timing as he chases a bonus win in the group 2 Chelmsford Stakes (1600m) on Saturday at Randwick. Rawiller was to ride Godolphin star Beiwacht in the group 1 Winx Stakes at Randwick two weeks ago, with hopes Chris Waller-trained stablemate Lindermann would be scratched and saved for him to partner in the Memsie Stakes a week later at Caulfield. Nash Rawiller pushes Lindermann to victory in the Chelmsford Stakes last year. Getty Images A slight temperature for Beiwacht forced a late change, putting Rawiller on Aeliana in the Winx and back to Beiwacht instead for the group 1 Memsie, which the pair then dominated with a front-running, three-length victory. Seven-year-old Lindermann faded when first up in the Winx Stakes to finish more than seven lengths ninth. It was a similar effort to his 2025 run when 10th, and Rawiller hopes history can repeat in the Chelmsford, which they claimed with a gritty performance out front to hold off Sir Delius. Rawiller has won five times on the Lonhro gelding and they were second, ahead of Autumn Glow, in Sir Delius’ Queen Elizabeth Stakes victory last time together.



Rawiller was forgiving of Lindermann’s Winx run and keen to get him back on track. Nash Rawiller returns a winner on Lindermann in the Hill Stakes. Godolphin Australia boss Andy Makiv has said the Manikato Stakes could be next for the three-time group 1 winner before possibly going to Australia’s two richest races. “I think with the Everest, being a strong 1400m horse, it could be an advantage, so it will be interesting,” Rawiller said. “If he can keep his confidence up and show he’s ready to go there, I think he would be one of the main chances.” Rawiller was also confident about his chances with another warhorse on Saturday, Private Eye ($3.90), in the group 2 Tramway Stakes (1400m) after the nine-year-old was strong to the line when second to Cosmic Crusader in the PB Lawrence Stakes (1400m).



Nash Rawiller winning the PB Lawrence Stakes last year on Private Eye. Rawiller has picked up the ride on Screen Icon ($21) in the Furious Stakes, and he will chase back-to-back Highway wins on Mrs Goldberg ($4.20). “I think it’s important for [Screen Icon] not to work too hard early and leave her with a good kick at the 300,” he said. “Mrs Goldberg looks well weighted again and she enjoyed sitting off that hot tempo last time. She was pretty explosive.”

World.title: Emergency powers used to open Southland's Waituna Lagoon
World.content:
Southland's regional council will use emergency powers to open Waituna Lagoon to the sea after weeks of unusually high water levels.

The council said the lagoon near Invercargill had stayed above 2.2m since late July, affecting nearby roads, paddocks and farms.

For the past five days it had been above 2.3m, the council said.

General manager integrated catchment management Lucy Hicks said the lagoon's opening should reduce pressure on surrounding land and lower the risk of ecological damage in warmer months.

"There are trade-offs in opening the lagoon at this time of year," she said.

"We need to reduce the risk of nutrient-rich water sitting in the lagoon and fuelling algal growth, while also considering spring and summer growth for Ruppia and other aquatic plants."

Diggers will carve a channel through the gravel bar separating the lagoon from the sea so the water can drain out.

Hicks said the lagoon could not be closed mechanically once it was open.

"It requires the right combination of wind and sea conditions to push gravel back into the channel that we will be creating with the digger."

Waituna Lagoon is part of the internationally significant Awarua-Waituna Wetlands.

It has previously been plagued by algal blooms and deteriorating water quality.

World.title: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon won't say what level of Taiwanese government will be invited to Pacific Islands' Forum
World.content:
The Prime Minister won't say what level of Taiwanese government representation will be invited to the Pacific Islands' Forum (PIF) when New Zealand hosts next year.

Christopher Luxon said New Zealand would revert to its "normal protocols and the normal engagement," but wouldn't say what that looked like.

It comes as Taiwan's Foreign Minister told Australian media in Palau he - or another minister - was keen to attend the New Zealand meeting.

There had been some tension at this week's forum in Palau - a republic in free association with the United States - after it invited Taiwan. Its foreign minister, Lin Chia-lung, accepted.

Leaders at the round table for the 55th Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting Plenary in Koror, Palau. 2 September 2026. TMC Palau/Ohanna Rabo Galo

That led to China warning of consequences.

It comes as both Luxon and his Foreign Minister Winston Peters deny that foreign interference could compromise the strength of the Forum as a centralising force for the region, helping pacific nations make collective decisions about issues that face them.

New Zealand adheres to the One China policy, which means it doesn't hold formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

Asked repeatedly by reporters on Thursday, Luxon couldn't answer whether the foreign minister would be invited next year.

"We will just revert back to the long established norms that we've had around managing that issue, and it won't be a problem at all.

"We'll just go back to our normal protocols and the normal engagement.

"We've managed this issue since 1992 very well. It's actually been managed here pretty well too, within those norms as well," he added in relation to PIF.

He said there had always been an opportunity for Taiwan to engage with partners.

Asked if that was at the ministerial level, he said that would be worked through next year.

Luxon wouldn't specify exactly what the normal protocol was, and blamed the media for making the China-Taiwan dynamic a distraction.

"Inside the PIF that hasn't been a focus," he said.

"I know there's been a lot of focus on the China-Taiwan dynamic, but actually, we think it has been fairly well managed that tension here.

World.title: US unveils more than $150 million deal in Pacific investments and assistance
World.content:
The United States will spend upwards of US$150 million on projects and initiatives in the Pacific.

The US State Department said the Trump Administration is reorienting Pacific relationships towards "championing US enterprise and investments", mirroring its approach to much of the developing world.

US commits millions to various Pacific projects Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

The State Department's second top diplomat, Christopher Landau, has been on the Pacific meeting circuit regularly since February, when leaders were invited to Honolulu to hobnob with US investors and military officers.

Its biggest spend is a fuel security deal that, pending US Congress, would dole out US$60m to fix up energy infrastructure and build storage capacity.

The big winners of the US' lolly scramble are the Cook Islands - with US$50 million for its Penhryn Atoll port announced on Tuesday, and the Compact of Freely Associated States; Palau, Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.

Palau, this year's Pacific Islands Forum leaders summit hosts, will walk away from the meeting with cash for a new hospital upgrade, support to test and clean its drinking water, and a co-chair role on a new US-backed Pacific Policing Forum.

The Marshall Islands will receive technical assistance to modernise its mobile network, and each of the Compact states will see the return of the US Peace Corp, the highly sought after band of American volunteers.

Tonga, which is subject to a harsh travel ban into the US, is being given feasibility studies for fuel storage and data centres.

World.title: More banks pass on OCR increase
World.content:
Is there any point in KiwiSaver if I'm on a total remuneration package? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

BNZ, ASB and Kiwibank have become the latest to move on interest rates, after the official cash rate was increased on Wednesday.

The rate lifted 25 basis points.

Westpac and ANZ increased interest rates on Wednesday afternoon.

On Thursday, Kiwibank said it was increasing its variable home loan rate and offfset variable rate by 25 basis points, to 6.25 percent.

Its revolving loan rate increases from 6.05 percent to 6.3 percent.

It is also passing on increases to savers, but to a lesser degree.

Barbara Edmonds responds to OCR rise by Reserve Bank Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Its 90-day and 32-day notice saver rates lift by 15 basis points, to 2.75 percent and 2.2 percent, respectively.

Its standard online call, PIE online call and business online call interest rates are also lifting by 15 basis points.

BNZ is passing on the full 25 basis point increase in the OCR to its variable housing rates, effective 17 September.

ASB said it too was increasing its variable home loan rate by the full 25 basis points, its Savings Plus product by the same margin and its Headstart rate by 10 basis points.

In its monetary policy statement, the Reserve Bank criticised banks for not passing on increases to term deposit rates.

It said the monetary policy committee had noted a "more limited pass through of higher wholesale interest rates to term deposit rates", which made funding cheaper for banks.

"A greater pass through to deposit rates would be more consistent with the desired stance and transmission of monetary policy."

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen told RNZ on Wednesday it was fair criticism from the Reserve Bank.

"There hasn't been quite as much of a lift in term deposits as wholesale interest rates have increased but retail mortgage rates of course have moved up faster than term deposits.

"Even some slim difference between passing on interest rate increases to retail mortgage rates versus term deposits can start to create some larger margins for banks - and what the Reserve Bank is saying here is that, if both retail mortgage rates and term deposits were seeing more equal pass-through, the signalling from interest rates would be more balanced.

"Higher mortgage rates and other lending rates suggest that everyone should spend and invest relatively less than they did before, and higher savings rates, like term deposits, also send a signal that you'll get a bit more if you save rather than spend/invest. That's the transmission the Reserve Bank is talking about."

World.title: 'Imagine if all of us showed up': Young voters urged to enrol
World.content:
The number of young people enrolled to vote has increased over the past month, but almost 188,000 18- to 24-year-olds remain unenrolled ahead of this year's general election.

The youth enrolment rate rose from 53.89 percent at the end of July to 57.45 percent at the end of August. There are currently 253,158 18- to 24-year-olds enrolled to vote.

On A Roll, a rangatahi-led non-partisan campaign, is now urging young people to get on the roll before the 25 October deadline.

Ethan Reille (Kāi Tahu), 22, is one of the rangatahi behind the kaupapa and said young people need to see voting as something bigger than political parties.

"This shouldn't be about political parties. It should be about our communities, the kind of future we want to inherit, and also just ensuring that we have a seat at the table."

Reille said young people's low participation could become a cycle, with a lack of trust in politicians making young people feel disconnected from the political system.

"We know that young people don't feel prioritised by politicians. Therefore, they don't see themselves in the system, and therefore they don't vote. And because they don't vote, politicians will continue to not prioritise those very young people."

VNP / Daniela Maoate-Cox

Barriers to voting

On A Roll was created in response to changes made through the Electoral Amendment Act, including the removal of same-day enrolment.

"By virtue of that, there are more barriers for young people to be voting in this year's general election," Reille said.

"We know that young people, particularly 18- to 24-year-olds, are the least likely to be enrolling and voting, and that's by virtue of the statistics."

Reille said 16,000 more young people had enrolled in the past month, which he described as "really good" progress.

"That shows that we're making moves."

But he said there was still a long way to go.

"Imagine if all of us showed up," he said.

"Imagine what kind of future Aotearoa would look like if all of us showed up and enrolled to vote for this year's general election."

22-year-old Ethan Reille (Kāi Tahu) wants rangatahi to imagine an Aotearoa where every young person turned up to vote. Supplied / Ethan Reille

Why are young people less likely to be enrolled?

Reille said young people's disengagement was not necessarily about indifference, but a lack of confidence that voting would make a difference.

"I think the goalposts keep on shifting. For a long time now, young people have been excluded from the system and the way our election cycles are set up. There's the sense of a self-reinforcing cycle."

He said the campaign wanted to make the process easier to understand, while moving the focus away from political parties.

"The conversations we're having on the ground is voting does seem hard.

"Our job in Aotearoa is to make voting as seamlessly easy as possible and to be able to demystify and break down those barriers."

He said their kaupapa was focused on encouraging young people to think about the issues and future they cared about, rather than telling them who to vote for.

"As a non-partisan campaign, we really want to depoliticise the idea of enrolling and voting. This has everything to do about young people and the kind of future they want, no matter their beliefs or the issues they care about."

Reille said cost of living was one issue young people were consistently raising.

But he said the campaign wanted to reach young people before they even got to the question of which party or candidate they might support.

"It's having a real honest conversation about how enrolling and voting brings a sense of community.

"And it's, again, taking away this idea that voting is about an individual, it's about a collective.

World.title: Christopher Luxon defends taking second plane overseas after criticising Hipkins for the same
World.content:
The prime minister is defending the deployment of a second Defence Force plane for his Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) mission, having previously criticised the use of a back-up plane when in opposition.

Christopher Luxon is in Palau for the annual PIF leaders meeting. Both of the RNZAF Boeing 757s have been deployed on the mission, with one staying in Cairns as a back-up.

Luxon said it was a Defence Force decision to take two planes, with 88 people from New Zealand heading to PIF.

"We've taken 14 delegations up here, we've got a lot of people to take home on Sunday as well, and we're taking some home when I go out on Friday as well."

Luxon said connectivity was a big challenge at PIF, and he had talked about the importance of connectivity at the realm leaders' meeting with Tokelau, Niue, and the Cook Islands last week.

"It makes the case for why we need a good, reliable Air Force plane."

An RNZAF Boeing 757, pictured in 2015. RNZ / Alexander Robertson

Air Component Commander Air Commodore Andy Scott also spoke of the PIF meeting's remote location.

"This important meeting is being held in a comparatively remote location where air services and options are limited, and therefore a back-up aircraft has been positioned to assist if required for any reason."

New Zealand is hosting next year's leaders meeting.

Christopher Luxon. RNZ / Nick Monro

In 2023, the Defence Force sent a back-up plane for then-Prime Minister Chris Hipkins' trip to China.

The back-up plane, which was sent in case the first broke down, was left in Manila. It attracted strong criticism from then-opposition leader Luxon, who said it "doesn't seem a good move" in a climate challenge.

Luxon vowed not to use Defence Force planes to travel internationally if he became prime minister - a promise he quickly reneged on.

On Thursday, Hipkins said Luxon was changing his position based on what was convenient for him.

"Well, well, well," he said.

"Hypocrisy knows no ends."

The government is currently purchasing two new Airbus A321XLR planes on a lease-to-buy arrangement, to replace the ageing 757s.

The current planes, which were purchased in 2003, are mostly used for transporting cargo around the Pacific. But they have a recent history of unreliability when it comes to prime ministerial travel.

In 2024, Luxon had to fly commercially to Melbourne after the 757 broke down.

He also left a business delegation in Papua New Guinea after a 757 broke down during a refuel stop en route to Japan.

In 2016, Sir John Key was forced to cancel the first day of a trip to India after the 757 broke down in Townsville, while in 2019 Dame Jacinda Ardern flew commercially back from Melbourne after a breakdown.

World.title: New Zealand pilgrims narrowly escaped Nepal flash flood
World.content:
More than half a dozen New Zealanders narrowly escaped last week's deadly flash floods on the Nepal-China border after their Auckland-based tour operator decided to cross the border a day earlier.

A massive flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through a Himalayan valley last Wednesday, burying villages.

Eight New Zealanders were among a group of 20 pilgrims who crossed through the Gyirong Port immigration centre just a day before it was completely washed away by the deluge.

Dixit Chauhan, owner of Royale Travels, said he made the decision to take the group across the border one day earlier than planned because previous experience on the pilgrimage had taught him the benefits of acclimatisation before attempting the trip.

The gruelling 53-kilometre pilgrimage around Mount Kailash is undertaken at altitudes exceeding 5000 metres, and pilgrims are advised to spend some time in the area before making a gradual ascent in elevation.

Chauhan's decision to cross earlier than planned to spend time at altitude meant the New Zealanders were safely on the other side of the border when the flash flood struck.

Wire agencies have reported that more than 1200 people have been confirmed dead in the disaster, with another 4200 missing, including five New Zealanders.

Pilgrims stand in front of the Gyirong Port Immigration Building and the Nepal-China Friendship Bridge last month, both of which were washed away in a flash flood last week. Amar Prakash

Chauhan was leading the group on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar.

Mount Kailash is believed to be the resting place of Hindu deities Lord Shiva and his wife, Parvati, and is considered one of the holiest places for Hindus, Buddhists and Jains.

The mountain is also viewed as a "cosmic pillar", a central axis connecting the physical world and higher spiritual dimensions.

It is believed that Lord Shiva sits on the mountain top in perpetual meditation, sustaining cosmic equilibrium.

For that reason, pilgrims are prohibited from climbing to the summit.

Nearby Lake Manasarovar is also considered sacred.

Hindu devotees believe completing the pilgrimage and taking a holy dip in Lake Manasarovar can cleanse a lifetime of sins and help attain moksha, or liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

"We were all shocked by what happened," Chauhan said from Darchen in China's autonomous region of Tibet.

The group had completed its physically demanding walk around Mount Kailash.

"We were initially planning to cross the border on Wednesday when the floods happened but, because this was my second time, I told our operators we need to go a day earlier for the group to acclimatize to the conditions," he said.

Chauhan believed the decision to cross a day earlier was guided by Lord Shiva.

"I think it's not me who saved their lives but Lord Shiva," he said. "It's not my decision but the god's."

Chauhan said the group left New Zealand on 20 August and would return at the weekend.

He said the group was at the Gyirong Port immigration building as well as Rasuwa a day before the flash flood struck.

"We left Kathmandu in the morning [on Monday] and arrived [at Rasuwa] at 5pm and spent the night," he said.

"The next morning [on Tuesday] we left for the border, spent a couple of hours at the building and then crossed the border."

Chauhan said the group only learnt of the flash flood sometime later because it had limited connectivity in the mountains.

Amar Prakash (second from left) at Mount Kailash in July. Supplied

Remembering past visits

Auckland resident Amar Prakash has completed the pilgrimage twice.

Prakash arrived in Nepal in July, circled Mount Kailash and crossed the border from Tibet back into Nepal on 2 August.

"We were devastated and shocked because we have been through that border four times now," he said.

"We just couldn't believe the force of the water, the rubble, everything coming down," he said. "[It] is just heartbreaking."

Prakash said the hotel where they had stayed a few weeks earlier had been washed away and the guide who helped the group in China was missing.

"Without her, our pilgrimage wouldn't have been complete," he said.

Prakash said it took a while for him to fully accept that the places he had walked through just a few weeks earlier were completely gone.

Prakash first went to Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar in June last year.

"I was going through a big life event transition in my life, going through divorce. I was at a very low point in life, I guess, and I needed something to sort of help me get back on my feet again," he said.

"It's quite a tough journey to go on because it challenges you emotionally, mentally and physically in all various aspects."

Prakash said the trip genuinely helped him, and he started to see positive changes in his life upon returning to New Zealand.

Inspired, he took some family members, including his parents and a cousin, on the pilgrimage this year.

Prakash said he spent a lot of time in Syabrubesi last year and walked around the bazaars of Rasuwagadhi this year as well.

He said the trip cost him somewhere between $10,000 and $12,000.

Unlike his first trip in 2025, Prakash noticed a significant increase in the number of Tibetan pilgrims this year.

"Because it is the Year of the Fire Horse, one that only happens every 60 years, the number of pilgrims from the China side increased this year," he said.

Pilgrims walk towards Mount Kailash in China's autonomous region of Tibet. Amar Prakash

'We shouldn't let this devastation stop us'

Monark Panchal, another Aucklander, also made the pilgrimage this year.

"It was my long wish to go to Mount Kailash since I was young but somehow it got delayed until this year," Panchal said.

He said the pilgrimage was very tough, and he was asked by his tour operator to train in advance.

"The parikrama (clockwise circumambulation) around Mount Kailash is a tough hike and takes three days to complete," he said.

The walk enables pilgrims to see the mountain from all sides - north, south, east and west.

Panchal said members of the group had to take medicine because of the high altitude.

"Every 20 minutes we had an alarm set just for drinking water," he said.

Panchal said the third day of the trek was the toughest.

There were horses and porters to help pilgrims carry their luggage and provide a ride if anyone needed one, he said.

Panchal said the high altitude, lack of oxygen and tough terrain combined to make the pilgrimage physically demanding.

"When we reached Dolma La Pass, we were more than 5600 metres above sea level," he said.

"If you go up [another] 3000 metres above sea level, you'll be on top of Everest and so you can imagine how tough it must be."

Panchal said the climb down from the Himalayan plateau was equally treacherous, requiring hikers to navigate steep seven-kilometre drop.

He said most pilgrims crossed into Nepal through Gyirong Port because it was the shortest way back.

Panchal said he tried to get in touch with a few people he met during the trip but had been unable to do so.

"We have been trying to reach them," he said. "It's all washed out actually and very sad.

"Since the disaster, I'm really disturbed and a bit stressed thinking about all the people that I know."

Pilgrims travel by horseback on the Mount Kailash and Lake Mansarovar trek. Amar Prakash

Chauhan, Panchal and Prakash said they were keen to make another trip.

Prakash vowed to return to Mount Kailash next year.

"Nepal is a beautiful country and so is the Tibet side. The journey is a big economic industry for both areas," Prakash said.

"The pilgrimage creates a lot of jobs, creates a lot of money flow within the economy and so I think it's important that, where possible, we should still support and go through this journey because we shouldn't let this devastation stop us [from visiting]."

Five New Zealanders remain missing following the deadly flash flood: Dejan Kuzmic, Shweta Mhatre, Mihir Patel, Kinnari Patel and Suhasini Reddy.

Three hundred and thirty foreign nationals have been rescued, according to an update from the Nepal Tourism Board early Tuesday morning.

No New Zealanders have been included in that number.

RNZ understands Mhatre was also part of the Isha Foundation's pilgrimage, and Sadhguru had previously said two New Zealanders were missing from his trekking group.

Meanwhile, Reddy's family has called on rescuers not to stop searching for the 44-year-old after conflicting reports of her status emerged online.

Reddy's brother, Rajeev, and his wife, Lauren, urged people to keep searching for survivors in a Facebook post.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Thursday there had been no change to the status of the five missing New Zealanders.

"Challenges on the ground mean that new, verified information is going to take time to emerge," the spokesperson said, describing the situation on the ground as being "very bleak".

World.title: Hampshire ditches New Zealand all-rounder after fan backlash
World.content:
Hampshire Cricket has cancelled the contract of Kiwi international Scott Kuggeleijn minutes before he was set to take the field after backlash from supporters.

The 34-year-old fast bowler was named in a social media post as part of the 15-man squad to take on Warwickshire in the County Championship match.

The club had not announced the three-Test player's signing on their social channels.

The presence of the New Zealand international bowler in the squad was met with furious resistance from the club's supporters and some staff members, with reaction including comments of "disgraceful" and "shameful" on social media.

"Having reflected and listened to feedback from our staff and supporters, Hampshire Cricket can confirm that Scott Kuggeleijn will not represent the club," a statement from the club read.

"We value the passion of our fanbase and thank everyone who took the time to share their views."

Kuggeleijn had been signed for the final four games of Hampshire's County Championship season as a replacement for South African Delano Potgieter, who was called up for the South Africa A series against Bangladesh last month.

Kuggeleijn faced a rape charge in 2015 and was acquitted in 2017 after the first trial resulted in a hung jury.

The Hamilton-born player made his international debut after his acquittal in an ODI series against Ireland in Dublin in 2017.

There was backlash in New Zealand when Kuggeleijn was initially selected in the squad, with then-coach Gary Stead forced to defend the call-up.

In addition to his three Test matches, Kuggeleijn has played two one-day matches and 18 T20 games for the Black Caps.

He has not played for New Zealand in any format since the second Test against Australia at Hagley Oval, Christchurch in March 2024, which the Aussies won by three wickets.

Prior to his signing for Hampshire, Kuggeleijn was playing for the Kingsmen in a Darwin T20 league.

He is a regular player in first-class cricket for Northern Districts in New Zealand.

World.title: Aviation authorities to review low flyover at Cape Town rugby match
World.content:
A low-altitude flyover by two Airlink passenger jets before a rugby match at Cape Town Stadium is being reviewed by South African aviation authorities after it drew safety concerns, officials say.

The South African Civil Aviation Authority (SACAA) said it had obtained flight data recordings and requested additional information from regional carrier Airlink as part of its assessment. A full report with recommendations will be issued once the review is complete.

"It is therefore critical that we interrogate this past weekend's events … to determine if there were any safety concerns which warrant a review," the agency said in a statement.

Airlink has withdrawn plans for another flyover at the upcoming rugby match in Soweto, according to the SACAA, which regulates aviation safety and security.

The flyover ahead of the Springboks and All Blacks match on August 29 drew huge cheers from an estimated crowd of about 56,000, but it also sparked a debate over safety risks after video footage from spectators inside and around the stadium spread online.

Deandra Peters, 25, a pilot and aviation enthusiast attending her first live rugby match, said the spectacle electrified the crowd in the stadium in a way that was difficult to capture on video.

"You can watch the planes fly over, but you can't recreate what it felt like to be inside a stadium full of Springbok supporters absolutely losing their minds," she told The Associated Press.

"The atmosphere was electric — the noise, the pride, the emotion. It was a very uniquely South African moment."

Airlink on Wednesday said the manoeuvrer had been carefully planned and rehearsed and that safety was "the first consideration at every stage of the process." It said each aircraft had three senior captains aboard, with more than 75,000 combined flight hours across the crews.

Earlier this week, Airlink had provided the data from the aeroplanes' black boxes to the civil aviation authority for review.

The SACAA said it would examine flight data to determine whether any safety concerns warranted a review.

The airline acknowledged the enthusiasm generated by the spectacle while also recognising what it described as the "valid questions and concerns" that followed.

"We never intended to become the news or upstage rugby's greatest rivalry," Airlink chief executive de Villiers Engelbrecht said in a statement.

The regulator said the airline had made applications for three flyovers. The most recent one in Cape Town was the second, while the first flyover took place in Johannesburg on August 22. Both were approved in line with the requirements for special air events.

Airlink has withdrawn its application for a flyover scheduled for September 1, over Johannesburg's Soccer City Stadium. The airline said forecast weather conditions were unfavourable for a safe formation flyby. SACAA confirmed that the application had been withdrawn.

South African rugby has a long tradition of stadium flybys at major matches, dating back to the 1995 Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg, when a Boeing 747 swept over Ellis Park before the Springboks faced the All Blacks.

Last Saturday's flyby was unusually low and dramatic, drawing international attention, with some aviation experts later questioning whether the aircraft had left too little margin for error.

World.title: Prime-time era Magbegor leads Opals' World Cup charge
World.content:
The Opals have produced a consistent pipeline of global superstars throughout their silverware-packed history, an impressive feat in one of the world's most competitive sports.

In the 2026 incarnation of the Opals, Ezi Magbegor, 27, carries that tag.

After bursting onto the international stage as a highly promising 18-year-old, she is now a defensive linchpin, a leader, and the type of player whose influence will likely dictate how far the Opals go at the Women's Basketball World Cup.

And she is in her prime-time era.

Magbegor was part of the team that won bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

Throwing a fit

Magbegor entered this WNBA season as a hot commodity — becoming the equal highest paid Australian player in the league, and one of the richest female Australian athletes overall.

But an Achilles injury, then broken nose, wiped her out for most of the season, delivering a harsh reality check for the Seattle Storm forward-centre.

Magbegor has been wearing a mask for the Seattle Storm, since returning from a broken nose. (Getty Images: Olivia Vanni)

"I've been so blessed to not have many injuries at all in my first seven years of my W season," she told ABC Sport.

"You just realise injuries are a part of sport and it's about how you reset your mind and bounce back and prepare for the next thing.

"And so, yes, I was injured, but I just used it as a great opportunity to work on my body and put myself in the best position to be ready."

It also gave her a chance to spend some time on her 'tunnel fits', aka the casual outfits that players wear when arriving at arenas, which have become a core part of the WNBA.

"This year I really wanted to lean into my Nigerian culture and heritage, and my mum's been begging me to wear traditional clothing," she said.

"My favourite was definitely my traditional attire. My parents had bought the material from Nigeria and then one of our friends had sewn it together in Melbourne.

Loading Instagram content

"I worry about being too dressed up sometimes, but my mum's like, yeah, it's not enough, nothing's too dressed up. So, it was really fun to be able to share that with her."

She traded high fashion for a protective face mask when she returned to the court for the Storm in late July, adding to her already intimidating aura as one of the league's best shot blockers.

And while her domestic season has been stunted, she is coming back to full fitness and form just in time for the World Cup, tipping-off in Berlin this weekend.

Opals going big

Magbegor was part of the team that won World Cup silver in 2018, bronze at home in Sydney in 2022, and bronze at the Paris 2024 Olympics.

Magbegor is known as an elite rim defender and shot blocker. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

There has been substantial turnover since Paris with the emotional core of the team including Tess Madgen, Lauren Jackson, Cayla George, and Marianna Tolo, all missing.

And with captain and point guard Sami Whitcomb belatedly ruled out of this World Cup, the side's star power now largely shines around Magbegor and Alanna Smith.

"It's expected for me to pass on the cultural values and expectations onto the next group coming up," Magbegor said.

"But for me it's just about leading by example, touching base with my teammates, making sure that I'm being the best professional, best teammate, best person I can be come tournament play, and in the lead up as well.

"I've been in the Opals team and squad for a while now and I want to have an impact for the team in any way I can, whether that's on the floor, off the floor.

"But definitely looking to play my best basketball for the group and hopefully come away with the medal."

Smith, who was last year named WNBA defensive player of the year, had her own injury interrupted start to the season.

Alongside Magbegor, Dallas Wings player Alanna Smith is regarded as one of the Opals' best players. (Getty Images: Stacy Revere)

Coach Sandy Brondello is confident Magbegor and Smith are recovered and ready to lead Australia's charge in Berlin.

"They can hold themselves with any of the best post players in the world here. And that's what we're going to need from them without putting pressure," Brondello told ABC Sport.

"I've coached [Ezi] since she was 18. And this is her time, back healthy.

"The best is to come to her, but I'm just excited for her to get out, her athleticism, her rim protection. But now she's a three-level scorer, so that's a great asset.

"And Alanna was our best player in Paris, most consistent player over the whole tournament.

"And it's good to see her getting some rhythm now and getting that confidence back because we need them. We have to lean into them. They're our two best bigs."

Chasing the elusive gold

The Opals enter the World Cup ranked third. The Olympic bronze was followed by a breakthrough Asia Cup win last year, without any WNBA players, and they had a limited preparation for this tournament.

Coach Sandy Brondello says the team's culture is key to its continued success over many years. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

"The results that we've had, it shows that the continuity that we've developed over many years, not just one year, is showing because our chemistry is strong, our culture is strong," Brondello said.

"Everyone's accepting their roles and coming in and playing at a high level. And that's the beauty of Australian teams that we have."

Culture is always the constant with the Opals and what they attribute their sustained performance over decades to.

"It really just comes down our sisterhood and how gritty and tough we are and how we play together and we'll play whatever role to help us to have great success," Brondello said.

"These players, they've become family.

"Playing at the highest level just means everyone has to buy into the values for the success of the program. And there's no one player bigger than the program."

While the Opals are perennial podium finishers at major tournaments, gold has eluded them since their one and only world title in 2006.

Players from the 2006 World Champion Opals met with the current squad during a series in Melbourne in July. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

"It's just something that comes with being an Opal, that legacy piece and recognising and acknowledging who put us in this position and who started that legacy," Magbegor said.

"Medals is quite synonymous with Opals, and we've won in the past and want to continue to win."

As had been the case for decades, the world number one USA is a seemingly immovable object from the top step of the podium, although was pushed all the way by France in the gold medal match at the Paris Olympics.

"[The USA are] the best of the best and they're great, but they've got the best talent," Brondello said.

"But we've got a talented group, we've built some more chemistry over the years, and that's what we have to lean into."

Growing the game

Half the Opals squad plays in the WNBA, the rest are in the local WNBL, and both leagues have experienced significant changes in the past year.

Zitina Aokuso is one of the local WNBL players in this World Cup squad. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

After drawn out, often bitter negotiations, the WNBA and players' association finally signed a new collective bargaining agreement which saw player salaries skyrocket.

Magbegor went from earning $US186,000 ($260,000) a year to $US1.25 million, a figure matched by Smith at the Dallas Wings, and significantly larger than the base salaries of other leading Australian female athletes in team sports, including the top Matildas and cricketers.

"I think that's just a testament to people that came before us and really pushing for the growth of women's basketball in particular, but just women's sports in general," Magbegor said.

"And I think now is a greater time than ever to push forward, invest in women's sports and just advocate for ourselves, but each other as well."

The WNBL has been making its own moves on a much smaller scale, including a new ownership group taking over last year.

And after starting her career there, Magbegor hopes it too can thrive.

"That's what is probably lacking right now, exposure, and knowing that it's going to pay off in the long run," she said.

"People need to see the product and see the game and realise that women's basketball, basketball is incredible.

"We have great athletes, especially coming up, and I think it's just a matter of investing, a matter of showing up and a matter of supporting."

World.title: More Aussies tumble as de Minaur finally concludes first round match
World.content:
Taylah Preston's US Open adventure has ended abruptly in the second round.

The first Australian through to round two was the first to exit following a 6-1, 6-1 loss to big-hitting American Taylor Townsend.

The 20-year-old wildcard was eliminated in just 48 minutes.

Preston was one of five Australians scheduled for day-four action at Flushing Meadows.

Australian women's number one Daria Kasatkina was also removed from the draw, but not before offering more considerable resistance against Spaniard Paula Badosa.

The pair resumed their stop-start affair that was halted on Tuesday morning (AEST) in sensational fashion.

After first being forced off court because of rain early in the second set while trailing Badosa 6-1, 1-2, Kasatkina was delighted when officials called it a night immediately after she saved a third match point.

Badosa was furious and had to return 15 hours later trying to serve out the contest at 5-4 and deuce in the second set.

Kasatkina saved her first two match points in an epic 22-point game serving at 3-5 in the second set, before fighting off another six more.

Kasatkina also conjured two break point chances to level up at 5-5 before Badosa, a one-time world number two, finally closed out the contest to book a second-round date with 2023 champion Coco Gauff.

Maya Joint is scheduled to take on ninth seed Elina Svitolina this morning, hoping to reach the third round in New York for a third straight year.

Meanwhile Kim Birrell is up against Russian Ekaterina Alexandrova believing she can also topple the Russian 18th seed after taking down world number five and 2024 US Open finalist Jessica Pegula at the French Open.

De Minaur through after delay

New York's lousy weather dealt Alex de Minaur's US Open title hopes another setback with the top-ranked Australian's first-round clash delayed further by rain.

Former champion Daniil Medvedev and American home hope Alex Michelsen were already safely through to round three before de Minaur even made it on court for his tournament opener.

When he finally opened his campaign on day four, de Minaur looked intent on making up for lost time, racing to a 6-2, 4-2 lead over Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri in just 49 minutes.

Then the heavens opened again, forcing de Minaur scampering back to the locker room.

He eventually went on to win 6-2, 6-2, 6-4.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Record warm winter brings disappointing end to snow season
World.content:
Australian ski resorts are winding up operations early in 2026 after the warmest winter on record.

Along with mild temperatures, winter also brought frequent rain to the high country, preventing a seasonal snowpack from establishing across lower alpine elevations.

This year also marks three very lean years in the past four, continuing the long-term decline in snowfall across the Australian Alps, which is proving to be one of the most tangible signs of our warming climate.

Ski fields above freezing most of winter

This year's snow season was a challenge from the start.

June was unseasonably warm and wet, and when it was not raining, it was mostly too warm for snowmaking at ski resorts.

Heavy rain in late August caused a major melting event and a swelling of the Perisher Creek. (Supplied: SMSkier)

A remarkable statistic for early winter was the Perisher Valley weather station measured 301 millimetres of precipitation from June 1 to July 2, of which only 25mm fell at a temperature below 0 degrees Celsius.

A modest dump of snow finally arrived in July, but the month was generally mild and occasionally rainy; although a snow base developed on higher slopes, a full cover across lower alpine regions never formed.

Last month brought no relief, with further rain and above-average temperatures — during the final days of the month, alpine maximums even climbed above 10C, including a new all-time winter record of 14.4C at Perisher on Saturday, August 29.

Three warmer-than-normal months meant the average winter temperatures across the high country were easily the highest on record, and by a fair margin.

The longest-running BOM station in the Australian alpine region is Cabramurra, where this winter's mean of 4.0C was well above the long-term average of 1.8C and nearly half a degree above the previous record in 2023.

Across the border, the Mount Buller station has been operational since 1985 and also exceeded the previous record by nearly half a degree, coming in at 1.9C versus a long-term average of 0.1C.

Snow depth in 2026 is historically low

Before: Pictures of Frostbite Kiosk at Thredbo on August 30, 2025, versus August 30, 2026. . . After: (Supplied) . . Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Before and after images SLIDE Pictures of Frostbite Kiosk at Thredbo on August 30, 2025, versus August 30, 2026. / (Supplied)

In a typical year, snow accumulates through winter and peaks in August or early September.

However, this year, discounting the improbable arrival of a major polar storm this spring, snow peaked two weeks earlier than average and was at historically low levels, which heavily restricted the amount of open terrain for skiing.

The table below shows peak snow depth in 2026 compared to average; however, there are a few caveats when analysing snow data in Australia*.

What is evident this season is that, for higher elevations, it was the worst season for natural snow since 2006, while for lower regions it was the worst on record.

Despite the setbacks, CEO of Snow Resorts Australia Josh Elliott was confident the industry had the infrastructure to mitigate poor seasons.

"While conditions and available terrain have differed between resorts, continued investment in snowmaking and snow management has meant that skiing, snowboarding and snowplay have been available in NSW, Victoria and the ACT since the June long weekend," he said.

Winter finished with almost no snow cover on many alpine slopes and an early end to the season for most of the terrain. (Supplied: Perisher)

But even extensive snow curation eventually lost out to the elements, and two of the lower resorts, Mount Selwyn and Mount Baw Baw, already shut down operations for the season a fortnight ago.

Mount Hotham is also due for a premature finish this Sunday, and with more heavy rain ahead this weekend, it is hard to see the other major resorts lasting until the traditional closing weekend in early October.

The downhill slide continues

Loading...

In isolation, a winter without much snow is nothing new in Australia — 1973 and 1982 were both very lean years — but it is the sharp downward trend over recent decades that is concerning.

And unsurprisingly, the marginal lower alpine areas are most vulnerable to a warming climate, since more winter precipitation is now falling as rain, and above-freezing temperatures are melting the snow cover between storms.

Between 1955 and 2000, the peak annual snow depth at Three-Mile Dam, at an elevation of 1,460 metres, averaged 55 centimetres, but during the past 25 years that figure has fallen to 34cm, a reduction of 38 per cent.

A few hundred metres higher, Mount Buller's drop during the corresponding period is 21 per cent, from 117cm to 93cm, while for Spencers Creek at 1,830m, the decline is 13 per cent from 205cm to 178cm.

In other words, the winter snowline is clearly rising, and projections from several studies this century show that by 2050, maximum snow depth at major resorts, relative to the late 20th century, may decline by more than 50 per cent even under a low emissions scenario.

However, Mr Elliott said Australian resorts were leveraging against future climates.

"While those projections may be relevant to understanding changes in the natural alpine environment, they are not forecasts of future skiable terrain, resort operating periods or the visitor experience," he said.

"Snowmaking has been a core component of the Australian snow experience for more than 35 years. New technology, including All-Weather Snowmaking Systems, now allows resorts with these systems to produce snow in ambient temperatures of up to +20C."

*Victorian statistics are sufficiently robust with daily natural snow depth readings taken by resorts; however, Mount Hotham did not report during the COVID-19 winters of 2020 and 2021. In NSW, Perisher and Thredbo quote snow depth data from Snowy Hydro at Spencers Creek, normally measured weekly or fortnightly. Snowy Hydro also takes readings at Deep Creek and Three-Mile Dam, however these datasets suffer from inconsistent measurement intervals, with intervals between readings of up to three weeks.

World.title: Tiger Woods loses driving licence for five years after plea deal
World.content:
Golfing champion Tiger Woods has pleaded no contest to a reckless driving charge following a rollover crash in March near his home in Florida where he initially was accused of driving under the influence.

Woods appeared in a courtroom in Martin County where he agreed to the reduced charge.

A judge ordered that his drivers licence be suspended for five years.

Woods, 50, said little during the hearing and beforehand sat at the defence table, looking back at the courtroom gallery.

He arrived at the courthouse with his girlfriend, Vanessa Trump, President Donald Trump's former daughter-in-law.

She sat behind him during the hearing. Woods left the courthouse without addressing reporters.

Tiger Woods stands by his overturned vehicle following a crash in Florida. (AP: Jason Oteri)

He also pleaded no contest to refusing to submit to testing and was fined court costs, according to court documents.

A no-contest plea is not an admission of guilt, but means the accused will offer no defence.

The plea is treated as a conviction in the criminal justice system.

Woods was arrested after his SUV clipped a truck and rolled over on its side on a beachside residential road on Jupiter Island.

A sheriff's report said deputies found two pain pills in his pocket and he showed signs of impairment. He did a breathalyser test, which came out negative, but refused to take a urine test.

He had pleaded not guilty to the original DUI charge.

Neither Woods nor the person in the other vehicle were injured in the crash, according to officials.

But his Land Rover caused $US5,000 ($7,000) in damage to the truck, according to a police report. Woods had told a deputy that he was looking down at his phone and changing the radio station when he hit the truck.

Woods is among the most influential figures in golf, but his career has been derailed by multiple back and knee surgeries, car crashes and dependence on pain medication.

Woods has been involved in four crashes over the years.

He took a leave from the golf tour after the 2009 crash and again after the latest crash and has yet to return to tournament play.

He left the United States to seek treatment at an inpatient treatment facility, according to court records.

Woods made his first public appearance since returning from treatment on June 23 when he introduced the PGA Tour's plans to revamp its schedule for 2028.

Woods remained as chairman of the tour's Future Competition Committee after his arrest. He did not take questions during that appearance.

AP

World.title: Ciraldo calls out NRL over delayed rule-change communication
World.content:
Cameron Ciraldo wants rule changes for 2027 to be communicated to clubs well in advance of the season's start date as Canterbury prepares to become the latest crash-test dummies in trials for the NRL's kick-off experiment.

With the Bulldogs and Thursday's opponents Brisbane both out of finals contention, the NRL has again opted to stress-test changes to the kick-off rules, where teams conceding a try can opt to kick or receive from the restart.

The concept was widely panned by players in Melbourne's win over Brisbane, and Ciraldo claimed on Wednesday he only learned his team would be guinea pigs in their regular-season game via email.

Beach sprinting was just the start of Damien Cook's NRL story It's been a long time since Damien Cook was known merely as a beach sprint champion, but ahead of the champion hooker's final NRL game, all the old stories are being told one last time.

Ciraldo would have a right to feel aggrieved by the NRL's constant tinkering, given his side were firmly entrenched in the top four last year.

The Dogs slipped back in the pack when the NRL changed the six-again threshold from the 40-metre line to the 20-metre mark weeks out from the season starting.

Canterbury has righted the ship since officials have eased off on calling six-agains.

And while Ciraldo won't solely attribute his club's early-season form slump to the changes, he would prefer clearer communication so clubs can plan their conditioning and roster management accordingly.

"If you look at our form at the start of the year you can blame that, but I think there's a lot of factors that went into our results at the start of the year," Ciraldo said.

"We'll look to address those over the next few weeks.

The Bulldogs have corrected their form of late after referees eased off on the six-again calls. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

"As the rules came back to what they were last year, we sort of found our rhythm a little bit more, and were able to get back to our style of footy.

"I think it coincides with a number of other things as well.

"I think everyone would like to know what the rule changes are to start the pre-season and not find out about them during the trial period."

Ciraldo said Canterbury had little time to put the trialled kick-off interpretations into practice this week.

"I don't check my emails that often, so someone had to tell me," Ciraldo said.

Canterbury's clash with Brisbane will be the last for Bronson Xerri (Melbourne) and Josh Curran (Perth) before they move on to new clubs in 2027.

Ciraldo paid tribute to the pair for being key parts of the Dogs' revival, and confirmed Sean O'Sullivan had agreed to a contract at Belmore for 2027, despite interest from the Super League.

AAP

World.title: AFL boss backflips by scrapping controversial 'Opening Round' experiment
World.content:
The AFL has scrapped the Opening Round experiment after three seasons and will return to a traditional nine-game first week.

League boss Andrew Dillon today confirmed the demise of the much-criticised concept that featured four games played exclusively in Queensland and New South Wales between only a selection of eight clubs.

Designed to build a foothold in rugby league heartland, it instead drew criticism given the fixturing created a staggered start and early-season byes.

Defending it in March, Dillon said Opening Round was "key" to growing the sport north of Victoria, citing record attendances and membership rises.

Australia and England will play a one-off Test next year at the MCG to celebrate 150 years of Test cricket, pushing the AFL season back. (Getty Images: Robbie Stephenson/PA Images)

"What we've found in the last couple of years is that focus on NSW and Queensland is helping to grow awareness in NSW and Queensland and at the same time it hasn't taken away from our round one," Dillon said at the time.

But, with the season to begin a week later next year due to the MCG hosting the 150th anniversary cricket Test between Australia and England, it has been taken out with the trash.

"We have been working through alternative options to deliver the start of the AFL season," Dillon said in a statement.

"After important feedback from fans and stakeholders, and consultation with clubs and broadcasters, round one will see the return of a traditional nine-game round played across the country."

The first round will be played from Wednesday or Thursday, March 17 or 18, just days after the final day of the historic Ashes Test.

The 24-round home-and-away season will conclude on Sunday, August 30, with the five-week finals series beginning with two wildcard finals in the first week of September.

The grand final will be held on Saturday, October 2 and Gather Round in South Australia is locked in for April 8-11.

AAP

Tech.title: Uber beats Waymo as first to launch robotaxis in London
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Uber beat out Waymo in launching a commercial robotaxi service in London, the city’s first. The vehicles use autonomous driving tech developed by Wayve, a UK-based startup, and will initially feature safety drivers behind the wheel.

The launch is a milestone for Uber, which has been plotting a UK launch with Wayve for several years. In beating Waymo to the punch, it allows Uber to set the standard for the robotaxi experience for thousands of Londoners. It’s also an early test of whether there’s appetite for driverless ridehailing beyond the US and China, where most of the world’s robotaxis are currently clustered. (There’s a smattering in the Middle East, too.)

London-based Uber customers who want to try out these new robot-controlled cars can indicate their preference in the app’s settings. When booking a ride through UberX, Uber Comfort, or Uber Electric, riders may be paired with a Wayve-developed autonomous vehicle, but it’s not a guarantee. Wayve is using Ford Mustang Mach-Es for its fleet, followed by the Nissan Leaf in the future.

Safety drivers will monitor the driving from the front seat, though Uber says they won’t control the driving and will gradually be phased out in favor of fully driverless vehicles. Safety drivers are licensed by Transport for London, the city’s transit authority.

Uber says there will be no geofence — the virtual boundary within which robotaxis are programed to operate — because Wayve’s AV2.0 system is designed to move “beyond the constraints of traditional AV systems.” Wayve describes AV2.0 thusly:

The traditional AV1.0 approach relies on hand-engineered stacks, HD maps and a rule-based approach – this limits scalability and the ability to rapidly generalize to new environments or complex scenarios. Wayve’s AV2.0 takes a different path – a single, learned AI driver trained to understand the world, anticipate risk, and adapt to new environments.

The robotaxis will be maintained and serviced by Uber in partnership with UK fleet operator Otto Car. Wayve will stay in charge of the autonomous driving system.

Wayve, which was founded in 2017 by a pair of machine learning PhD students from the University of Cambridge, says its autonomous driving system can learn on the go, adapting to new roads, weather, or driving scenarios much like a human driver. The vehicles use cameras and radar as part of their perception system — but notably do not use lidar, the laser sensor that Waymo and many other robotaxi operators rely on. This puts Wayve in a similar camp as Tesla, which also doesn’t use lidar for its robotaxis.

Still, Wayve claims its system is hardware agnostic, thanks to a software stack that can run on whatever sensors and chips an automaker uses for its vehicles. While additional sensors like lidar can theoretically be integrated if a car manufacturer prefers them, Wayve’s AV2.0 is built to operate autonomously without HD maps or expensive sensors, the company says. In addition to Uber, Wayve is also working with Stellantis on hands-free driving tech. And earlier this year, the startup raised $1.2 billion from Uber, Nvidia, and Stellantis, as well as Nissan and Mercedes-Benz, according to TechCrunch.

Waymo has said it will launch its robotaxis in London before the end of the year. In addition, Lyft is working with China’s Baidu on its own robotaxi service in the city, starting with the neighborhood of Brent.

Uber has been lobbying for a hybrid network made up of human drivers and robotaxis, which clashes with Waymo’s vision of a driver-free, rider-only system. Waymo and Uber still work together in several cities, including Austin and Atlanta, but the companies have increasingly found themselves on opposite sides of the debate — prompting rumors of an imminent breakup. Meanwhile, Uber has made a big to-do about linking up with a variety of AV partners, including Zoox, Avride, Nuro, Motional, Waabi, and of course, Wayve. The company has said it plans on spending upwards of $10 billion to build out its robotaxi business over time.

Tech.title: Google says its new Gemini 3.8 Flash model ‘works harder’ but might cost more
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google launched Gemini 3.8 Flash, arriving just a few weeks after its predecessor. The company claims the new model “works harder” than Gemini 3.7 Flash by performing more reasoning steps on complex tasks and “calling tools iteratively.” It has the same introductory pricing as 3.7 Flash, $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, but could still end up costing users more. Google warns that “the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels.” Developers can keep using Gemini 3.7 Flash if they want to minimize token usage.

Gemini 3.8 Flash’s launch was followed by some early impressions online. Artificial Analysis highlighted the model’s pricing, saying Gemini 3.8 Flash is “the cheapest we’ve measured at this level of intelligence. This is up ~40% from Gemini 3.7 Flash despite unchanged per-token pricing, driven by a 30% increase in output tokens per task and more turns on agentic evaluations.”

Aigora.ai CEO John Ennis compared Gemini 3.8 Flash to Anthropic’s models, saying it offers “Opus 5 coding quality but at a fraction of the cost and super fast,” adding, “This is going to be so awesome for things like making remotion videos.”

Google says Gemini 3.8 Flash offers “significant improvements” for software engineering and autonomous AI agents. It outperforms its predecessor and other frontier models on the DeepSWE v1.1 software engineering benchmark, including Anthropic’s Fable 5, which got an upgrade earlier this week that also promises stronger performance at a lower price, by cutting the price to use cached data.

Google’s new model also outperformed its competitors on the Vals Finance Agent V2 benchmark and Harvey’s Legal Agent benchmark. However, the new model also “ships with safeguards against misuse in the domains of Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) and cyber offense.”

Google also released Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber alongside its new Fairwind Program, which is limited to governments and “trusted partners.” The program, whose 650 members include CrowdStrike and the Center for Internet Security, offers access to 3.8 Flash Cyber and Google’s CodeMender agent, which Google says can help “autonomously find and fix vulnerabilities, protecting critical infrastructure, public services, and national security.” Gemini 3.8 Flash is available now for consumers with a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription, as well as developers and enterprise users.

Tech.title: Here are some of REI’s best Labor Day sale deals
Tech.content:
In case you weren’t aware, REI members can take an extra 20 percent off a single outlet item with the coupon code LABORDAY26 . A lifetime membership is only $30 , and there are a number of items available where the discount covers that upfront cost.

If you’re open to suggestions on what to check out during the sale, I’d like to call particular attention to Darn Tough socks while they’re 25 percent off.
